The widespread adoption of autonomous vehicles (AVs) is anticipated to transform automotive networks into a vast edge computing infrastructure, where numerous AVs and roadside units (RSUs) act as computational nodes. This potential is significant because leveraging distributed edge computing can enhance safety and efficiency through data sharing and collaborative processing. However, the high data volume and intensive processing demands of edge cognition tasks often result in excessive data transmission and redundant computations, which can compromise data privacy. To address these challenges, this paper introduces a novel Collaborative Structure (CS) designed for privacy-preserving edge cognition within automotive networks. The CS comprises two main components: a data sharing module and a computation module. The data sharing module enables vehicles to exchange information with RSUs and other vehicles while maintaining privacy. Subsequently, the computation module facilitates collaborative processing by multiple vehicles and RSUs on shared data to improve cognition performance. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed CS significantly reduces both data transmission and computational complexity compared to existing methods. Furthermore, the collaboration among vehicles and RSUs enhances overall cognition performance. This study offers a new perspective for developing practical edge computing systems in automotive networks. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2020/Privacy-Preserving-Edge-Cognition. Significance surfaces serve as visual tools for identifying the most relevant feature values within predictive models. While numerous methods exist for linear and tree-based classifiers, as well as for regression and density estimation, many are restricted to low-dimensional contexts. This paper introduces the Euler Significance Surface (EulerSig), a novel approach capable of projecting the significance of any smooth multivariate function $f(\mathbf{x})$ onto an arbitrary submanifold of any dimension. The method is versatile, accommodating a broad spectrum of multivariate functions, including predictive models, density estimates, and even non-statistical functions like artistic color maps. Significance surfaces can reveal the importance of multivariate features, complementing univariate techniques by highlighting interactions and dependencies. Furthermore, they offer visualization capabilities beyond standard plots, such as 3D renderings, color-coded images, and animated sequences. The core of EulerSig is the integral of the model's Hessian along a path, which quantifies the curvature of the model around a specific location. This approach draws inspiration from the mean curvature flow, a concept from differential geometry. We demonstrate the method's effectiveness through examples involving multivariate density estimation and machine learning classifiers. This study integrates Allee effects into a Holling type-II predator-prey model, analyzing three scenarios: weak Allee effects in both species with logistic self-limited growth (yielding three equilibria and two dynamical regimes), strong Allee effects in both species (yielding five equilibria and three dynamical regimes), and a strong Allee effect in the prey with the predator exhibiting linear self-limited growth (yielding four equilibria and two dynamical regimes). For each scenario, the weak or strong mutualistic Allee effect is examined through the lens of the critical threshold value $\theta_c$ and its associated stability properties. The analysis reveals that the Allee effect can be weak, strong, or non-existent depending on $\theta$, with the transition between these states occurring at $\theta_c$. Furthermore, the stability of the Allee effect is determined by the eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix evaluated at $\theta_c$. Finally, numerical simulations are employed to illustrate the theoretical findings. The results demonstrate that the Allee effect exerts a significant influence on the dynamics of the Holling type-II system, a factor that must be carefully considered when applying this model to real-world biological systems. This underscores the critical role of the Allee effect in the coexistence of predator and prey populations. Additionally, the paper offers a comprehensive review of the Allee effect, its various types, and its relevance to ecological systems. The study concludes by suggesting several avenues for future research. This study investigates the impact of off-shell effects in $t$-channel single-top production and the associated influence of these off-shell contributions on the top quark mass extraction from $t\bar{t}+j$ events. To address off-shellness, we employ an effective field theory (EFT) framework, utilizing Wilson coefficients to adjust various off-shell sources within this specific event topology. Our analysis demonstrates that incorporating off-shell effects enhances the sensitivity of the extracted mass value, with EFT Wilson coefficients playing a crucial role in this process. Furthermore, we examine how these coefficients affect the statistical uncertainty of the mass determination. Finally, we provide projections for the potential precision of the top quark mass measurement achievable with the High-Luminosity LHC. These findings are based on an analysis of simulated data for $t\bar{t}+j$ events, where the off-shell treatment is derived from the ATLAS $t\bar{t}$ simulation. Additionally, we explore the potential for improving this precision by including $t\bar{t}+$ heavy jets events. This work serves as a proof of concept for the proposed EFT approach to modeling off-shell effects in $t$-channel single-top production. Such an approach is essential for performing precise measurements of the top quark mass using $t\bar{t}$ data. The developed methodology will be utilized in our upcoming top quark mass extraction studies. The results of those investigations will be presented in a forthcoming paper. This manuscript serves as a proof of concept for the Wilson coefficients, which will be employed in our future mass extraction analyses. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 provides an overview of the event selection criteria and the analysis framework. Section 3 details the construction of the off-shell Wilson coefficients. Section 4 presents the results of the analysis. Finally, Section 5 offers a discussion of the findings. The human face serves as a primary identifier, making it a frequent target for spoofing attacks. To address this, face countermeasures are employed to distinguish between live faces and spoofing attempts. This study evaluates the efficacy of Vision Transformers (ViTs) compared to Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) in detecting deepfake attacks. Our findings indicate that CNNs achieve superior performance in ViT-dependent countermeasures, suggesting that ViTs are less effective in zero-shot scenarios. Furthermore, ViTs show reduced performance in non-adaptive countermeasures relative to CNNs, highlighting the need for further research to enhance their efficiency in these areas. Additionally, we introduce a novel deepfake dataset, FFD, which is more challenging than existing alternatives. The FFD dataset comprises 1,000,000 frames featuring 10,000 source images across 10 sources, 10 targets, and 10 back-ends, covering 10 attacks generated using Face2Face and Roop. It further incorporates 10,000 FFD images per source and target to simulate diverse age, gender, and ethnicity variations. We conducted extensive experiments on FFD and two established datasets, reporting state-of-the-art results for CNN-based methods. Additionally, we explored the potential of Vision Transformers in this domain, with results available at https://github.com/AbdulrahmanAlshammari/FFD. The dataset can be accessed at https://github.com/AbdulrahmanAlshammari/FFD/tree/master/FFD. Source code is hosted at https://github.com/AbdulrahmanAlshammari/FFD/tree/master/FFD_Code. The paper is accessible at https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.00001. We hope the FFD dataset will advance research in face countermeasure and deepfake detection. His research focuses on face recognition, anti-spoofing, and deepfake detection. This paper introduces a reinforcement learning framework designed to train a vehicle controller for a driving simulator. The simulator provides the controller with a bird's-eye view of the environment, including the vehicle itself and all other agents. The controller's objective is to navigate the vehicle to a designated destination while adhering to traffic rules and avoiding collisions with other agents. We developed a novel reward function that incorporates a distance-based penalty to prevent the vehicle from entering restricted zones, such as highways and pedestrian crossings. Additionally, the simulator tracks the vehicle's path and compares it against real-world road maps to evaluate adherence to traffic regulations. Our approach utilizes the Deep Q-Network (DQN) algorithm, which employs double Q-learning to mitigate overestimation of state values and applies experience replay to enhance training stability. We conducted extensive experiments to assess the controller's performance, measuring its ability to reach destinations, comply with traffic laws, and avoid crashes. The results indicate that the trained controller successfully reaches the target in approximately 80% of scenarios, while the remaining 20% involve violations of traffic rules or collisions. Furthermore, the simulator was developed using the Unity engine, leveraging its extensive asset library and physics capabilities. We believe this system offers a valuable foundation for future research into autonomous driving using reinforcement learning. To foster further advancement, we have made the code and trained models publicly available. We hope this work inspires additional research in autonomous driving and contributes to the development of safer and more efficient self-driving technologies. This paper introduces a novel asynchronous parallel evolutionary algorithm designed to mitigate evaluation time bias. Unlike traditional approaches, this method prioritizes fitness function evaluations based on the algorithm's operational frequency rather than individual evaluation time. By employing a straightforward yet effective parent selection mechanism, the approach ensures that more mature individuals are chosen for offspring generation. The proposed frequency-centered parent selection is integrated into the Asynchronous Multi-Objective Breeder Algorithm, resulting in the Asynchronous Multi-Objective Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm (AMOSA). Extensive experiments across diverse benchmark functions demonstrate that AMOSA significantly outperforms the current state-of-the-art Asynchronous Multi-Objective Non-Dominated Sorting Evolutionary Algorithm. Furthermore, the method is versatile and can be readily incorporated into other asynchronous parallel evolutionary algorithms to reduce evaluation time bias. The comprehensive experimental results are available at https://github.com/leopoldo-g/AMOSA. Finally, the authors conclude by identifying promising directions for future research. Keywords: Asynchronous Parallel Evolutionary Algorithms, Multi-Objective Optimization, Evaluation Time Bias.

The Adaptive Optics Near-Infrared Exoplanet Direct Imaging and Spectroscopy (Keck Adaptive Optics Exoplanet Direct Imaging and Spectroscopy, or KAEDIS) instrument at the W. M. Keck Observatory has confirmed the planetary companion OGLE-2017-BLG-1434b, which was originally identified via microlensing. The host star, OGLE-2017-BLG-1434L, is a low-mass star ($0.11 \pm 0.01 M_{\odot}$) located approximately $1.8 \pm 0.2$ kpc from the Sun, orbiting a more massive primary star ($0.41 \pm 0.02 M_{\odot}$) with a binary separation of $0.6 \pm 0.1$ AU. By employing the Floquet-Suslin representation, we demonstrate that the Floquet operator admits an expansion with an explicit error term at every order, valid for sufficiently high rates. Furthermore, we establish that the rates of these expansions are independent of the initial state. These findings are achieved through the application of Fourier series expansions, series reordering techniques, and Floquet theory. As a practical application, we derive an expansion for the Floquet pure dephasing map applicable to any two energy levels, which is relevant for analyzing dynamical decoupling protocols. Additionally, we prove that the rates of this expansion are also state-independent. Our results are supported by numerical simulations. Finally, we outline several promising directions for future research. Notably, we conjecture that the derived expansions remain valid even at finite rates, a hypothesis that could be tested experimentally. This offers a potential pathway to experimentally validate the high-rate expansion of time-regular quantum Markovian dynamics without relying on numerical simulations. Furthermore, our methodology may be adaptable to other areas of quantum physics, such as the study of time-regular many-body systems. Specifically, we propose that these techniques could facilitate the analysis of Floquet topological insulators and the design of Floquet superconductors. In these contexts, the ability to determine error bounds for high-rate expansions is essential for ensuring the accuracy of theoretical predictions. Finally, we suggest that these findings could be experimentally verified using trapped ions, which offer high control precision and the capability to implement arbitrary quantum operations. This would enable the direct observation of Floquet dynamics and the testing of expansion validity without the need for quantum state tomography. To facilitate such experimental tests, we have made our code publicly available. We conducted a 12.27 GHz Very Large Array (VLA) survey of the high-mass star-forming region G176.51+00.20, detecting 11 compact HI narrow-line self-emission sources. These sources are situated within a HI cavity, with 8 of them located in the cavity's center. The average line width at the half maximum (FWHM) for these 11 sources is 1.2 km s$^{-1}$, and their average HI mass is approximately 1.1 $\times 10^5 M_{\odot}$. The spatial distribution of these HI narrow-line self-emissions is highly asymmetric, with a higher concentration on the south-west side of the region. We propose that the HI narrow-line self-emissions are generated by the interaction between the south-west HI ridge and the HI cavity. Furthermore, the asymmetric distribution of these HI self-emissions may be influenced by the south-west HI ridge, which is elongated along the south-west direction. Additionally, the HI self-emissions detected in the cavity's center may result from the interaction between the two HI ridges on either side of the cavity. Finally, the HI self-emissions found within the cavity could serve as a potential source of HI gas for the star-forming region. This study represents the first detection of HI narrow-line self-emissions in G176.51+00.20. Our findings suggest that the HI cavity in this region is not empty but contains several compact HI self-emissions. These results may aid in understanding the formation of HI cavities and the evolution of HI gas within star-forming regions. Future observations with higher resolution and sensitivity are required to further investigate the HI cavity in G176.51+00.20. Deep neural networks are extensively applied across various fields, including image recognition, yet they often struggle with domain shifts. This study evaluates four state-of-art techniques designed to adapt these models for identification tasks: data augmentation, transfer learning, adversarial training, and style transfer. We introduce a unified framework to assess their efficacy in training deep neural networks for identifying images from unseen sources. Our experiments involve identifying images from the iNaturalist 2018 dataset, utilizing models pre-trained on the larger iNaturalist 2018 training set and the Stanford Dogs dataset. Our findings indicate that the proposed framework offers a comprehensive approach for evaluating these domain adaptation strategies. Furthermore, we demonstrate that combining multiple methods can yield superior performance compared to using any single approach in isolation. We demonstrate that the number of arcs in $\mathbb F_q^2$ (where $q$ is odd) with cardinality $s$ (for $2 \leq s \leq q+1$) is precisely $q+1 - \binom{s}{2} \left( \frac{2}{s} \right) q^{\frac{s-3}{2}}$. Consequently, this yields a novel, rigorous enumeration of $k$-secant arcs in $\mathbb F_q^2$ that holds for all $k$ and $q$, thereby extending the findings of Ball, Blokhuis, and Szonyi [J. Combin. Theory. Ser. A 80 (1998), 167–175]. Furthermore, our approach provides a fresh proof of the upper bound $s \leq q+1$ for arcs in $\mathbb F_q^2$. Our methodology relies on the Chevalley-Warning theorem, the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, and the application of a system of quadratic equations to model point-arcs configurations. Additionally, we offer a comprehensive analysis of arcs in $\mathbb F_q^2$ for the specific case $s=4$, deriving the count of such arcs as $q(q-1) + 3 \left( q^{\frac{1}{2}} - 1 \right) \left( \frac{q}{-1} \right)$. This result refines the earlier work of Beutelschies [J. Reine Angew. Math. 255 (1972), 192–199]. Our results also establish the non-existence of arcs in $\mathbb F_q^2$ with cardinality $s$ when $q < s-1$ and $s$ is even, thereby resolving an inquiry posed by Beutelschies [op. cit.]. Finally, we extend our findings to point-arcs configurations, deriving several novel identities and inequalities. In the process, we identify the exact number of point-arcs configurations for every $s$ and $q$, and we offer a new, elementary proof of a theorem by Ball, Blokhuis, and Szonyy [J. Combin. Theory. The discovery of multiple substructures within the galaxy cluster RXCJ0232.2-4420 offers valuable insights into its formation history. Utilizing X-ray data from the Chandra and XMM-Newton observatories, we identified two distinct substructures, designated as Sub1 and Sub2. By analyzing the X-ray surface brightness profile, we determined that Sub1 is located at a projected distance of 120 kpc from the cluster center, while Sub2 lies 200 kpc away. Our spectral analysis revealed that both substructures exhibit a temperature of approximately 10 keV, indicating they are likely part of the cluster's core. Furthermore, we observed a significant temperature gradient in the central region of RXCJ0232.2-4420, with the temperature rising from 7 keV at 100 kpc to 10 keV at 200 kpc. This temperature profile suggests that the cluster is undergoing a merger event. Additionally, we examined the morphology of the cluster's core and found that the pressure profile is asymmetric, with higher pressure detected on the northern side. These findings imply that the merger axis is oriented along the north-south direction. Finally, we compared the properties of RXCJ0232.2-4420 with other merging clusters to better understand its formation process. Our results indicate that RXCJ0232.2-4420 is a merging cluster that has undergone multiple interactions. This conclusion is supported by the presence of a temperature gradient, an asymmetric pressure profile, and the detection of two substructures within the cluster. These observations collectively suggest that RXCJ0232.2-4420 is currently in the process of merging. The study of its substructures provides crucial information for understanding the formation and evolution of galaxy clusters. Future research should focus on investigating the detailed properties of these substructures to further elucidate the cluster's formation history. Additionally, we recommend conducting a dynamical analysis of RXCJ0232.2-4422 to gain a more comprehensive understanding of its formation process. This analysis could be achieved through the examination of the cluster's velocity profile and the identification of substructures via weak gravitational lensing. Such future investigations will significantly enhance our understanding of the formation and evolution of galaxy clusters. The paper is available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.00010

The Legendre memory module (LMM) is a recently introduced variant of the transformer memory module (MM) designed to enhance performance through superior expressiveness and computational efficiency. Despite these benefits, the training process for LMM remains constrained by data parallelism. This paper introduces a novel approach to training LMM within a data parallel framework by leveraging the Legendre polynomial basis and its Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization. We demonstrate that this basis can be represented in a tensor product form, which decomposes the training objective into independent subproblems. Furthermore, we establish that the training objective can be reformulated as a constrained optimization problem, solvable via a straightforward iterative algorithm. We provide a detailed implementation of this algorithm and evaluate its performance against standard training methods. Our results indicate that the proposed method achieves a 2.5x speedup in training time. Additionally, we extend this work to address the training of multi-layer LMM architectures. Experimental outcomes confirm that our approach scales effectively across hundreds of GPUs. Finally, we validate the efficacy of the proposed training algorithm on the ImageNet dataset. Our findings demonstrate that LMM trained with this method surpasses various state-of-the-art transformer models, achieving a 1.5x improvement in both training and inference speeds. This paper presents a modeling approach to linguistic consistency within labeling games, where participants from a migrating population interact with objects possessing intrinsic properties. Consistency is defined by the alignment between participants' interpretations of these objects and the objects' actual nature. The study examines two primary sources of inconsistency: (1) the lack of initial alignment between objects and participants, and (2) the emergence of inconsistency arising from labeling interactions. To address these issues, the migration of participants is utilized as a mechanism to mitigate both types of inconsistency. The analysis covers two distinct information structures: a setting where participants possess no prior knowledge of object properties, and a setting where participants hold prior beliefs that may or may not align with the objects' true nature. Furthermore, the evolution of language itself is incorporated into the analysis, demonstrating that inconsistency within a labeling game can drive linguistic evolution. The paper concludes by outlining several avenues for future research. This work extends the author's prior publication, "A model of labeling games with migrating participants," which offered a simpler analysis of labeling interactions. The current study offers a more comprehensive examination of inconsistency and migration, alongside an exploration of how inconsistency influences linguistic evolution. The primary contribution lies in the analysis of linguistic evolution, which is grounded in a detailed investigation of inconsistency and migration. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 provides a preliminary overview of labeling games; Section 3 outlines the model; Section 4 analyzes the case where participants lack prior knowledge; Section 5 analyzes the case where prior beliefs exist; and Section 6 concludes with suggestions for future research. Additionally, Appendix A provides a detailed analysis of linguistic evolution, while Appendix B offers a preliminary discussion of inconsistency and migration. The Appendix is intended for readers seeking further insight into labeling games. Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) have recently emerged as a powerful method for solving partial differential equations (PDEs). However, recent research indicates that PINNs often suffer from spectral bias, tending to prioritize learning low-frequency components over high-frequency ones. This study offers theoretical insights into this phenomenon and demonstrates its validity through numerical experiments. Our analysis reveals that the spectral bias stems from the gradient descent optimization process applied to fully connected feedforward networks. We further prove that adding momentum to the optimizer can mitigate this bias, a finding supported by additional numerical evidence. Consequently, incorporating momentum into PINNs presents a promising strategy to address spectral bias. Overall, this work provides new theoretical perspectives on optimization within PINNs and introduces momentum as an effective solution to spectral bias. This paper investigates a coupled system featuring two wave equations, where one includes full Kelvin-Voigt damping and the other only locally disrupted Kelvin-Voigt damping. By employing energy methods, we demonstrate that the coupled system's energy decays at a rate of $t^{-1/2}$, matching the decay rate of the system when both equations possess full damping. This result relies on the assumption that the intersection of the damping supports is non-empty and that the products of the coupling operators are sufficiently small. Furthermore, we extend our findings to the scenario of local damping interaction. Notably, our analysis does not require geometric conditions on the coupling or damping, nor does it necessitate smallness conditions on the size of the domains. The paper concludes by presenting examples that illustrate the applicability of these results. Additionally, we provide an example of a system that fails to exhibit stability, thereby highlighting the sharpness of our main theorems. Finally, we outline several open questions and potential avenues for future research. This work serves as an extension of the authors' previous study, where both subsystems possessed full damping. In that earlier paper, we established sharp decay rates for the energy using a frequency domain approach based on maximal $L^p$-regularity estimates for the coupled system's generator. In contrast, the current study achieves stability through energy estimates, which are more straightforward to apply. However, this advantage comes with a trade-off: the decay rate obtained here is less sharp than the one derived via maximal $L^p$-regularity estimates. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 introduces the coupled system and its governing equations; Section 3 presents the main results; Section 4 contains the proofs of these results; and Section 5 offers examples demonstrating the applicability of the findings. Finally, Section 6 addresses open problems and suggests directions for future research. This current version represents a significant revision of an earlier draft, incorporating substantial improvements and corrections. Specifically, the earlier version did not address the case of locally disrupted damping, whereas this revised paper does. Furthermore, the earlier work claimed a logarithmic loss in the decay rate, whereas this paper proves that no such loss occurs. These enhancements are the result of a thorough re-examination of the proofs and the inclusion of additional technical details. Although deep reinforcement learning (RL) agents excel at solving complex tasks, they often lack interpretability, making it difficult for humans to grasp the decision-making processes of black-box models. This opacity hinders the deployment of RL in safety-critical domains. To address this, we introduce a hierarchical RL framework that utilizes inductive logic programming (ILP) to render the agent's behavior interpretable to humans. By training an ILP model on the states and actions generated by the deep RL agent, we produce a high-level policy that mirrors the agent's decisions while remaining understandable to non-experts. We validate the efficacy of our proposed explainable model-driven hierarchical RL agent through a case study involving a simulated autonomous vehicle navigating a roundabout. The results demonstrate that our method successfully produces interpretable policies and effectively learn high-level policies for the specified scenario. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/rajkumarvishwanath/Explanable-Model-Driven-Hierarchical-RL. Given its ability to generate interpretable policies, this approach holds significant potential for facilitating the adoption of deep RL agents in real-world applications. Furthermore, the method is versatile and can be applied to various other scenarios, such as robot navigation and medical diagnosis. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the first application of hierarchical RL with model-based explanations to enhance the interpretability of deep RL agents. Asymmetry in light scattering is a fundamental and ubiquitous phenomenon observed across diverse contexts, including non-centrosymmetric materials, directional light propagation, and structural disorder. In this study, we introduce a novel method to achieve light scattering asymmetry by compressing one transverse dimension of an incident beam into a highly non-classical state. This quantum-induced scattering asymmetry relies on the spatial redistribution of both photon probability and quantum fluctuations within the compressed beam. We demonstrate this effect in a simple yet instructive scenario: an incoming single-mode squeezed light beam scattered by a disordered screen. Our findings indicate that the asymmetry ratio can surpass that of the incident beam, potentially reaching several orders of magnitude. Furthermore, we show that this phenomenon can be readily detected through photon counting at specific output modes. These results pave the way for new applications of quantum illumination and enhanced metrology, leveraging the significant amplification of quantum effects. Additionally, our approach offers a new perspective on quantum-compression-induced phenomena, highlighting the critical role of quantum fluctuations in interacting with matter. Finally, we outline the experimental requirements and confirm that the necessary equipment is currently accessible. This research was conducted using the Quantum Asymmetry Lab, a dedicated facility at the University of Geneva designed to explore fundamental questions in quantum optics. The lab is equipped with a versatile platform for generating, characterizing, and manipulating non-classical light, alongside a collection of passive and active disordered samples. These samples were specifically engineered to maximize quantum-induced scattering asymmetry, thereby enabling a deeper investigation into the underlying physics. We introduce a direct detection experiment designed to identify spin-dependent interactions between dark matter and nucleons in $\mathbf{^{6}Li}$. This approach offers two primary benefits: first, the nucleus's spin is predominantly carried by the proton, simplifying nucleon contributions; second, the nontarget neutron can still generate spin-dependent nuclear responses via meson exchange currents. We establish a framework for designing such an experiment and calculate the resulting cross sections. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this method can achieve sensitivity to $\mathbf{^{6}Be}$-like nuclear states, which are crucial for detecting dark matter with a mass below approximately 100 MeV. Finally, we discuss the experiment's potential to constrain spin-dependent interactions mediated by light mediators. Our findings indicate that a 100-kg spin-polarized $\mathbf{^{6}Li}$ target, operating for 100 days with a 10% detection efficiency, could detect a proton-mediated cross section as low as $\sigma_{p}^{\rm SD} \sim 10^{-40} \, \mathrm{cm}^2$ for mediators with masses between 10 and 1000 MeV. For mediators lighter than 10 MeV, the experiment would be sensitive to $\sigma_{p}^{\rm SD} \sim 10^{-30} \, \mathrm{cm}^2$. These projections are contingent upon the availability of a highly efficient spin-polarized $\mathbf{^{6}Li}$ target. Additionally, we show that the proposed setup can probe spin-dependent mediators lighter than 10 MeV, a range that has remained largely unexplored by other direct detection methods. This capability stems from the significant enhancement of nuclear cross sections caused by the presence of a $\mathbf{^{6}Be}$-like state. For mediators between 10 and 1000 MeV, we predict a 90% C.L. upper limit of $\sigma_{p}^{\rm SD} \lesssim 10^{-36} \, \mathrm{cm}^2$, while mediators lighter than 10 MeV could be constrained down to $\sigma_{p}^{\rm SD} \lesssim 10^{-42} \, \mathrm{cm}^2$. These results are expected to surpass the sensitivity of existing direct detection experiments.

Blind image restoration (BUR) is an inverse problem that seeks to recover original images from blurred observations without knowledge of the blur kernel. This study introduces a novel kernel mixture model designed to simultaneously estimate the blur kernel and reconstruct the original image. The proposed method is grounded in a nonparametric Bayesian framework, utilizing a Dirichlet process (DP) to define a nonparametric prior for an infinite kernel model. By applying a mean-field variational inference approach, the algorithm achieves efficient and rapid estimation of both the blur kernel and the latent image. Experimental results demonstrate that the method outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques in terms of peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) and structural similarity index (SSIM). Furthermore, the proposed method exhibits robust performance across a diverse range of blur kernels. The implementation is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi-1998/KernelMixture. Keywords: Blind image restoration, blur kernel estimation, kernel mixture model, Dirichlet process.

Nonuniform algebras serve as a generalization of associative algebras, designed to facilitate the study of discrete integrable systems. This paper investigates bialgebra structures on discrete integrable systems derived from nonuniform associative algebras, with a specific focus on the discrete two-dimensional Yang-Baxter equation. We present multiple examples of systems satisfying this equation, including the discrete Hirota three-wave interaction model, the discrete Toda lattice, and the discrete two-dimensional Yang-Baxter equation. Subsequently, we derive nonuniform analogues of the associative and R-matrix properties, which allow for the construction of solutions to the discrete two-dimensional Yang-Baxter equation. Finally, we establish the nonuniform associative Yang-Baxter equation, a concept that extends the classical associative Yang-Baxter equation, and explore its relationship with the discrete two-dimensional Yang-Baxter equation. Additionally, we provide examples of solutions to the discrete two-dimensional Yang-Baxter equation generated by the nonuniform associative Yang-Baxter equation. This work represents a preliminary step toward developing a nonuniform version of the Drinfel'd-Sklyanin theory. This paper introduces a formal framework designed to validate programs annotated with logical forms of natural language descriptions. Its primary objective is to enable formal reasoning about program correctness based on assertions expressed in the logical forms of statements found in natural language. To achieve this, we propose a formalization of Hoare logic within a natural language framework and utilize typed lambda calculus to model the meaning of these statements. Furthermore, we present a validation system for Hoare logic formulas using Coq, a proof assistant. Our framework facilitates formal reasoning about program correctness by leveraging the formal semantics assigned to natural language descriptions. Additionally, we demonstrate the applicability of this system by validating a substantial number of formulas related to the Y combinator and Fibonacci numbers. The complete formalization is accessible online. Our results indicate that this system can effectively validate programs derived from the meaning of natural language descriptions, thereby supporting formal reasoning about program correctness. We believe this framework offers a valuable approach for validating programs originating from logical forms of natural language. Canopus is a Byzantine fault-tolerant (BFT) replicated state machine (RSM) designed for cloud environments, featuring a streamlined protocol that reduces the number of client interactions per consensus round to just two. However, Canopus's reliance on a centralized coordinator renders it susceptible to coordinator failures, which can stall the RSM. This paper introduces RCanopus, an enhanced version of Canopus that eliminates the need for a central coordinator by distributing its responsibilities. We present a prototype implementation of RCanopus and validate its efficacy through extensive experiments. Our findings demonstrate that RCanopus offers superior fault tolerance compared to the original, while also delivering a 1.5x to 2x performance improvement under heavy loads. Furthermore, we observe that the original Canopus experiences a significant performance degradation when the coordinator fails, whereas RCanopus maintains consistent performance under such failures. Additionally, we show that the original Canopus is vulnerable to Byzantine attacks targeting the coordinator, while RCanopus effectively mitigates these attacks. Finally, we demonstrate that RCanopus is more resilient to network failures than the original Canopus. The RCanopus source code is accessible at https://github.com/CloudLab/rcanopus. This study examines the impact of cholesterol on the mechanical properties of lipid membranes. We begin by analyzing experimental data on how the bending modulus varies with the mole fraction of cholesterol, revealing a linear relationship. Subsequently, we apply a statistical mechanical framework to investigate the lateral interactions between lipids and cholesterol, as well as between distinct lipid species. Our model demonstrates that cholesterol induces ordering in the hydrocarbon chains of phospholipids, thereby increasing the membrane's bending modulus. Finally, we compare our theoretical predictions against both experimental findings and results from molecular dynamics simulations. The agreement with simulations is excellent, whereas our theory tends to overestimate the magnitude of the bending modulus. Nevertheless, the derived theoretical expressions for the bending modulus and lateral interactions offer valuable insights into the ordering of lipid tails and the phase behavior of membranes. These findings are essential for developing more accurate computational models of membranes containing diverse lipid and cholesterol components. Furthermore, the theoretical methodology employed can be extended to investigate the effects of other membrane constituents, such as sphingolipids and proteins. The underlying code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/abhishekdatta1992/cholesterol_lipid_membrane. We examine the Hamiltonian constraint within the loop quantum gravity (LQG) framework, utilizing the standard ADM Hamiltonian formulation. By employing a specific gauge choice, the constraint is expressed as a function of holonomies and the basic flux variables associated with the electric field components. We then apply the quantization procedure to this Hamiltonian constraint. The resulting quantum constraint equation is derived and analyzed. This analysis yields an infinite set of difference equations, where the difference variable corresponds to one of the fundamental flux variables. We demonstrate that, under a suitable gauge choice, this basic flux variable functions as a momentum, enabling the difference equations to be interpreted as the dynamics of a free particle. Furthermore, we explore the relationship between this result and the dynamics of a free particle in a non-relativistic context. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for the understanding of spacetime dynamics. In this regard, we find that the basic flux variables, which represent the area of surfaces intersecting a spatial slice, can be interpreted as the radii of a hypersphere surrounding a spatial slice. This interpretation suggests that the dynamics of a free particle may reflect the behavior of a hypersphere expanding into an extra dimension. Additionally, we note that the difference equations are free of the zero mode problem. Consequently, the quantum dynamics of a free particle are characterized by a minimum length, a phenomenon that can be understood as the quantum gravitational effect of a black hole. This approach offers a new perspective on the relationship between black holes and the fundamental length scale of Planck's scale. Ultimately, this provides a novel interpretation of the Planck length and a new understanding of the quantum gravitational regime. We conclude that the quantum dynamics of a free particle, derived from the Hamiltonian constraint in LQG, offer a fresh perspective on the quantum gravitational problem. This approach may pave the way for a new understanding of the quantum gravitational regime. Specifically, it suggests that the quantum gravitational effect of a black hole could serve as a fundamental length scale. This conclusion is supported by the observation that the minimum radius of a black hole, known as the Schwarzschild radius, is directly proportional to the Planck mass. In this view, the quantum gravitational effect of a black hole is not merely a derived phenomenon but a fundamental aspect of spacetime dynamics. Deep object detectors are widely used across diverse fields, yet their predictions lack uncertainty quantification, which is essential for safety-critical applications. To address this, we introduce BayesOD, the first Bayesian framework for object detection. This approach employs a Bayesian perspective to model the deep network's output, enabling the propagation of uncertainty from individual bounding box predictions to the final detection results. By utilizing a novel Bayesian NMS algorithm, the method effectively accounts for uncertainty during non-maximum suppression. Evaluated on the COCO dataset, BayesOD achieves state-of-the-art performance in uncertainty estimation, significantly outperforming previous methods. Accurate short-term traffic prediction is essential for intelligent transportation systems. This study introduces a new dataset comprising 5-minute traffic flow snippets for each of the 1,000 busiest roads in Tokyo, Japan, covering the period from 2017 to 2019. The proposed method trains a regression model on these snippets to forecast traffic flow 15 minutes ahead. Experimental results demonstrate that the method achieves a 10% improvement in prediction accuracy compared to state-of-the-art approaches. Furthermore, the method is shown to be robust against variations in the length of the input snippets. We demonstrate that coherence, interpreted as invertibility within a proof-theoretic framework, can be modeled in a 2-category where 1-cells are implementations and 2-cells are mappings between them. This implementation concept, introduced in our prior work, is grounded in the observation that incoherent structures possess canonical modifications that preserve composition and duality. Our proof relies on the existence of an adjunction between the category of coherent structures and the category of implementations. This paper extends our previous findings by incorporating weak invertibility and proving that the aforementioned adjunction restricts to an equivalence on coherents. Additionally, we establish that invertibility and canonical invertibility are equivalent when invertible transformations are defined categorically. Finally, we illustrate the utility of these findings by applying them to linear and classical logic. The code referenced in this paper can be found at https://github.com/brunocampos/categorical-coherence. Keywords: coherence spaces, coherence, coherence geometry, coherence logic, coherence structures, coherence geometry, coherence logic, coherence structures, coherence geometry, coherence logic.

This study introduces a novel deep learning framework designed to analyze brain MRI scans for classifying Alzheimer's disease and seizures. The process begins with segmenting the hippocampus using a 3D U-Net architecture, followed by classification via a suite of deep convolutional neural networks, including ResNet, VGG, and Inception models. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves a Dice coefficient of 0.81 for hippocampus segmentation and a 96.5% accuracy for the classification task. The source code is publicly accessible at \url{https://github.com/abdullahkaya1995/hippocampus-classification}. This framework is particularly well-suited for clinical settings where limited data availability necessitates the use of transfer learning. Furthermore, the modular design facilitates the independent evaluation of each component, such as the segmentation network or the ensemble of classifiers. The comprehensive code repository includes detailed instructions for implementation and evaluation. The paper also outlines the dataset used for training and testing, as well as the specific methodologies employed for hippocampus segmentation and classification. Additionally, the study addresses the computational challenges associated with training multiple networks and their integration into a unified framework. Finally, the work discusses the broader applications of this method in medical imaging and suggests potential future research directions. The authors hope this research will inspire further advancements in the field. The source code can be found at \url{https://github.com/abdullahkaya1995/hippocampus-classification}. The dataset is available at \url{https://github.com/abdullahkaya1995/brain-mri-dataset}. We examine the Pigeonhole phenomenon, which asserts that two transversal modes sharing the same photon number can be distinguished by a single photon passing through a beam splitter. Our analysis demonstrates that this phenomenon is not universal; rather, its feasibility relies entirely on the specific linear independence of the two multimode photons. Consequently, we establish that the ability to detect the transversality of pigeonhole modes is constrained by the amount of information contained within the modes. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the pigeonhole phenomenon can be utilized to generate nonclassical correlations between the output ports of the beam splitter. These outcomes are achieved through the explicit construction of the relevant states and by deriving a necessary and sufficient condition for the existence of such states. Finally, the framework developed is sufficiently general to encompass various quantum sensing applications. In this context, we illustrate that the quantum Fisher information regarding the transversality of the modes can be maximized by preparing the two multimode photons in an N-uniform state. This approach enables the precise estimation of the integer $N$ using a minimal number of photons. Additionally, we show that the quantum Fisher information can be enhanced by preparing the two multimode photons in a symmetric W state. These results highlight the utility of nonclassical correlations in quantum sensing. Our findings are validated through numerical simulations. Notably, the proposed states are readily available in numerous quantum systems, including those used for quantum metrology. This suggests that the pigeonhole phenomenon can be effectively employed in practical quantum sensing tasks. Our work thus provides a comprehensive theoretical foundation for the application of the pigeonhole phenomenon in quantum sensing. This study presents a new model for time-dependent, low-energy cosmic ray protons at low Earth orbit (LEO), incorporating the effects of geomagnetic and atmospheric cutoffs. The model is derived from a large ensemble of 100 Monte Carlo simulations of the Earth's atmosphere, each utilizing a different geomagnetic field configuration. These simulations span a range of International Geomagnetic Reference Field (IGRF) indices from 0 to 100, covering a 10-year period between 2015 and 2025. The model is validated against the AP-8AEN proton flux data. Results indicate that the IGRF index correlates with the rate of change in cosmic ray protons, with a correlation coefficient of 0.99. Furthermore, the model demonstrates that the rate of change in protons is 1.5 times greater at the top of the atmosphere compared to LEO. This finding is critical for accurately predicting the Single Event Upset (SEU) rate in Low Earth Orbit satellites. The IGRF index can be readily obtained from the World Data Center for Magnetism, which provides weekly updates. The IGRF data, along with the proton model, is available at https://github.com/abhishekkumar1994/CRAND_LEO. This model is particularly valuable for Low Earth Orbit satellites operating in Low Earth Phenomena (LEP) regions, such as the International Space Station (ISS) and the International Sun-Earth Explorer-3 (ISEE-3). The ISEE-3 satellite, which orbits the Sun, experienced a 100% increase in SEU rates during its closest approach to the Earth in 1982. Additionally, the model is essential for accurately predicting the total ionizing dose (TID) on LEO satellites, as the IGRF index influences the dose rate by a factor of 1.5. The study concludes that the IGRF index is a significant factor in LEO LEP events, including SEU and TID. The paper also discusses the relationship between the IGRF index and solar activity, noting that the index is 1.5 times higher during solar maximum than solar minimum. This relationship is crucial for accurately predicting the total dose rate on LEO satellites. We introduce the Universal Pyramid-like Shrinkage Skeleton (UPSS), a framework that simplifies the design of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) by reducing them to a pyramid-like shrinkage skeleton. This approach is grounded in the observation that most existing GNN architectures, despite their apparent complexity, ultimately follow this fundamental skeleton. By focusing on UPSS, we aim to eliminate redundant design efforts and facilitate the systematic exploration of GNNs. To achieve this, we propose a minimal and universal design rule: Local Structure Link Rewiring (LSLR). LGSR provides a local perspective on network design, enabling the construction of diverse GNNs through the straightforward rewiring of links within a pyramid-like structure. Furthermore, we propose an efficient algorithm that achieves this optimal rate and conduct a comprehensive numerical analysis to evaluate its performance. The Attenuation, Emission, and Polarization (AEP) framework from dust in the Diffuse Interstellar Medium (ISM) is a rapidly evolving field. This Atti et al. (2021) study aims to provide a thorough review of the most recent findings and theoretical models. We begin by examining the fundamental properties of attennuation and polarization caused by dust grains, followed by an analysis of the mechanisms driving the emission of Atomic Polarization (PAH) molecules. Subsequently, we explore the structure of the ISM and the characteristics of the grain size distribution. Finally, we address the challenges in modeling AEP data and conclude with a discussion on future research directions. Attenation and polarization data reveal a universal dust grain size distribution, while the polarization fraction of PAH emission is approximately 0.01% and remains independent of wavelength. The Diffuse ISM is characterized by a two-phase structure: a low-density phase comprising 80% of the volume and a high-density phase occupying only 20% of the volume but containing 90% of the mass. The polarization of PAH emission is attributed to the alignment of molecules within the low-density phase. Furthermore, Attenuation, Emission, and Polarization (AEP) data indicate that dust grains in the Diffuse ISM are not spherical. The Attenuation, Emission, and Polarization (AEP) properties of dust in the Diffuse ISM are governed by the grain size distribution, which is determined by the balance between growth and destruction processes. Theoretical models suggest that the grain size distribution in the Diffuse ISM is non-universal and varies with the local environment. Finally, we discuss the challenges in modeling AEP data and outline future research directions. The primary challenge in modeling AEP data is the lack of accurate grain size distributions, which can be addressed by combining AEP data with other observational data. We report the detection of a gap in the gas disk of the very low-mass star CIDA 1, observed via ALMA at a separation of 100 au. This gap is best explained by the presence of a massive planet with a mass of 10 Jupiter masses orbiting at a semi-major axis of 100 au. This system represents the first instance where a gap in a low-mass star's disk is attributed to a planet. The planet's migration is likely halted by the disk's inner edge, which is defined by the boundary between the accretion shock and the star's photosphere. Additionally, we identify a second gap at 20 au, suggesting another planet with a mass of 1 Jupiter mass. We also present new optical photometry of CIDA 1, indicating a stellar mass of 0.015 solar masses and an age of 10 million years. Finally, we discuss the implications of this system for planet formation theories around low-mass stars. The existence of a massive planet at 100 au challenges current models, which typically predict that planets around low-mass stars are either very small or located very close to the star. This study underscores the necessity of studying planet formation around low-mass stars to understand the full range of planetary systems. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the gap at 100 au can be modeled using the linear gap-opening formalism, a method traditionally applied only to solar-mass stars. This finding suggests that the linear gap-opening formalism may be more broadly applicable than previously believed. Additionally, we show that the gap at 20 au can be successfully reproduced using the linear gap-opening formalism. These results indicate that the linear formalism is more versatile than previously thought, as it can account for gaps in both the gas and dust components of the disk. This work highlights the critical role of high-resolution, high-sensitivity observations in investigating planet formation around low-mass stars. The disk around CIDA 1 offers a unique opportunity to study how planets form in these environments, and we anticipate that future observations will reveal more planets within this disk. This study is part of the ALMA Large Program "Gaps and Planets in Disks around Low-mass Stars" (ALMA-GLAD), which aims to identify and characterize planets in the disks of low-mass stars. The program utilizes the ALMA Large Program's high angular resolution and sensitivity to detect gaps in both the gas and dust components of these disks

This paper introduces an extension of the classic game "Lights Out," framing it as a problem in linear algebra over finite fields. We provide a detailed description of this challenge and offer a heuristic approach to solving it. Furthermore, we present a specific variant known as the "Maximum Clicks Challenge," which requires players to light up all bulbs using the greatest possible number of moves. We demonstrate that this objective can be modeled as a system of linear equations, solved via the method of undetermined coefficients. Additionally, we illustrate the application of this method with a 3x3 grid example. The paper concludes with a discussion of findings and suggestions for future research. This work was conducted as a project within the Applied Mathematics course at the University of Puerto Rico, Mayaguez. The authors are: J. A. Gonzalez, J. A. Jimenez, and J. A. Rodriguez. Abstract Interpretation is a well-established framework for static analysis that operates by relaxing precision to achieve computational efficiency. This paper examines the fundamental efficiency-precision trade-off within this framework. We demonstrate that the standard "flattened" approach to managing this trade-off—where the rising phase adjusts precision through over-approximation and the "flattened" phase adjusts efficiency through over-scheduling—is not optimal. We introduce a new theoretical framework that separates these phases to resolve this suboptimality. We validate this framework using a simple but illustrative example, showing that our method offers greater flexibility in balancing precision and efficiency compared to the traditional approach. Finally, we illustrate the practical benefits of this framework through a case study involving a static analysis of JavaScript code. The code for this case study is accessible at https://github.com/PranavKumar2000/decoupled-abstract-interpretation. This work expands upon the first author's PhD thesis, P. Kumar, *Decoupling the rising and falling phases in abstract interpretation*, University of Cambridge, 2021. The full thesis is available at https://www.repository.cam.ac.uk/handle/1810/310004.

We introduce a theoretical framework for modeling the interaction between photons and phonons in oxide perovskites. Our analysis demonstrates that the electron-phonon coupling is predominantly governed by the $\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{p}$ mechanism, with contributions from polarization and spin-orbit coupling being negligible. We establish that this coupling is largely independent of photon polarization but is strongly modulated by photon momentum. Furthermore, we identify specific momentum values where the coupling reaches its maximum, corresponding to the momentum transfer of Lattice Polarons. These findings offer a basis for designing new experiments to investigate geometric phonons and enhance the coupling between electronic excitations and phonons.

Identifying anomalies is a critical challenge across numerous domains, including finance, medicine, and security. While many methods exist, they often depend on specific data characteristics, such as linearity or the absence of noise, which limits their generalizability. To address this, we introduce a novel anomaly identification framework grounded in the Closeness Graph, a metric-based approach that offers greater adaptability. We also develop a new feature engineering technique to enhance the classifier's performance. Extensive experiments conducted on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that our proposed framework achieves superior accuracy compared to current state-of-the-art solutions. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2000/Closeness-Graph. Furthermore, we have released a new real-world dataset, the UCI-Medical, which comprises 1,000 samples of patients diagnosed with either myocardial infarction or acute pancreatitis. This dataset can be found at https://github.com/ChenYi2000/UCI-Medical. The findings from this study are detailed in the paper titled "A Closeness Graph-based Method for Anomaly Identification in Metric Spaces," published in the Proceedings of the 2021 IEEE International Conference on Data Mining (ICDM 2021). The project's website is located at https://cheyi2000.github.io/CGM/. The corresponding author is Chen Yi, who can be contacted at chen.yi@uwaterloo.ca. The paper's title in English is "A Closeness Graph-based Method for Anomaly Identification in Metric Spaces." The authors are Chen Yi, Chen Liang, and Wang Shu. The abstract states: "Anomaly identification holds significant importance in diverse fields such as finance, medicine, and security. Although numerous techniques have been proposed, most are constrained by the need for large volumes of labeled data or are limited to specific data types. This paper presents a new approach leveraging the Closeness Graph, a method that is more adaptable to various data characteristics. We also propose a novel feature engineering method to further improve the classifier's performance. The results indicate that our method outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques." This study examines an atom oriented against a slender, dielectric wall by developing a Green's function for the electromagnetic field within a half-space characterized by an orientation-dependent dielectric tensor. We demonstrate that the atom's motion generates a stimulation effect, which can be interpreted as the atom absorbing two virtual photons with opposite signs arising from the anisotropic environment. Furthermore, we show that the atom's electrodynamics can be modeled as a system comprising an electric dipole and a magnetic dipole. Additionally, we calculate the electromagnetic emission characteristics of a moving atom in this dielectric medium, revealing that the emission rate is enhanced by a factor of two compared to the stationary case. These findings offer new perspectives on the interaction between atoms and dielectric media. The theoretical framework is applicable to various scenarios, including the design of efficient light sources and the investigation of quantum phenomena such as the dynamical Casimir effect and atom cooling. Finally, we outline the potential for extending this theory to more complex geometries and dielectric configurations. The research was conducted using the open-source Python package `pydielectric`. The accompanying Python code is available at https://github.com/abdelrahim-b/pydielectric. The package is distributed under the MIT license. This interface allows users to input the dielectric tensor, atomic velocity, and atomic frequency to compute the normalized Purcell factor, which represents the ratio of the Purcell factor in a moving medium to that in a vacuum. The community equity problem seeks to identify a community of nodes within a graph that maximizes a specific objective function. This study examines the trade-off between the size of these communities and their quality, introducing the localized community equity problem. This variant restricts solutions to communities of a predefined size and demonstrates that understanding graph locality is essential for achieving high-quality results. We present an algorithm capable of generating high-quality communities in sublinear time relative to the graph's total size, with performance controlled by a locality parameter. Experimental results indicate that our algorithm outperforms state-of-the-art methods in identifying high-quality communities across various real-world datasets. Furthermore, we show that our approach surpasses high-quality community detection algorithms from Google, Facebook, and Microsoft when applied to localized datasets. Finally, we evaluate the algorithm's effectiveness in local graph understanding, revealing that identified communities offer valuable insights into the operational mechanisms of real-world networks. This study introduces a new iterative method to solve master equations governing reversible enzyme reactions, grounded in the principle that the time-dependent probability density function (pdf) at any given time can be derived from its steady-state counterpart. The efficacy of this approach is demonstrated using a specific instance of the equation for the same type of pdf. The iterative solutions are validated against both exact solutions and results from the Runge-Kutta fourth-order method. Furthermore, an examination of the steady-state pdfs reveals that, for this particular equation, the time-dependent pdfs rapidly converge to their steady-state forms. Consequently, the proposed iterative method is shown to be highly effective for these systems. Additionally, the computational efficiency of the method is compared with the Runge-Kutta fourth-order approach, demonstrating that the iterative scheme is significantly faster. Finally, the method's application is extended to other kinetic equations describing reversible enzyme reactions. In these additional cases, the time-dependent pdfs also quickly approach their steady-state limits, confirming that the iterative method remains highly effective and efficient for these systems as well. Overall, the findings indicate that this iterative scheme is a powerful tool for obtaining accurate solutions to kinetic equations in enzyme reaction systems. This study examines the production of jets and missing transverse momentum in proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV, with a focus on simplified models featuring vector mediators that decay into neutrinos. The analysis incorporates both soft and parton-level cuts, utilizing Monte Carlo simulations processed through Pythia 8.215 for parton showering and CMS software for detector-level reconstruction. By employing a multivariate discriminant, the investigation determines the most stringent 95% confidence level limits on the mass of vector mediators and their associated couplings, based on the ATLAS experiment's 2016 dataset, which corresponds to an integrated luminosity of 36.1 fb$^{-1}$. Furthermore, the study explores the potential for detecting supersymmetric particles in proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV by employing a jet missing ET signature. It compares two distinct data-taking strategies: a fully merged approach and one incorporating jet-parton matching. The research concludes that the fully merged signature offers superior sensitivity for jets originating from the decay of supersymmetric particles, specifically those with low transverse momentum. Additionally, the analysis highlights the necessity of including jet-parton matching in simulations to accurately describe the kinematic properties of jets with low transverse momentum. This study examines the stochastic dynamics of the Standard & Poor's 500 Index (S&P 500) over the period from January 1950 to December 2019, employing a stochastic resetting framework. This model incorporates a primary stochastic phase characterized by heavy-tailed, mean-reverting durations, interrupted by rare, unpredictable resettings that restore the system to an initial state. Consequently, the effective stochastic dynamics are governed by a continuous-time renewal process featuring inter-event times with heavy tails and infinite variance, resulting in a continuous-time random walk with divergent av-advancing times. These dynamics yield a continuous-time probability density function (PDF) for the time interval between successive record highs, which asymptotically follows a power law with an exponent of $\gamma=5/2$. Furthermore, at large times, the PDF exhibits a linear time dependence, a feature attributed to the stochastic nature of mean-reverting durations. The findings support the hypothesis that record highs in the S&P 500 are governed by a sequence of independent events, with the linear time behavior of the PDF serving as a critical indicator of the stochastic character of these financial swells. The analysis also explores the implications of these results for financial forecasting. Finally, the study extends the stochastic resetting framework to other fields, including finance, physics, and biology. The paper concludes with a discussion of the forecasting implications of these findings. To facilitate replication, the authors provide a Python package, `stochastic_resetting`, available at https://github.com/alejandro-garcia-ortega/stochastic_resetting. This package includes a class, `S&P500`, which contains the time series data of the S&P 500 from January 1950 to December 2019, along with a `resetting_statistics` method to compute resetting statistics. Additionally, a Jupyter notebook, `resetting_analysis.ipynb`, is included to demonstrate the application of the `S&P500` class. The package also offers a `stochastic_duration` class to model stochastic durations and a `forecasting` class to calculate forecasted probabilities for record highs. The `forecasting` class includes a `predict_next_record_high` method to predict the next record high and a `predict_record_highs` method to forecast multiple future record highs. The `predict_next_record_high` method predicts the time to the next record high, while the `predict_record_highs` method forecasts multiple future record highs.

This study introduces a path integral approach to analyze a quantum harmonic oscillator subjected to external propulsion. The proposed technique employs Markov chain Monte Carlo strategies to numerically evaluate the influence functional, thereby bypassing the need for complex numerical integration. We demonstrate that the time-dependent probability density function can be computed with high precision using this method. Furthermore, we show excellent agreement between our numerical results and those obtained via the Schrödinger equation method. Our findings indicate that the oscillator's behavior is highly sensitive to the propulsion path; specifically, an appropriately chosen propulsion path enables the system to settle into its ground state within a significantly shorter time frame compared to the unpropelled case. Additionally, we observe that the propulsion force is not necessarily constant and may vary with time. Finally, we demonstrate that the technique remains effective even when the potential energy function is modified. These results suggest that the proposed method is a versatile tool for investigating quantum systems subjected to external propulsion. The accompanying code is available at [1].

In recent years, item recommendation has garnered significant attention within the recommender systems community. While most research has centered on user-item interactions, the growing influence of online reviews and ratings has made evaluating user-item interactions an increasingly vital area of study. Although some studies have incorporated review texts and ratings into recommendation models, they often overlook the substantial value of sentiment information contained in these reviews. To address this gap, this paper introduces a new task: Sentiment-insensitive and Fusion-based Item Recommendation (SIFN). This framework utilizes user review data to extract sentiment features and integrates them with user-item rating data to generate personalized items for each user. Extensive experiments conducted on a real-world dataset demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, ablation studies confirm the efficacy of the proposed sentiment-insensitive and fusion-based strategies. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi1998/SIFN. The dataset can be found at https://github.com/ChenYi1998/ReviewSentimentAnalysis. This paper investigates the potential of Arabic-English code-switched data to generate supplementary training sets for various machine learning tasks. Our methodology involves substituting words from one language with lexical items from another, thereby creating information-augmented datasets. We introduce a straightforward yet effective algorithm designed to perform successful lexical substitutions within code-switched text. Our methodology was evaluated across two tasks: sentiment analysis and part-of-speech tagging. The results demonstrate that our approach yields significant improvements in both tasks. Specifically, our method surpasses the baseline by 10.6% in sentiment classification accuracy and achieves a 1.5% gain in F1-score for POS tagging. Furthermore, we find that substitution algorithms based on lexical similarity outperform those relying on word embeddings. Finally, we release our code and data as an open-source resource to facilitate future research. The accompanying code can be accessed at https://github.com/abdelrahmanelkafrawy/Information-Augmentation. The dataset is available at https://github.com/abdelrahmanelkafrawy/Information-Augmentation/tree/master/data. Keywords: Arabic-English code-switching, information augmentation, lexical substitution, sentiment analysis, part-of-speech tagging.

We demonstrate that any Roelcke-precompact collection of homeomorphisms acting on degree $d \geq 2$ surfaces must possess a uniform modulus of continuity relative to the spherical metric. This finding offers a negative response to a query by M. Gromov concerning whether non-constant maps on degree $d$ surfaces can have an infinitesimal that is infinitesimally close to their modulus of continuity when measured against the hyperbolic metric. Furthermore, we establish that the modulus of continuity relative to the spherical metric serves as a Roelcke invariant for groups of surface homeomorphisms. These findings generalize earlier work by M. Gromov and J. Lohkamp specifically to the context of surfaces. Additionally, we present a self-contained proof of the fact that the modulus of continuity with respect to the hyperbolic metric is the largest sharp asymptotic invariant for surface homeomorphisms. Finally, we extend our findings to include spherical manifolds. The paper concludes with several open questions. We investigate the integrability of non-linear sigma-model membranes, focusing on their solvability through both inverse scattering and inverse collisionless evolution methods. These approaches are applied to spaces arising from $\lambda$-transformations of six-dimensional Minkowski space, where membranes are defined as maps from a two-dimensional world-sheet into the resulting six-dimensional manifold. By analyzing a specific subclass of these membranes, we demonstrate their integrability and derive their equations of motion using both methods. Furthermore, we generalize these findings to include membranes that depend on two light-cone coordinates and explore the possibility of solving their equations via both techniques. Finally, we establish the integrability of membranes mapping the world-sheet into the general space of $\lambda$-transformation. This is achieved by identifying an infinite set of conserved quantities and demonstrating that the membrane equations can be reconstructed from a Lax pair. Among the various membranes examined, we pay particular attention to those that are holomorphic. We also discuss the construction of higher conserved quantities and the associated integrability structures. Additionally, we examine the integrability of membranes with a world-sheet topology of a two-dimensional torus. The solvability of such membranes is proven by solving the equations of motion and constructing a periodic tau-function. This construction enables the determination of the membrane's position within the manifold at any time, based on its initial configuration and conserved quantities. We also address the integrability of membranes with a world-sheet topology of a two-dimensional plane, which can be viewed as a limit of toroidal membranes. We show that the equations of motion for these membranes can be solved using the inverse scattering method. Finally, we discuss the integrability of membranes with more complex topologies, such as a two-sheeted torus, and illustrate how the equations of motion can be solved by reducing them to a system of ordinary differential equations. This reduction is accomplished by considering membranes that depend on only one spatial coordinate. We also examine the integrability of membranes with a two-sheeted sphere topology, showing that their equations can be solved by reducing them to a system of ordinary differential equations. This is achieved by considering membranes that depend on only one light-cone coordinate. The paper concludes with a discussion of the general integrability structures of membranes and their potential applications in string theory and M-theory. We also discuss the general construction of membranes and their role in the study of non-linear sigma-models. We introduce a new algorithm for solving the hex board game Hex on boards featuring regular hexagonal grids of hexahedra, commonly known as hex meshes. This approach, termed Hex-Mesh, leverages the mesh structure to achieve exceptional performance, reaching speeds of up to 58 Tets/Hex on an AMD Ryzen 9 5950X CPU. By utilizing tetrahedralization to bypass the traditional "convergence theorem" found in Hex-Mesh literature, the method accelerates both the simulation of random games and the evaluation of winning positions. Furthermore, the algorithm offers a clear victory path for completed games and provides specific move suggestions for active ones. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/AndreasKraemer/Hex-Mesh. To demonstrate the algorithm's capabilities, we have created a web-based hex solver (https://hexsolver.net) that allows users to input board configurations and instantly receive visualized solutions or optimal moves. The paper also explores the application of Hex-Mesh in computer graphics, including its role in procedural texture generation and a comparison with the texture quality produced by folding sheets of paper. Finally, the discussion addresses the challenges of porting the algorithm to GPUs and concludes with an analysis of the game's complexity. The source code is available at https://github.com/AndreasKraemer/Hex-Mesh. Supplementary material can be found at https://hexsolver.net. Keywords: Hex, Hex meshes, texture generation, computer graphics, tetrahedralization, texture synthesis, procedural texture.

Relation extraction is a core NLP task focused on identifying the relationship between a subject and an object within a sentence. However, models often struggle to identify all semantic entities and their connections, particularly when dealing with multiple relations in a single sentence. This paper introduces a new method that leverages pre-trained language models for knowledge graph connection prediction to enhance relation discovery. By integrating a connection prediction task into the relation extraction framework, the model can simultaneously identify entities and determine their links. Furthermore, we developed a multi-task learning approach that utilizes a knowledge graph connection prediction task to boost performance on relation extraction. Empirical results show that this method achieves state-of-the-art performance on the ACCMERGE dataset and reaches 85.0% F1-score on the REMBER dataset, outperforming previous approaches. The code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi-1998/MultiTask-KE. Additionally, the paper can be found at https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.00020. This paper introduces a novel framework grounded in the concept of rough-grained smoothness, which we argue is both necessary and sufficient for ensuring convergence in model-based reinforcement learning. We propose a model-based algorithm that leverages this property to achieve a sample complexity of $\tilde{O}(H^2S^2A)$, matching the theoretical lower bound established by Jin et al. (2021) and Liu et al. (2021) for model-free methods. Furthermore, we extend our analysis to incorporate uncertainty-aware dynamics, resulting in an improved complexity of $\tilde{O}(H^2S\sqrt{A})$. Our theoretical findings are supported by experiments on both Atari and Pong benchmark tasks. Notably, our model-based approach surpasses several state-of-the-art model-free techniques, including DQN, A3C, and PPO. Additionally, we demonstrate that our method outperforms recent model-based algorithms, such as those by Li et al. (2021) and Yu et al. (2021). To our knowledge, this represents the first model-based algorithm to attain the optimal sample complexity in a metric space.
