We investigate tidal features and merger rates for early-type galaxies (ETGs) at redshifts $0.01 \lesssim z \lesssim 1.5$ by analyzing 1.2 million galaxies from the Hyper Suprime-Cam Subaru Strategic Program (HSC-SSP). Tidal features are quantified using the flux ratio $F_{\rm sub}/F_{\rm main}$, which compares the light of the brightest substructure to the primary component. Our findings indicate that the distribution of $F_{\rm sub}/F_{\rm main}$ for ETGs is bimodal, with one peak near unity and another around 0.1. The latter aligns with the distribution observed in nearby galaxies, suggesting that the presence of substructures is not uncommon among ETGs. Furthermore, the fraction of galaxies exhibiting significant substructures ($F_{\rm sub}/F_{\rm main} \gtrsim 0.1$) remains relatively constant across redshift, implying that the specific fraction of ETGs with prominent substructures stabilizes after an initial decline. Additionally, the redshift evolution of the merger rate for ETGs with $M_{\rm Ks} \lesssim -23.5$ is approximately $10^{-11} \, {\rm yr}^{-1}$, a value that is independent of redshift and mass. This evolution is roughly 100 times lower than that of early-type spirals, a discrepancy likely attributable to differences in stellar mass. Finally, we observe that the merger rate of ETGs with $M_{\rm Ks} \lesssim -23.5$ decreases by a factor of approximately 100 between $z=0$ and $z=1$, a trend that is more pronounced in the most massive galaxies. These results suggest that the majority of early-type galaxies have already completed their growth phase by $z \lesssim 1$. The HSC-SSP dataset offers a unique opportunity to study the tidal characteristics of early-type galaxies at high redshift with exceptional precision. We anticipate that this work will facilitate a more accurate understanding of the formation and evolution of these galaxies. The data and analysis code are publicly accessible at https://github.com/hiroyuki-koike/ETG_tidal. This research is based on observations from the Hyper Suprime-Cam (HSC) on the Subaru Telescope, operated by the National Astronomical Observatory

This work extends the Azimuthally Symmetrical Theory of Gravitation (ASTG), previously outlined in Part I, by introducing the concept of bipolar ejections. This phenomenon is characterized by a negative mass density within the ejecta, resulting in a net negative force that expels matter from the equatorial plane of the source. The bipolar ejection mechanism offers a compelling explanation for the formation of bipolar jets observed in various astrophysical contexts, including protostars, protogalaxies, active galactic nuclei, pulsars, black holes, and the galactic center. The paper begins by deriving the equation of motion for bipolar ejections and subsequently applying it to the case of the galactic center. Furthermore, the study examines the dynamical evolution of the galactic center, demonstrating that the observed bipolar jets can be attributed to the bipolar ejection of matter from the galactic center. Additionally, the evolution of the galactic disk is analyzed, revealing that the rotation curve of the Milky Way is accurately described by ASTG. These findings underscore the efficacy of the ASTG framework. Finally, the paper concludes with a discussion of the astrophysical implications of bipolar ejections. The methodology employed here is notably straightforward, as it relies on the principle of superposition applied to the ASTG-derived equation of motion. This simplicity suggests that ASTG holds significant potential for explaining diverse gravitational phenomena. Ultimately, the ASTG provides a unified framework for understanding the formation of protostars and protogalaxies, as well as the development of jets in galactic nuclei and the galactic center. The theory also addresses the dynamical evolution of galactic disks and the origin of their rotation curves. Ultimately, the gravitational field equations of ASTG offer a comprehensive approach to describing gravitational phenomena across galactic and sub-galactic scales. The simplicity of the theory and the accessibility of its gravitational field equations further highlight its effectiveness. Consequently, ASTG represents a viable alternative to General Relativity for describing gravitational phenomena at galactic and sub-galactic levels. The success of ASTG in explaining the bipolar ejection phenomenon serves as additional evidence supporting its validity. The ASTG is grounded in the concept of mass flow, which is defined as the azimuthal flow of matter along the equatorial plane of the source. This azimuthal mass flow generates a negative mass density in the equatorial plane, thereby producing a negative force that repels matter away from the plane. The origin of fast radio bursts (FRBs) remains uncertain, with a leading hypothesis suggesting they result from the collapse of massive stars. This scenario necessitates the production of electromagnetic radiation across a broad spectrum, spanning radio to gamma rays. However, optical emission from these bursts has yet to be detected. We conducted a targeted search for optical transients coincident with the well-localized FRB 20201124A using the ZTF optical telescope, analyzing data from 2020 to 2022. Our investigation revealed no concurrent optical emission. Additionally, we examined archival ZTF data to search for optical signals following the burst, a method that yielded a 95% confidence upper limit of $1.1 \times 10^{-10}$ on the fluence of any delayed optical emission. These findings impose significant constraints on the optical signatures of the progenitor systems responsible for FRBs. Specifically, we establish a lower limit of $10^{51}$ erg for the optical energy released by the progenitor of FRB 20201124A, a constraint that is independent of the specific emission mechanism. This result aligns with the energy output of a typical core-collapse supernova, thereby supporting the hypothesis that the progenitors of FRBs are massive stars. Furthermore, we identified a new FRB with a high signal-to-noise ratio at 1.4 GHz, designated FRB 20220911A, which exhibits a dispersion measure of 1000 pc cm$^{-3}$ and a redshift of $z=0.012$. The burst's duration of 1.2 ms and energy of $10^{40}$ erg are comparable to those of FRB 20201124A. The source is located in the outskirts of the galaxy NGC 4013, and its dispersion measure is consistent with the intergalactic medium of the nearby galaxy cluster, A1656. The optical upper limit for FRB 20220911A is $1.2 \times 10^{-9}$, which is approximately ten times higher than that of FRB 20201124A. This non-detection of optical emission is consistent with the optical luminosity of the host galaxy, suggesting that the burst's optical signature is either heavily absorbed or intrinsically faint. Although language models are increasingly employed to generate text, they currently lack visual oversight, which hinders their ability to produce high-quality outputs. We introduce a new framework that integrates visual controls into textual creation, allowing text to be steered by image-based prompts and adjusted in real-time based on modifications to these prompts. This system empowers users to direct text generation, refine existing output, and continuously monitor a model's progress. We have implemented this framework using three distinct modalities: image captions, image features, and image features paired with comparison operators. Our results demonstrate that training a multimodal image-text model on a carefully curated dataset yields a flexible and intuitive mechanism for controlling text generation. Furthermore, we show that generation can be refined through incremental updates to image prompts, and we evaluate the system's efficacy via user studies. Ultimately, our findings indicate that visual controls enhance both the quality and utility of text generated by language models. The code and data required to replicate our experiments are available at https://github.com/ashwinbhat/VMOT. Our findings are presented at the 2021 Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR). Video: https://youtu.be/2222222222.

This paper introduces Delegated RingCT, a novel ring signature and ring confidential transaction scheme. The primary innovation is the ability to verify a ring signature by checking only a subset of signed transactions. This approach significantly lowers verification costs, both computationally and in terms of bandwidth, compared to traditional ring signatures. We detail the security properties of our scheme and provide a formal proof of security. Additionally, we present performance evaluations that demonstrate the advantages of Delegated RingCT. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/BitsharesC/delegated_ring_ct. BitsharesC, the development team behind Delegated RingCT, can be contacted at dev@bitshares.org. The paper itself was authored by J. Kaczmarek.

The proposed system is designed to measure transverse intensity profiles of high-current, short-bunch particle beams. It operates without requiring beam capture or external diagnostics, utilizing only the machine's own RF system and a fast feedback system to adjust the longitudinal bunch intensity. The technique is applicable to beams ranging from a few picoCoulombs down to a few femtoCoulombs and functions across a broad frequency spectrum, from roughly 10 MHz up to the RF frequency. The core concept involves injecting a small amount of noise into the beam via a dedicated pick-up, causing beam particles to oscillate transversely. These oscillating particles interact with an on-beam diagnostic, such as a button or broadband pick-up, generating a current signal. By adjusting the transverse noise amplitude and frequency, the transverse position of the beam particles can be scanned. A fast feedback system then varies the RF voltage to modify the beam's longitudinal intensity, thereby changing the number of oscillating particles and the resulting current signal. This process is repeated at different transverse noise frequencies and amplitudes to map the beam's transverse profile. The system is currently being developed for the LHC and is scheduled for installation in 2018. A prototype has already been tested on the SNS, and a demonstration on the LHC is expected to commence in 2018. A key advantage of this method is its ability to detect and localize beam halo, which is critical for minimizing beam loss and mitigating machine protection risks. Furthermore, the system can be adapted to measure other on-beam quantities, such as emittance and centroid position, by adjusting the feedback mechanism. This paper outlines the principle, design, and status of the development. It also presents initial results from a prototype test conducted at the SNS. Finally, the paper discusses the technique's potential for other applications, including the measurement of other on-beam quantities. The proposed approach for measuring centroid position is demonstrated using simulated data. Additionally, a method for determining the beam phase profile is illustrated using simulated and measured data. The paper concludes with a discussion of the technique's potential for other applications, with the proposed centroid position measurement method demonstrated via simulated data. Finally, the technique for measuring the beam phase profile is demonstrated using both simulated and measured data. Data-informed modeling (DIM) represents a synergistic approach that integrates data-driven and modeling-based techniques to enhance the performance of individual components. This survey examines recent advancements in DIM, with a specific focus on reinforcement learning (RL) and control. We begin by outlining the fundamental principles of DIM, followed by a review of its applications within model-based RL and control contexts. Additionally, we address critical challenges and open research questions, aiming to provide a comprehensive perspective on the field and inspire further investigation. This work serves as a summary of our recent survey paper, Collaborative data-informed modeling, published in ACM Computing Surveys (2021). The corresponding source code can be found at https://github.com/ChenYi2020/Review_DIM. Furthermore, the video presentation is available at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=42222222222. Soft robotics is a rapidly evolving field characterized by the use of inherently compliant materials and the need to interact with dynamic, unstructured environments. These robots typically employ continuous deformations for movement and rely on sensing and control systems that account for complex nonlinear dynamics. This paper reviews the application of continuum mechanics models to control soft robots. It begins by outlining the fundamental characteristics of soft robots and their modeling approaches, followed by an examination of various modeling techniques, including finite element models, geometric models, and physics-informed neural networks. The discussion then addresses control strategies derived from these models, covering optimal control, model predictive control, and reinforcement learning. Finally, the paper identifies and analyzes key challenges and future research directions within this domain. By synthesizing concepts from mechanics, control theory, and machine learning, this review aims to provide a comprehensive overview of current advancements and highlight open issues for future inquiry. It serves as a valuable resource for researchers in robotics, mechanics, and control, offering a clear perspective on the state of the art and potential avenues for continued research. Additionally, the paper provides a curated list of relevant resources, including textbooks, articles, and software tools, to assist readers in navigating the field. (This work was supported by the European Research Council under the European Union's Horizon 2020 research and innovation programme, Grant Agreement No. 805137.) Keywords: Soft robotics, continuum mechanics, optimal control, model predictive control, reinforcement learning. The literature on the {\em Jacobi group} is extensive and frequently contradictory, often resulting in mathematical structures that are difficult to visualize. This paper aims to clarify the most fundamental instance of the Jacobi group, which corresponds to the {\em authentic} version. We begin by examining the {\em abelian cover of the Euclidean plane}, a structure that is both intuitive and essential for understanding the authentic Jacobi group. Subsequently, we demonstrate that the {\em abelian Jacobi 1-cocycle}, a critical element in defining the Jacobi group, arises naturally from a specific function associated with a point on this cover. Finally, we derive the {\em Jacobi bundle} as a natural extension of the abelian cover. By presenting the authentic Jacobi group through the lens of this bundle, we illustrate how its elements can be concretely realized. We conclude by emphasizing that the abelian cover of the Euclidean plane serves as a valuable model for grasping the authentic Jacobi group. Furthermore, we note that this cover provides a natural framework for the {\em inhomogeneous quantum harmonic oscillator}, a system that is both intuitive and significant. We show that the {\em inhomogeneous propagator}, a fundamental component of the authentic Jacobi group, is naturally generated by the {\em inhomogeneous oscillator Hamiltonian}. Additionally, we demonstrate that the {\em inhomogeneous oscillator path integral} is naturally derived from the propagator, thereby establishing a clear connection between the authentic Jacobi group and the inhomogeneous oscillator. Ultimately, we contend that the abelian cover of the Euclidean plane offers a natural perspective on the authentic Jacobi group. This approach not only clarifies the group's definition but also reveals its deep relationship with the inhomogeneous oscillator. We anticipate that this perspective will prove valuable for future research. Specifically, we believe that the abelian cover of the Euclidean plane will serve as a useful model for the authentic Jacobi group, facilitating a more comprehensive understanding of the group's nonabelian extension. Furthermore, we anticipate that this framework will aid in elucidating the connections between the authentic Jacobi group, the inhomogeneous oscillator, and the rich web of relationships surrounding the authentic Jacobi bundle. We introduce a novel task: table-oriented fact verification, which involves confirming whether a specific assertion holds true based on data from a provided table. To accomplish this, we examine various strategies, including information retrieval, sentence disintegration, and their integration. We also compile a new dataset, TabFact, covering three validation scenarios. Experimental results demonstrate that leveraging both retrieved information and disintegration significantly enhances performance. Generative Confrontational Networks (GCN) are a class of generative adversarial models designed to create samples from complex distributions. While GCNs excel at modeling intricate data patterns, they often struggle with unstable training, which hinders their ability to reach the data manifold. This paper introduces a novel approach called Hidden Space Conditioning (HSC) to enhance GCN training. By utilizing an autoencoder to embed generated samples into a low-dimensional latent space, we can monitor and regulate the training process. Furthermore, HSC enables the generation of samples that lie closer to the manifold of the training data. Our experiments on the MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets demonstrate that our method consistently improves the training of GCNs. Additionally, we explore how the trained model can produce samples that were not present in the original training data, thereby expanding the manifold. These results indicate that our method successfully generates samples near the manifold of the training data. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/abhishekkumar12345/GCN_HSC. This work was conducted while the first author was a visiting scholar at the University of Notre Dame.

Phase samplers are compact oscillators that generate a phase signal, which, when integrated, produces a frequency signal. This mechanism is fundamental to phase-locked loops (PLLs) and is also utilized in the hierarchical sampling technique for measuring low frequencies. However, the phase of a PLL is susceptible to various noise sources, including quantization noise, jitter, and low-frequency phase noise. This study examines how different sampling strategies and phase sampler characteristics influence the accuracy of hierarchical sampling. The research begins by analyzing the impact of quantization noise, jitter, and phase noise on the sampling process. Subsequently, a model of hierarchical sampling using a phase sampler is developed, from which an expression for the root mean square (RMS) error is derived. Finally, an approximation for the RMS error is proposed to facilitate a more efficient comparison of different samplers. The paper concludes by comparing several phase samplers based on their respective advantages and limitations. Furthermore, a comparison between hierarchical sampling and direct sampling is provided, highlighting the suitability of each method for specific frequency ranges. Additionally, the influence of jitter on phase samplers is discussed, and a comparison of various samplers is made in the context of measuring frequencies affected by jitter. Ultimately, the study demonstrates that quantization noise is the primary limiting factor in hierarchical sampling, whereas jitter emerges as the main constraint in direct sampling. Consequently, hierarchical sampling is identified as the superior approach for measuring low frequencies. Finally, the effects of phase noise are examined, and a comparison of different samplers is presented regarding their performance under low-frequency phase noise conditions. The paper also addresses the impact of high-frequency phase noise, noting that while high-frequency noise can be filtered out in hierarchical sampling, it remains a significant limitation in direct sampling. The study further explores the consequences of aliasing in hierarchical sampling, and the effects of non-ideal samplers are analyzed. Ultimately, the research establishes that hierarchical sampling is the preferred method for low-frequency measurements, with quantization noise serving as the primary constraint. In contrast, for direct sampling, jitter is the most critical limitation. Additionally, phase noise is recognized as a significant factor in hierarchical sampling, whereas aliasing is the main constraint in direct sampling. Finally, the effects of non-ideal samplers are discussed, with the conclusion that the choice of sampling method depends on the specific application requirements. The paper also examines the impact of non-ideal samplers on hierarchical sampling, and the consequences of non-ideal samplers in direct sampling are analyzed. We introduce a resilient algorithm designed to assign non-negative integer distances to the vertices of a graph. This method leverages a specific class of distance-noncontractive taggers originally developed by Even-Zohar et al. (2018) for the problem of noncontractive embedding. We demonstrate that our tagger successfully handles edge failures within the standard Hamming metric. Furthermore, we establish that this approach achieves optimal resilience, meaning it can tolerate failures up to a number equal to the magnitude of the assigned tags. The algorithm operates in linear time, $O(m)$, where $m$ represents the graph's edge count. Additionally, we present a novel algorithm that constructs a $c$-noncontractive tagger for planar graphs with an Euler genus of $g$, requiring tags of size $O((g+1)c\log^2 n \log\log n)$, and proves its resilience against $O((g+1)c\log^2 n \log\log n)$ edge failures under the Hamming metric. This result surpasses the resilience of all existing noncontractive taggers for planar graphs. Our implementation runs in $O(m)$ time, improving upon the $O(mn)$ time complexity of previous methods. The proposed algorithm is straightforward to implement and utilizes only elementary data structures. Finally, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the algorithm's performance and resilience across various graph families. This paper investigates non-autonomous elliptic equations in divergence form within a measure space $(X, \mathcal{B}, \mu)$, where the underlying structure involves a current $T$ on $X$ with norm $\|T\| \leq C_0 < \infty$ and a symmetric, non-negative definite matrix field $A \in L^2(T; \mathcal{B})$. The study focuses on the solvability of equations defined by $L u := \mathrm{div}(A \nabla u) = \mathrm{div} f - \mu u$ for $u \in L^2(X, \mu)$. The matrix $A$ exhibits divergence-type regularity with respect to the specific measure $\mu$ and current $T$, implying that $A$ is not necessarily a function. Consequently, the operator $L$ is defined as a distribution. The analysis demonstrates that the operator $-L$ generates a strongly continuous contraction semigroup on $L^2(X, \mu)$, which is strongly analytic whenever $\mu$ is absolutely continuous with respect to the control measure of $T$. Furthermore, it is established that $L$ is a maximal monotone operator, thereby guaranteeing the existence of weak solutions. Additionally, the existence of distributional solutions is proven, contingent upon the specific form of the measure $\mu$ and the current $T$. Finally, the paper explores the connection between the Muckenhoupt $A_2$ condition and the solvability of these equations. A key innovation in this work is the development of a novel method for deriving Caccioppoli-type inequalities, which are essential for establishing semigroup properties. This method relies on a specific type of capacity, which is shown to be closely related to the capacity defined by the divergence-form operator $L$. The paper concludes with several examples illustrating the applicability of these findings. Notably, these results are applicable to the study of the Laplacian on the Heisenberg group equipped with a non-doubling measure, a topic addressed in a companion paper. Our results demonstrate that the distributional GP approach outperforms the probabilistic GP method, achieving state-of-the-art performance on a benchmark aneurysm detection dataset. Furthermore, we show that GPs offer a flexible and effective solution for anomaly detection in time-series data, with the distributional GPs specifically proving their utility in identifying out-of-sample anomalies. Finally, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the method's performance across various datasets. The Alexandrov Maximum Theorem serves as a fundamental instrument in the study of the Monge–Ampère equation, particularly within the context of Kähler geometry. This paper presents a refined version of the Alexandrov Maximum Theorem, establishing the uniform Hölder continuity of solutions to the Monge–Ampère equation subject to specific constraints on the right-hand side. Notably, this enhanced formulation of Alexandrov's theorem holds independent significance beyond its application to Kähler geometry. As a practical application, the authors derive the uniform Hölder continuity for the Kähler–Einstein–Atinger equation. The methodology employed relies on the technique of doubling variables, originally developed by Crandall, Ishii, and Lions. Furthermore, the authors demonstrate the Hölder continuity of the solution to a parabolic complex Monge–Ampère equation, thereby extending the applicability of the Alexandrov Maximum Theorem to parabolic settings. These findings generalize the results of Song and Tian. The primary innovation of this work lies in the direct application of the enhanced Alexandrov Maximum Theorem to address problems in Kähler geometry. Additionally, the authors introduce a novel approach to the Alexandrov Maximum Theorem that circumvents the need for the deep regularity theory of the Monge–Ampère equation, thereby simplifying the original proof. The paper concludes with a discussion of the limitations of this approach. Finally, the authors anticipate that the enhanced Alexandrov Maximum Theorem will prove valuable for other areas of Kähler geometry, including the study of special metrics and geometric flows. Optical clocks represent the most precise timekeeping instruments available. While current research predominantly focuses on their repetitive operation, non-repetitive modes offer distinct advantages for specific applications. This study characterizes the temporal structure of these optical clocks using both time and frequency domains. By analyzing the time-domain signal, we identify the primary noise contributions, which are subsequently modeled through a frequency-domain approach. This methodology is demonstrated using an optical clock based on a single $^{171}\mathrm{Yb}^{+}$ ion. The developed frequency-domain model is subsequently applied to other non-repetitive optical clocks. These models are constructed from experimental data via a straightforward fitting procedure, enabling the efficient characterization of optical clock performance. Furthermore, this approach facilitates the rapid assessment of new clock candidates and aids in identifying the dominant noise sources. Consequently, it supports the optimization of existing clocks and the design of future systems. The methodology is implemented using the Qucs-S circuit simulator. All necessary files, including the simulator and Python scripts for data processing, are publicly accessible. The code is designed to be easily adaptable for simulating other optical clocks. Additionally, the code is open-source and can be utilized to analyze experimental data from any optical clock. This enables researchers to compare the performance of their experimental setup against state-of-the-art systems. The analysis is performed using data from our laboratory's optical clock. We demonstrate that the proposed model accurately describes the clock's performance. Furthermore, we illustrate how this model can be employed to optimize the clock by adjusting various parameters. Finally, we discuss potential applications of non-repetitive optical clocks. These include measuring time-varying quantities, such as the gravitational potential of the Earth, and facilitating distributed quantum networks. The latter application leverages the quantum properties of optical clocks, which are essential for quantum information processing. We show that the quantum nature of optical clocks can be analyzed using the time-domain signal. This analysis is performed with the Qucs simulator, which is integrated into the Qucs-C quantum simulator. The code used for this analysis is also publicly available. We conclude that the time-domain signal of an optical clock contains valuable information regarding its performance. The model presented in this work allows for the efficient characterization of optical clock performance. We demonstrate that this model can be utilized to optimize the clock. We also show that the quantum nature of the clock can be analyzed using the time-domain signal. These findings suggest that non-repetitive optical clocks can be used for various applications, such as measuring time-varying quantities and supporting distributed quantum networks

This study introduces a fog-assisted software-defined network (SDN) framework designed to enhance service chaining (SFC) within fog computing environments. The proposed solution utilizes a distributed algorithm to optimize resource allocation for SFC services, incorporating collaborative failure recovery and fault mitigation mechanisms. By integrating asset management strategies, the system achieves energy efficiency. Furthermore, a distributed approach is developed to minimize the end-to-end delay between the service chain and the fog core. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed framework outperforms existing schemes in terms of reliability, fault tolerance, energy efficiency, and end-to-end delay. Additionally, the paper provides a comprehensive analysis of the algorithm's computational complexity. The simulation outcomes indicate that the algorithm operates in polynomial time. Finally, the study concludes that the proposed solution is highly suitable for real-time SFC services in fog computing. To the best of the authors' knowledge, this represents the first work to address the joint optimization of SFC, failure recovery, fault mitigation, and energy-efficient asset management within a fog-assisted SDN. This paper introduces a novel, controlled gradient manipulation technique designed to isolate the impacts of different loss function components. By applying this method, we demonstrate that standard loss functions, such as MSE, can be engineered to mimic the behavior of parametric alternatives like LSTMs. The study evaluates this framework across multiple domains, including classification, clustering, and recommendation systems. Our findings indicate that a carefully selected loss function can achieve performance on par with, or superior to, more sophisticated models. Furthermore, we show that these approaches are compatible with distributed training frameworks, such as TensorFlow's Parameter Server. Ultimately, we argue that loss functions play a more significant role in deep learning than previously recognized, and that this research offers a systematic framework for analyzing the effects of various loss functions within specific application contexts. The code for these methods is available at https://github.com/ashishgupta1997/Effect-of-Loss-Functions. Additional details can be found in our technical report at https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.00207.

This study investigates the three-dimensional distance distribution of fibers within the Galactic core, utilizing a sample of 1,000 fibers with a median parallax of 0.2 mas. The analysis employs the cumulative distribution function (CDF) and the probability density function (PDF) to characterize the distance distribution. The PDF is modeled using a two-component function, where the first component represents the dominant contribution from fibers with a distance $d < 100$ pc, and the second accounts for the remaining population. The parameters of this function are determined via a maximum likelihood estimation method. Additionally, the CDF is analyzed using a linear regression model. The research concludes that the mean distance between fibers is approximately 100 pc, and the PDF is effectively modeled by the aforementioned two-component function. These findings provide a quantitative description of the spatial distribution of Galactic core fibers, which can inform the design of future observational programs. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that the fibers are not randomly distributed in space. The implications of these results for the design of future Galactic core observation programs are also discussed. This work is part of a series; the companion paper will examine the radial velocity distribution of these fibers. This paper introduces an ideal conservation voltage reduction (CVR) scheme designed for primary-secondary integrated distribution networks. By lowering voltages and reducing power, distribution system operators (DSOs) can conserve energy, while end-users comply by adjusting their consumption to match reduced demand levels. The proposed distributed ideal CVR method enables local secondary DSOs to determine optimal voltage levels and switching configurations for energy savings without exchanging sensitive data with other local secondary DSOs or the primary DSO. This approach utilizes the ideal CVR model, which is more complex than standard models but yields superior results. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that this ideal model can be solved using a distributed subgradient algorithm, ensuring that all constraints are met. Simulation outcomes confirm the method's effectiveness in achieving ideal CVR outcomes within a distributed framework. Additionally, the paper explores the potential for extending this ideal CVR scheme to broader energy management applications. Finally, the study concludes by discussing current limitations and proposing future research directions. The paper is structured as follows: Section II presents the problem formulation; Section III details the proposed solution; Section IV provides simulation results; and Section V offers concluding remarks. This study examines a non-stationary bandit problem featuring arm-dependent lags, where pulling an arm temporarily removes it from selection for a specific duration. We demonstrate that a \emph{Specialist} algorithm, which dedicates itself to a single arm, can achieve a regret significantly lower than that of the \emph{Optimistic Index Policy (OSP)}, a well-established state-of-the-art online algorithm. Furthermore, we introduce a simple, efficient, and adaptive policy named \emph{NonRandom} that surpasses all current state-of-the-art methods. Our theoretical analysis relies on a novel concept called \emph{effective regret}, which we prove is upper-bounded by the classical regret metric. We also introduce a new parameter, $\kappa$, which quantifies the degree of non-stationarity and is essential for deriving regret bounds. This paper introduces a new framework for generating human-like text in dialogue. While current state-of-the-art systems excel at producing high-quality, contextually appropriate, and coherent responses, they often lack the emotional expressiveness and creativity found in human communication. To address this, we propose LEATHER, a new model designed to induce emotional expressiveness within a structured generation process. Our results demonstrate that the model successfully generates responses with higher emotional expressiveness, as validated by both quantitative metrics and qualitative assessments from human participants. Furthermore, we present an extensive analysis of the human ratings, which reveals that the perceived "human-likeness" of the generated text stems from the combination of emotional expressiveness and contextual appropriateness. This study employs linked Gaussian processes to create probabilistic models for predicting stress time histories and their spectral representations of offshore wind loads acting on turbine components. The methodology utilizes high-fidelity, time-varying wind-field data to generate stochastic surface and structural responses from an industry-standard aero-elastic simulation. The linked Gaussian process framework serves as a Bayesian surrogate for the original simulation, forecasting stress time histories and their corresponding power spectral densities. The resulting probabilistic proxy models are validated against the original simulation outputs and subsequently used to quantify uncertainties in wind-load statistics, including extreme values, probability distributions, and spectral parameters. These findings are applied to a specific offshore wind turbine scenario to illustrate the model's utility. The research demonstrates that the probabilistic proxy models achieve high accuracy in predicting stress time histories and spectral parameters, with a less than 1% discrepancy in power spectral density values. Furthermore, these models provide a robust means to quantify uncertainties in wind-load statistics, which is essential for assessing the reliability of probabilistic design methods. Ultimately, this study establishes a foundation for developing probabilistic tools that support the efficient design and risk assessment of future wind-turbine systems. The probabilistic proxy modeling approach is implemented via the linked Gaussian process framework, which is accessible through the open-source Python package, linkedgps. This framework is designed to be extensible for modeling various physical systems and is compatible with other modeling tools. The package includes a collection of example probabilistic proxy models for wind loads, alongside a framework for developing new models for different wind-load scenarios. These resources are available on GitHub at https://github.com/linked-gps/wind-load-models. The linked-gps package can be installed using pip with the command: pip install linked-gps. Additionally, the package includes example scripts that replicate the analyses presented in this study. Social media platforms have become integral to contemporary society, serving as vital channels for information dissemination. This study investigates the Izmir earthquake data from Twitter to analyze the event's impact and its connection to the platform. The primary objective is to identify the most active users and their locations, determine the languages employed in tweets, extract and visualize the core message, and assess the reliability of the information. The findings indicate that English is the most prevalent language in the dataset, followed by Turkish. The extracted key message reveals that the majority of tweets express sadness and sympathy for the earthquake's victims. Furthermore, the most active users are concentrated in Turkey, with the highest frequency of activity observed in Istanbul. These results align with the study's goals, confirming that Twitter serves as a significant source of information regarding the earthquake. The insights gained can assist researchers in extracting valuable data from social media for future research. Additionally, the methodologies employed can be applied to other natural disasters, such as floods, hurricanes, and fires. The study's limitations include the potential for unreliable information within the dataset, which could be mitigated by incorporating sentiment analysis. This paper investigates the $R_\infty$ property of generalized Baumslag-Solitar groups (GBS) by utilizing their nilpotent quotients. Specifically, we demonstrate that the torsion-free nilpotent quotients of acyclic GBSs retain the $R_\infty$ property. Furthermore, we extend our findings to GBs with torsion, proving that certain torsion-containing GBSs and their torsion-free nilpotent quotients both possess the $R_\infty$ property. These results are achieved through the application of a novel technique for counting inversions within braid groups. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the braid group inversion count required to establish these properties. Our work also includes a detailed examination of the $R_\infty$ property in torsion-free nilpotent quotients of specific GBSs, which were previously unresolved in the literature. We conclude by posing an open question regarding the $R_\infty$ property of general GBSs and their nilpotent quotients. Finally, we offer a characterization of the $R_\infty$ property for torsion-free nilpotent groups via their central series. Notably, this characterization relies on the properties of their nilpotent quotients, thereby generalizing findings from [10]. The study incorporates illustrative examples to elucidate these concepts. Our research was conducted within the framework of the 2022 Virtual International Conference on Algebra and Its Applications (VICA 2022). Time-resolved spectroscopy is a powerful method for monitoring how molecular systems evolve over time, yet extracting inversion data from these experiments is difficult due to noise, model errors, and the inherent ill-posed nature of the problem. This study introduces a forward-optimization strategy grounded in the geometric representation of the inversion process within a path-ensemble framework. By utilizing the mathematical properties of this framework, we develop a straightforward numerical approach that avoids complex algorithms. We validate the method's efficacy by applying it to time-resolved nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy, a key technique for tracking chemical reactions. The results demonstrate that this approach enables the rapid and accurate inversion of time-resolved data. Furthermore, the method is inherently extensible to other spectroscopic techniques, such as electronic spectroscopy, offering a promising avenue for future research. Context-aware naturalistic driving data is essential for investigating driver behavior and enhancing vehicle safety. However, existing datasets often fail to provide the necessary contextual details for precise behavioral analysis. To address this gap, we introduce SceNDD, a novel driving dataset featuring rich contextual information. This data was gathered using a custom-built in-vehicle system that logs driving trajectories, driver states, and surrounding context. The resulting dataset comprises 1,000 driving episodes, categorized into three scenarios: normal driving, near collisions, and intentional cuts. We evaluated the efficacy of various machine learning models for behavior analysis and scenario classification, demonstrating that combining sensor data with trajectory data significantly boosts classification accuracy. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that while vehicle sensor data is highly effective for crash prediction, video data is superior for classifying driving scenarios. The dataset is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2000/SceNDD. The accompanying paper can be found at https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.01000. This paper introduces a novel channel estimation framework designed for OFDM systems supporting reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RIS), specifically addressing the challenges of a flawed hardware reflection matrix and a deliberately shortened cyclic prefix (CP). The proposed method utilizes a single-antenna base station, a RIS, and a sparse array of RIS-reflecting elements to serve multiple single-antenna users. Channel state information is acquired during a training phase involving a sparse array of RIS-reflecting elements, followed by data transmission to the users. To overcome the limitations of existing methods, we propose an enhanced extreme learning machine (ELM) algorithm that accounts for the nonlinearity of the hardware reflection matrix and the reduced signal duration caused by a shortened CP. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed enhanced ELM achieves a 1 dB gain over the conventional ELM and a 2 dB gain over the least squares (LS) estimator. Furthermore, the enhanced ELM outperforms the conventional ELM by 1 dB in terms of convergence speed. Finally, the proposed enhanced ELM exhibits robustness against imperfect channel knowledge. Keywords: Channel estimation, RIS, OFDM, Cyclic prefix, Extreme learning machine, Flawed hardware.

This study introduces a non-invasive methodology to validate the IFt in freely diffusing individual particles, thereby eliminating the energy supply constraints inherent in prior IFt applications. To achieve this non-invasive approach, we developed a novel analysis technique that derives effective forces acting on particles from Brownian motion trajectory data. These forces are subsequently integrated to calculate the necessary minimum energy input. We validated this methodology by applying it to both computational models and experimental data regarding the diffusion of polystyrene beads in water. Our results demonstrate that the minimum energy input is contingent upon the specific system under study. Furthermore, we confirmed that the energy input derived from the IFt aligns with the energy consumption predicted by Brownian dynamics simulations. These findings establish a reliable framework for the non-invasive evaluation of the energy budgets of individual biological systems. Additionally, we demonstrate that the IFt can be validated without knowledge of the energy input by analyzing the time-reversibility of Brownian motion. This capability offers a novel approach for testing the IFt in biological systems, effectively circumventing the limitations of previous studies. We illustrate this by successfully testing the IFt in the diffusion of polystyrene beads within a microfluidic channel. Our findings indicate that the IFt holds true for the diffusion process, whereas it is violated when external forces are applied. These results provide a practical method for determining whether a biological system operates near thermodynamic reversibility. Finally, we show that time-reversibility can be quantified by analyzing the distribution of time-reversal entropy, a metric that offers a more intuitive interpretation of the IFt. This approach enables the quantification of irreversibility in biological systems, thereby offering a new perspective on the thermodynamics of biological processes. The Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID-19) has caused a global pandemic, prompting numerous nations to deploy contact tracing applications to curb its spread. This study evaluates the privacy safeguards of the Brazilian app Coronavírus-SUS, specifically its ability to protect the confidentiality of reported COVID-19 patients. We conducted a comprehensive analysis of the application's source code, revealing that it lacks mechanisms to prevent the leakage of sensitive user data. Our findings indicate that the app's design allows any registered user to identify and monitor the movements of other users. Consequently, we conclude that the app's architecture is fundamentally incompatible with the principle of individual privacy. Furthermore, we discuss the potential consequences of these design flaws and propose strategies to mitigate the associated risks. We hope this research raises awareness regarding the privacy implications of such applications and encourages future developments to incorporate privacy-preserving technologies. Additionally, we believe this work will stimulate further research into the privacy risks inherent in COVID-19 contact tracing applications. Quantum machine learning seeks to leverage quantum computing to address machine learning challenges, with a specific focus on algorithms that utilize quantum data. This study examines a specific application of quantum support vector machines (QSVMs) involving support vector data set completion, where missing data points must be reconstructed from existing ones. We demonstrate that certain problems within this domain cannot be solved efficiently by QSVMs, even when access to an arbitrary quantum data set is permitted. Furthermore, we establish that the quantum kernel employed in these protocols is not a positive definite kernel, indicating that the resulting quantum learning problem does not adhere to the standard definition. Consequently, we propose an alternative definition for quantum kernelized learning that encompasses these specific applications. Finally, we illustrate how this revised definition can be broadened to encompass a wider spectrum of learning tasks. Additionally, we explore the relationship between quantum kernelized learning and classical kernelized learning, showing that the former can be viewed as a generalization of the latter. This insight enables the identification of classical learning problems that can be solved more efficiently using quantum methods. This code creator generates syntactically valid C code, ensuring that the generated C program is semantically equivalent to its ACL2 representation. The author has also developed a new theorem establishing the correctness of this proof-generating code creator and integrated this correctness theorem into a more comprehensive correctness framework. This framework includes a theorem defining the semantics of our superficial C embedding and a more robust correctness assertion for the code-creating function. Our approach leverages the substantial body of existing theorems from a previous work on a theorem-based C program synthesizer to establish both the correctness of this new code-creating function and a related theorem concerning a different code-creating function. Additionally, we have proven a new theorem regarding that alternative code-creating function and extended its scope to cover a broader class of C programs. Our work also introduces a new theorem addressing soundness errors in C programs, which are utilized to strengthen both existing and newly developed theorems. The specific theorem discussed in this paper falls under the first category. A primary challenge in statistical learning theory is determining the capacity of a hypothesis space to represent functions over input data. In algebraic topology, the study of homology groups and cycles addresses analogous questions regarding the space's characteristics. This work introduces a methodology for applying algebraic topology to machine learning, specifically to analyze the topological structure of hypothesis spaces. Furthermore, we demonstrate the application of this methodology to kernel methods and support vector machines. Our findings indicate that the topological structure of these learning spaces is contingent upon the underlying data distribution. Additionally, we present a numerical simulation of the Ising model to explore the topological properties of learning spaces within statistical mechanics. Ultimately, our results suggest that algebraic topology serves as a valuable instrument for characterizing and comprehending various machine learning techniques. This framework not only offers a unifying perspective on established methods but also holds promise for guiding the design of novel approaches. Ultimately, we aim to leverage this framework to elucidate the relationship between learning spaces and generalization performance. By integrating algebraic topology with topological data analysis, we can investigate how data distribution influences the topological structure of learning spaces. This study investigates the angular distributions of $J/\psi$ mesons produced in association with charmonium states at $\sqrt{s} \approx 10.6$ GeV, specifically for the reactions $e^{+}e^{-} \to J/\psi + \eta_c$ and $e^{+}e^{-} \to J/\psi + \chi_{cJ}$ (where $J=0,1,2$). Utilizing the covariant constituent quark model alongside the potential one-loop correction framework, we compute the relevant cross sections and angular distributions at both leading and next-to-leading orders. Our results indicate that $J$-dependence in the angular distributions of $e^{+}e^{-} \to J/\psi + \chi_{cJ}$ persists even after incorporating one-loop corrections. Furthermore, the next-to-leading-order corrections significantly influence the production cross sections, necessitating their inclusion in future experimental analyses. Finally, we compare our theoretical predictions with existing experimental data. These findings offer valuable insights for the upcoming Beijing Spectrometer III experiment, which aims to explore the $J/\psi + \chi_{cJ}$ production process. Additionally, this work provides a reference for analyzing $J/\psi$ angular distributions in other hadronic reactions. Although the Signal app is a leading global encrypted messaging platform, its onboarding process remains a barrier for many potential users. This study investigates how existing Signal users perceive the app's PIN, a primary component of this process. We conducted in-depth interviews with 15 participants, analyzing their responses through a framework that examines three dimensions of PIN comprehension: knowledge (understanding of the PIN's purpose), attitude (views on the PIN's usability), and behavior (actions regarding the PIN during onboarding). Our findings reveal that while most users grasp the PIN's function, they often struggle with the specific onboarding steps, leading to frustration and a tendency to abandon the app. These results offer valuable insights for Signal's product and design teams to refine their onboarding strategy and enhance user acquisition. Furthermore, this research represents the first of its kind to explore end-user perceptions of a messaging app's PIN, a topic previously unexplored in the literature. We believe these insights will be valuable for other messaging applications seeking to improve their onboarding experiences. We develop a suite of quadrature rules, with the most precise being the Solar-Quadrature (SQ) family. This family encompasses high-order symmetric rules, including the Gauss rule, and low-order asymmetric rules, such as the Nyquist rule. The SQ family is constructed using node polynomials derived from generalized Chebyshev polynomials of the second kind. To determine optimal nodes and weights, we solve a system of nonlinear equations that correspond to the Stieltjes-Favard matrix associated with these polynomials. Furthermore, we establish necessary and sufficient conditions for the positivity of this matrix and for the existence and uniqueness of the associated quadrature rules. Finally, we apply the SQ family to integrate the probability density function of the random variable $X = \arcsin(U_1 + U_2)$, where $U_1$ and $U_2$ are independent and uniformly distributed on $[0,1]$. This application yields a highly accurate approximation of $P(X \leq \pi/2)$ with a negligible error of $10^{-14}$. The source code for the SQ rules is accessible at https://github.com/eduardogonzalez/SQ-rules. Additional resources, including a Mathematica package for symbolic computations and the Python package `pySQrules`, can be found at https://github.com/eduardogonzalez/SQ-rules/tree/master/SQrules. The Python package is also available on PyPI via `pip install SQrules`. The Mathematica package, however, remains under active development. This work is dedicated to Professor José M. Gutiérrez. This paper introduces the generalized Gauss-Newton matrix, a block-angular matrix that entry-wise characterizes the curvature of the objective function in nonconvex optimization. We demonstrate that the generalized Gauss-Newton matrix is low-rank in specific scenarios, including the blind image deblurring problem. Exploiting this low-rank property, we develop the ViViT algorithm, which utilizes a variable projection method to iteratively solve a sequence of rank-constrained least-squares problems. ViViT is proven to achieve linear convergence when applied to blind image deblurring. Furthermore, ViViT surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods on benchmark datasets, including the High-Frequency Blur Dataset and the Single Image Deblurring Benchmark. This study investigates how Grammatical Gender (GG) influences word embeddings within GG-labeling languages. We conducted a quantitative analysis of word vectors using three word2vec models trained on German, Russian, and Korean, which are selected for containing GG labels within their corpora. Our results demonstrate that GG significantly impacts lexical categories, particularly for animate nouns, and reveals distinct distributional patterns across these three languages. Furthermore, we examined the association between GG and semantic gender (SG), finding that while GG and SG are positively correlated, they are not equivalent. Finally, we explored the role of GG in embedding distortion, showing that it consistently affects GG-correlated categories and induces varying degrees of distortion across the three languages. These findings offer valuable insights for researchers working with word embeddings. The source code and pre-trained models are accessible at \url{https://github.com/ChenYi1998/GG-Embedding}. We demonstrate that for any locally compact, non-discrete group $D$ containing an open torsion-free subgroup, the group $\Gamma=\Gamma_D[G]$ constructed from a lattice $D$ in a simple Lie group and a finite-dimensional representation $G$ of $D$ is both charmable and rigid. Specifically, every finite-dimensional representation of $\Gamma$ is virtually conjugate to one defined on a lattice within another Lie group $D'$ associated with $\Gamma$. Furthermore, we establish that $\Gamma$ possesses the property $Q_{sep}$, signifying that it can separate points in any finite-dimensional space. These findings extend our prior work on representations of $SL_n(\mathbb A)$, where $\mathbb A$ denotes a locally compact totally real or $p$-adic field. Additionally, we present a novel approach to proving the point-separation property for lattices in $SL_n(\mathbb A)$. Our findings further imply that lattices in simple Lie groups are charmable and rigid, and that they can separate points in finite-dimensional spaces. The core technique involves the application of finite quotients of lattices, leveraging their substantial growth rates. This approach relies on the existence of lattices with large finite quotients, a property established by Burger and Kazhdan for lattices in non-discrete locally compact simple Lie groups. We also provide an alternative proof of this result specifically for lattices in $SL_n(\mathbb A)$. We introduce a new, straightforward method for estimating the positions of classes at the class-level zero-shot level. Our approach is straightforward: we first estimate the total count of each class, then synthesize a count map, and finally estimate the zero-shot class-level object response map by integrating the count map with a position prior. The efficacy of our method is validated across various object detection benchmarks, including COCO, KITTI, and Pascal VOC. Accurate traffic forecasting is essential for traffic management and control, yet it remains a difficult challenge. While deep learning models have been widely adopted, they typically depend on extensive data and struggle to generalize to unseen scenarios. To overcome these limitations, this paper introduces a novel, data-efficient framework for forecasting traffic flow across an extensive network. The method leverages the similarity among traffic networks at different locations to enhance prediction accuracy. Specifically, it extracts latent traffic attributes from an extensive sparse network using graph neural networks and temporal convolutional networks. These attributes capture the unique characteristics of each location, while the shared connectivity within the graph allows for the modeling of inter-location relationships. The proposed framework is demonstrated to significantly outperform existing approaches in terms of both accuracy and computational efficiency. The code is accessible at: https://github.com/ChenYi1997/Similarity-driven-Attribute-Extraction. The dataset can be downloaded here: https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1222222222222222222222222222222222222222. Future research will explore applying this framework to other domains, such as weather forecasting and disease prediction. We also plan to investigate how to incorporate additional information, including weather data and event schedules, to further boost performance. Finally, we will examine the impact of varying graph structures on the model's effectiveness. The authors thank the reviewers for their insightful comments and constructive feedback. Graphs serve as a universal method for representing and reasoning about complex systems, where nodes signify entities and edges denote their relationships. While graph representation learning has achieved significant success in learning representations for both entities and relationships, the graph system itself remains largely unlearned. In contrast, recent research on causal graph learning has demonstrated the potential to infer the unknown structure of a graph system. This paper introduces VACA, a new framework designed to learn the graph system—including nodes, edges, and its underlying causal structure—by integrating insights from representation learning and causal learning. VACA employs a causal graphical model to represent the graph system and utilizes a variational autoencoder to approximate this model. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach through various tasks, such as graph completion, intervention prediction, and counterfactual inference. Experimental results indicate that VACA can effectively reconstruct the graph system from a subset of nodes and edges and successfully predict the outcomes of both interventional and counterfactual queries. Real-time monitoring of the sky's transient population is a critical objective for modern radio telescopes. The LOw Frequency Array (LOFAR) in the Netherlands, originally designed for high-resolution imaging, has recently been adapted to detect radio transients. Concurrently, the Irish LOFAR facility (Ireland Low Frequency Array, ILOA) has been established in Ireland, featuring a dedicated backend named REAL-time Transient Capture (REALTA). This system is engineered to identify radio transients in real-time, enabling follow-up observations and archival storage. We present the initial results from REALTA, which were collected over a period of 10 days in late 2021. These early findings demonstrate the system's capability to detect both known and new transients, including Fast Radio Bursts (FRBs), the Fast Radio Burst afterglow from GRB 200424A, the Fast X-ray Burst from 4U 1820-30, the radio jet from the blazar 3C 273, and the radio flare from the supermassive black hole Sgr A*. Furthermore, we have identified a new repeating FRB, designated FRB 20211029A. This research underscores the significance of REALTA for both the transient community and the broader astronomical field. Additionally, we outline the future development of REALTA, which includes enhancing its sensitivity and expanding its field of view. Ultimately, these advancements aim to facilitate the study of FRBs and other radio transients, thereby advancing our understanding of the early Universe. The convergence of machine learning and photonics has driven the creation of numerous intelligent devices and systems. As a promising frontier, metaphotonics combines the advantages of metamaterials and machine learning to achieve superior performance. This review examines recent progress in metaphotonics, highlighting how integrating learning algorithms with light-matter interactions enables the design of high-performance smart systems. We begin by outlining the fundamental principles of metaphotonics, followed by a summary of its core components: data preparation and learning algorithms. Subsequently, we explore the latest developments in this field, including smart optical materials, metamaterials, and their constituent elements, as well as intelligent sensors and imaging systems. Finally, we discuss future prospects and potential applications for metaphotonics. This overview aims to inspire further research into the synergistic combination of metamaterials and machine learning. Keywords: Metaphotonics, Metamaterials, Machine learning, Intelligent devices, Intelligent systems. This paper introduces CurvedData, a novel dataset comprising 10,000 feature films from 1990 to 2019, sourced from IMDb. While existing datasets in this domain are significantly smaller, CurvedData offers a robust foundation for both clustering and classification tasks. Its unique structure allows for the analysis of various film attributes, including genre, director, actor, and production company. Furthermore, the study examines how pre-released features—such as trailers, reviews, and social media buzz—influence a film's box office performance. The findings indicate that pre-released materials do not guarantee commercial success, though they can generate significant interest. Ultimately, the research concludes that while pre-released features are valuable, they should not be the sole determinant for marketing strategies. This conclusion is supported by statistical analysis, clustering, and regression studies conducted on CurvedData. The dataset is accessible at https://github.com/curveddata/curveddata. Additionally, the authors have developed a Python package, curveddata, which facilitates data exploration and analysis through a collection of functions and classes. This paper introduces a model for a power system that incorporates auxiliary frequency regulation (AFR) devices, which link local frequency and voltage behaviors through a node-wise, nonlinear, and generally asymmetric function. The analysis covers both infinite bus (IB) systems and weakly synchronous networks. For a specific subset of AFR devices, the authors demonstrate that these findings extend to weakly synchronous systems as well. The study derives analytical expressions for steady-state voltage levels, investigates local stability, and utilizes a Lyapunov function to prove asymptotic stability under certain conditions. Additionally, the impact of AFR on oscillatory modes is examined, with results indicating that these devices can either enhance or diminish system damping. Finally, the paper presents a specialized AFR scheme designed to maintain positive voltages in a broader range of operating conditions. Simulation results are included to validate the theoretical analysis. The proposed AFR scheme is formulated as an optimization problem, where a dual-based algorithm is developed to solve it efficiently. This approach enables the calculation of AFR parameters with minimal impact on voltage and frequency dynamics, while ensuring the achievement of desired voltage levels at all buses. The effectiveness of this scheme is demonstrated through simulations on a 30-bus system. Furthermore, the study explores the influence of AFR parameters on system dynamics and proposes a method for selecting appropriate parameters based on a specific metric. Finally, the paper outlines potential extensions of this work. The results presented herein are drawn from the first author's PhD thesis [1].

The rise of cyberphysical systems (CPS) has driven the development of networks composed of these systems. However, current CPS are typically reactive, relying on external inputs to function. To address this, we propose a new class of cyberphysical systems characterized by cognition, termed cyberphysical systems with cognition (CPC). This paper introduces a comprehensive framework for CPC, detailing their fundamental characteristics, underlying cognitive architecture, and a formal mathematical model. We demonstrate that a CPC network exhibits emergent behaviors, such as self-organization, which are not present in traditional CPS networks. Furthermore, we outline a methodology for designing and implementing such networks, supported by a proof-of-concept example. The work concludes by discussing the potential applications of these cognitive systems within the context of a CPC network.

Keywords: Cyberphysical systems, cognition, design, implementation, cyberphysical systems with cognition.

The origin of the ultraviolet (UV) and soft X-ray excess in blazar spectra remains a debated topic, with two primary hypotheses: (i) thermal emission from the broad-line region (BLR) in type-1 active galactic nuclei (AGN), or (ii) partially polarized radiation generated by inverse Compton scattering (ICS) of UV photons by relativistic electrons within the jet. To distinguish between these mechanisms, we propose a testable prediction: the flux ratio between soft X-rays and UV ($F_X/F_{UV}$) should exhibit an inverse correlation with the degree of UV polarization ($P_{UV}$) if the excess arises from ICS. Specifically, hard X-rays produced by the upscattering of UV photons by relativistic electrons in the jet are expected to be more polarized than the UV photons themselves. We developed a Monte-Carlo framework to simulate the joint evolution of electron populations and photon fields, incorporating radiative cooling, adiabatic expansion, and photoionization. Our results indicate that the predicted inverse correlation between $P_{UV}$ and $F_X/F_{UV}$ is robust across various jet models and electron distribution assumptions. Furthermore, we applied this model to the AGN Mrk 421, which is known to display time-variable, highly polarized UV emission. Our simulations successfully reproduce the observed $P_{UV}$ versus $F_X/F_{UV}$ relationship, suggesting that the UV/X-ray excess in Mrk 421 is likely of non-thermal (ICS) origin. Additionally, our model accounts for the observed anti-correlation between $P_{UV}$ and flux ($F_{UV}$), a phenomenon that would be difficult to explain if the UV excess were BLR in origin. These findings support the hypothesis that ICS of UV photons by the jet electron population is a viable mechanism for producing the UV/soft X-ray excess in blazar spectra. Finally, we demonstrate that the proposed test can be applied to other AGN with sufficient photometric and polarimetric data. This analysis may help identify which sources are suitable for future investigations using the polarimetric capabilities of the upcoming Chandra Polarimetry Polarimeter (CHAMP). Such studies could provide critical insights into the nature of the UV/soft X-ray excess in AGN spectra. This study is the second in a series; the first, which details the Monte-Carlo model and its implementation, is available as \cite{2021MNRAS.500.

We present a method for creating an analytic extension of Cauchy's integral formula for the product of two functions, tailored to the specific requirements of geophysical data inversion. This approach utilizes the Generalized Cauchy Integral (GCI), which relies on the sampling theorem and the z-transform, alongside the Generalized Hilbert Transform (GHT). The GCI and GHT are implemented using the Lanczos algorithm, which offers superior accuracy compared to the traditional trapezoidal rule. The GCI is further extended to accommodate complex-valued terrains, a capability that proves essential for modeling electromagnetic data inversion in geologically complex environments. To validate the effectiveness of this analytic extension, we applied it to a 2.5D modeling scenario involving a complex terrain. The results demonstrate that the method achieves high computational efficiency, as evidenced by a significant reduction in calculation time. Furthermore, the precision of the solution is confirmed by the consistency of the imaginary part of the electromagnetic response, which remains below $10^{-10}$. These findings indicate that the proposed analytic extension is both highly accurate and effective for geophysical data inversion. We introduce a novel mechanism for baryon formation, termed "splintering," which occurs when a highly excited, helical string—possessing a wavy profile and significant internal energy—undergoes quantum decay into a lower-energy string and a particle-antiparticle pair. This process, which can yield mesons or baryons, is derived using a simplified model of a strongly coupled, quantized QCD string. The resulting analytical formula for the splintering rate aligns with the qualitative predictions of the corresponding classical equation. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this mechanism can account for the creation of baryon-antibaryon pairs observed in high-energy proton-proton collisions. Additionally, we find that the splintering rate is comparable to the rate of pair creation from the vacuum via strong quantum fluctuations of the string. This finding contradicts the classical expectation that splintering is the dominant channel for baryon formation. Consequently, our findings suggest that the conventional picture of baryon creation, based on the classical Schwinger mechanism, requires significant revision. Finally, we outline the necessary extensions to our model to incorporate backreaction effects and to apply it to realistic QCD strings. These generalizations are anticipated to provide a more accurate description of the string dynamics governing baryon formation. Our results also indicate that the quantized splintering mechanism may play a crucial role in the formation of baryonic matter in the early universe. We conclude by discussing the potential implications of this mechanism for the baryon asymmetry of the universe. Our findings suggest that the quantized splintering mechanism could be a key factor in explaining the observed baryon asymmetry. Solar active regions generate significant magnetic flux concentrations that drive strong currents and intense flows. This study examines how currents within these regions influence helioseismic travel-time measurements, specifically their impact on north-south bias. We analyze the contributions of currents located above active areas to helioseismic travel-time perturbations, utilizing a 1D magnetohydrostatic model of an active region to determine current strength. These values are then integrated into a 3D model of an active region situated above the solar surface to calculate travel-time perturbations. Our results indicate that the contribution of currents above active regions to the north-south bias in helioseismic travel times is negligible. Consequently, the observed bias is likely driven by other mechanisms, such as the interaction between solar rotation and surface currents. This finding supports the hypothesis that the north-south helioseismic bias is not caused by large-scale currents within active regions. Furthermore, our analysis demonstrates that the amplitude of currents above active regions is comparable to that of currents within the convection zone, suggesting that the latter may be a more probable source of the north-south bias. Finally, we explore the potential link between this bias and the solar magnetic field. We conclude that the north-south helioseismic travel-time bias is likely rooted in the solar interior rather than the surface. This conclusion is reinforced by the fact that the amplitude of currents above active regions is comparable to interior currents, and by the correlation between the north-south bias and the solar magnetic field's helicity. These results suggest that the solar surface is not the origin of this bias. Additionally, our findings align with recent research indicating that the north-south helioseismic travel-time bias is linked to the solar magnetic field and its associated helicity. Overall, this study underscores the critical role of currents in active regions in shaping helioseismic travel-time measurements. Our results provide a foundation for future research into the origins of the north-south bias and its connection to solar helicity. The pulsar timing spectrum (PTS) is defined as the range of pulsar timing residuals that cannot be explained by the Solar System ephemeris or Galactic and local gravitational potentials. This work investigates the potential of a pulsar timing array (PTA) to detect a gravitational wave background (GWB) linked to the stochastic evolution of magnetic fields. We demonstrate that a PTA is capable of identifying a GWB arising from the helical instability of ancient magnetic fields. Specifically, we establish that a next-generation PTA can achieve a signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of 3 within a 10-year observation period, provided the initial magnetic field strength is approximately $10^{-10}$ G and the gas density is around $10^{-24}$ g/cm$^3$. Furthermore, we show that a high-resolution PTA can detect this GWB in just 1 year under the same initial conditions. Our findings indicate that the detectability of this GWB is independent of the specific PTA configuration, as long as the array is optimized for the frequency range of the PTS. Additionally, we note that the SNR is directly proportional to the number of pulsars in the array and their spatial separation. We also examine the impact of the initial pitch angle, revealing that a lower pitch angle results in a higher SNR. Finally, we explore the possibility of distinguishing the helical background from other sources, such as supermassive black hole binaries (SMBHBs), by analyzing the polarization of the background. We find that the polarization of the binary background is primarily determined by the sky position of the SMBHB, whereas the polarization of the helical background is governed by the pitch angle of the initial magnetic field. These results suggest that polarization data can be utilized to constrain the properties of the initial magnetic field. Additionally, we propose that polarization data could serve as a valuable tool for characterizing the initial magnetic field. Finally, we suggest that the polarization of the binary background could be employed to constrain the orientation of the SMBHB's orbit. This paper introduces a learning-driven, multi-stream model for compressing light field (LF) images, which are inherently high-dimensional and difficult to compress. The approach separates spatial and angular information using a multi-stream architecture. To effectively capture spatial details, we employ a multi-scale encoder that aggregates data from various resolutions. Furthermore, to address the high dimensionality of angular information, we apply a series of autoencoders to extract compressed disparity representations. These spatial and angular components are then combined into a unified LF model through a spatial-angular fusion module. Additionally, we propose a new LF image quality metric that integrates spatial and angular fidelity, demonstrating a strong correlation with human visual perception. Extensive experiments across diverse LF datasets confirm that our method achieves superior compression performance compared to several state-of-the-art techniques.
