Interactive frameworks have demonstrated superior performance compared to non-interactive ones in various multilingual and cross-language information retrieval (CRIR) scenarios. However, current methods rely on ad-hoc strategies for selecting queries to present to users, lacking a principled approach. This paper introduces a novel method that leverages the strengths of both interactive and non-interactive paradigms. Specifically, it employs an interactive mechanism to choose non-presented queries, utilizing a new metric called "relevance gap." This metric quantifies the potential performance improvement achievable through user interaction and identifies which documents to prioritize for display. Experimental results indicate that this approach yields performance gains over existing methods. Furthermore, the study demonstrates the method's effectiveness across multiple languages, including English, French, and Spanish. This study introduces two estimation techniques to address the underestimation of cardiovascular disease (CVD) risks in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), a critical issue for public health planning. The first method, a model-focused approach, integrates country-specific covariates into the Global Burden of Disease (GBD) statistical model to forecast national-level CVD risks. The second, a design-focused approach, utilizes nationally representative survey data to estimate regional CVD risks. We applied these methods to forecast CVD risks in Bolivia, an LMIC, using the Demographic and Health Surveys (DHS) dataset. Results indicate that national CVD risks in Bolivia are higher than the GBD 2016 estimates, with the model-focused method showing a 10% increase over the original GBD 2016 levels. Furthermore, the model-focused approach produced more accurate estimates than the baseline GBD 2016 for all age groups, with the improvement becoming more pronounced in older populations. When comparing national versus regional estimates, the study found that the DHS-based regional assessment yielded lower CVD risks than the model-focused projections. These findings suggest that the GBD 2016 dataset may have underestimated CVD risks in LMICs, particularly among older adults. Additionally, the study highlights the necessity of incorporating country-specific covariates into the GBD model and the urgent need to collect and publish regional-level data to enhance small-region CVD risk estimation. This paper introduces a novel framework for developing quantum strategies within the Kelly Wager game. In this game, a quantum information carrier engages in repeated betting rounds against a casino, utilizing the fluctuations in a specific physical observable to determine stakes. While previous continuous variable strategies relied on the position observable, we demonstrate that the quadrature observable—which encompasses both position and momentum—yields a superior strategy. This enhanced approach enables the carrier to simultaneously exploit fluctuations in both conjugate variables, thereby achieving a higher average logarithmic return per round compared to existing methods. This optimal quantum strategy is applied to model classical casinos using a collection of continuous harmonic oscillators, as well as to quantum systems such as the electromagnetic field and the angular momentum of spin systems. We illustrate that for these modeled systems, the carrier can achieve non-zero logarithmic returns even when the casino operates with zero house edge. Furthermore, we establish that the strategy's performance is independent of the system's initial state, a distinct characteristic that sets it apart from other quantum wagering games. Finally, we examine the conditions under which the carrier can secure a positive logarithmic return despite the casino imposing a house edge. These findings are particularly relevant for analyzing scenarios involving continuous variable systems that are not strictly confined to the classical domain. Specifically, we show that the carrier can extract a return from a photon number state casino, a result that underscores the quantum nature of the proposed strategy. Additionally, we explore the relationship between the wagered observable and the system's uncertainty, revealing that the strategy is particularly effective when the chosen observable exhibits significant uncertainty. This insight is especially valuable for angular systems, where the strategy can be implemented using the angular momentum observable, which is intrinsically linked to angular uncertainty. These results suggest that the casino must possess precise knowledge of the system's state to prevent the carrier from extracting a return. Finally, we demonstrate that the strategy can be realized using a single harmonic oscillator, thereby eliminating the need for the initial entanglement required in earlier continuous variable strategies. This adaptability highlights the robustness and broad applicability of the proposed method across various quantum systems. Transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) have garnered significant interest for their unique electronic and optical characteristics, including band gap tunability, valley selectivity, and strong spin-orbit coupling. Recently, the class of materials known as monolayer group-IV monochalcogenides (MA$_2$Z$_4$) has emerged as a promising alternative to conventional TMDs, offering comparable two-dimensional properties alongside distinct features such as a non-zero Berry curvature, robust spin-valley locking, and band gaps that can be either indirect or direct. These attributes make MA$_2$Z$_4$ compounds highly attractive for applications in spintronics and optoelectronics. In this study, we utilize density functional theory to investigate the electronic and optical properties of MA$_2$Z$_4$ monolayers, specifically examining how variations in the metal atom (M) and anion atom (Z) influence their characteristics. Our findings indicate that the quasiparticle energy alignment between MA$_2$Z$_4$ and TMDs can be adjusted by selecting the appropriate constituent atoms. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the direct excitonic transition in MA$_2$Z$_4$ is stacking-independent, a trait that sets it apart from the direct excitonic transitions observed in TMDs. These results provide valuable insights for the design and development of optoelectronic devices utilizing MA$_2$Z$_4$ materials. Additionally, our analysis of the direct excitonic transition in MA$_2$Z$_4$ offers a deeper understanding of the optical properties of two-dimensional materials. The primary source of material for protoplanetary disks and solar system planets is the collapsing molecular cloud core that forms a prestellar object. This study investigates the potential for the prestellar core to directly generate a circumstellar disk. We model the disruption of a prestellar nucleus by a supernova shock wave, which fragments the core into a chain of dense clumps. These clumps collapse sequentially, creating a chain of protostars. The dense gas chain connecting these protostars is compressed by their gravitational fields into a disk-like structure. As the protostars evolve, they accrete matter from this disk, and the disk itself grows over time. We demonstrate that a prestellar object can naturally produce a disk with a mass comparable to the protostar and a radius of approximately 100 AU. The temperature within the disk is estimated to be around 1000 K, which is sufficient to vaporize silicates and ices, thereby supplying the necessary material for planet formation. This mechanism offers a straightforward explanation for the observed high gas-to-dust mass ratio in young stellar objects. Furthermore, the disk generated by this process is more massive than those formed via standard accretion, making it a promising candidate for the formation of super-Jupiter planets. This research suggests that the prestellar phase is a critical stage in the evolution of the solar system. The model's simplicity and its ability to explain several observational features indicate that the destruction of prestellar nuclei by supernova shocks is a common phenomenon. Consequently, the formation of the solar system likely occurred in a region of the molecular cloud heavily influenced by supernova activity. This finding has significant implications for the theory of panspermia. Additionally, the model provides a straightforward explanation for the existence of interstellar objects like 'Oumuamua and Borisov, which are believed to have an extrastellar origin. The paper concludes with a discussion of the implications of these findings. Atmospheric scattering significantly influences the appearance of celestial bodies, yet its complexity and dependence on atmospheric parameters make it challenging to model. This study introduces a novel method for characterizing scattering atmospheres using on-sky observations. We conducted a series of observations of the gas giant Jupiter across various phase angles to derive an atmospheric model. By analyzing the relationship between the phase angle and the scattering phase function, we determined the single scattering albedo and the asymmetry parameter. Furthermore, we applied the simplified adding-doubling method to generate synthetic images of Jupiter. The resulting model parameters align with existing literature, and the synthetic images successfully reproduce the key features of actual observations. This approach offers a straightforward and efficient means of characterizing atmospheric properties, which is particularly valuable for the imaging of exoplanets. We introduce a novel multi-term temporal sequence modeling approach designed to handle temporal dependencies of varying orders. This method employs an autoregressive framework where each term utilizes a distinct probability distribution to capture temporal order, with Bayesian Variational Inference (BVI) serving as the training mechanism. By leveraging the flexibility of diverse distributions, the model effectively learns temporal dependencies of different orders. Furthermore, we propose a sparse BVI technique to mitigate overfitting caused by the complexity of the multi-term structure. Experimental results on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods. This brief note aims to provide a more intuitive and conceptual understanding of Pontryagin dualism and its connection to Blum's work on continuous reasoning. While Pontryagin dualism establishes an equivalence between the category of topological abelian groups and the category of topological abelian groups, it is also valuable to consider it through the lens of duality in the sense of contravariant functors. From this perspective, we can derive a straightforward proof of Blum's conjecture. Furthermore, we will demonstrate that the claim of continuity in Pontryagin dualism is not only false but also fundamentally incompatible with this continuity requirement. Specifically, we will show that the dualization functor is discontinuous when equipped with a natural topology on the category of functors. Finally, we will outline an alternative dualization that satisfies continuity and possesses additional beneficial properties. Although this conceptual approach may lack the rigor of traditional proofs, it offers a more profound insight into the nature of dualization. We hope that readers will find this understanding more intuitive and beneficial for their own work. Additionally, this note may serve as a foundation for future research into continuous dualization. Federated learning (FL) is a machine learning approach designed to train models across multiple clients while safeguarding data privacy through confidentiality. This study investigates the impact of varying confidentiality levels on FL, specifically analyzing how differential confidentiality influences the model's fairness regarding sensitive client attributes. We demonstrate that FL models trained under differential confidentiality exhibit bias, whereas those trained with robust confidentiality mechanisms like secure multi-party computation (SMPC) maintain robustness. Furthermore, we introduce a novel confidentiality mechanism that surpasses the limitations of both differential privacy and SMPC. Our findings indicate that this proposed mechanism not only enhances the confidentiality of the federated training process but also improves the overall performance of the resulting FL model. Experimental results confirm the efficacy of this new mechanism, and we provide a theoretical analysis of the privacy guarantees offered by FL models when utilizing it. Finally, we examine the trade-off between model performance and privacy within the context of this proposed confidentiality framework. This paper introduces a new wireless network architecture that integrates intelligent reflecting surface (IRS) and wireless energy harvesting (W EH) to enhance throughput. The system operates in two distinct phases: first, the base station (BS) transmits a combined signal containing both data and energy to all users; second, active users who have harvested sufficient energy from the BS assist the network by reflecting BS signals toward the intended receiver to boost quality of service (QoS). To manage this two-phase operation, we propose a novel unsupervised learning method that jointly optimizes the phase shift matrix of the IRS and the users' energy harvesting rates, thereby maximizing the network's throughput. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the resulting throughput maximization problem is non-convex and non-concave. To address this, we develop a deep neural network (DNN) that learns the optimal solution from a large dataset of randomly generated parameters. Extensive simulations confirm that the DNN achieves significant throughput improvements compared to existing state-of-the-art schemes. Additionally, we prove that the proposed DNN approach is provably convergent. Finally, we show that the DNN exhibits strong generalization capabilities when tested on parameters outside its training distribution. Our results indicate that the proposed DNN outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in terms of throughput. We introduce a unified framework that interconnects the dark substance and leptogenesis. In this model, the dark matter candidate is the lightest neutralino, which is a substantial mixture of singlino and higgsino states. The dark matter abundance is primarily generated through coannihilation processes involving a nearly mass-degenerate right-handed smuon. Simultaneously, the required baryon asymmetry arises from the decay of a heavy right-handed neutrino, with the smuon acting as a crucial intermediate state. We demonstrate that a viable dark matter candidate can coexist with the observed baryon asymmetry within a specific parameter region. Furthermore, we show that a high-mass dark matter scenario is feasible, provided the mass of the heavy right-handed smuon is degenerate with that of the dark matter particle. Finally, we explore the connection between these two fundamental issues and discuss the potential for detecting the dark matter signal at the High-Luminosity LHC. Additionally, we examine the possibility of explaining the excess events detected by the IceCube collaboration within a specific sub-region of the parameter space. Reinforcement learning (RL) has demonstrated significant potential for deriving control strategies from data, yet it often demands extensive trials to reach a satisfactory policy. This paper introduces a data-informed control framework that accelerates the learning process by integrating supplementary information into RL. This additional knowledge, derived from data collected via simpler methods or human expertise, is embedded within the policy network to establish an informed initialization. This approach reduces the number of required learning trials and enhances the policy's interpretability. We validate this method by training a single network to execute four distinct locomotion tasks—swimming, walking, walking on uneven terrain, and flying—using data from simple controllers or human insights. The proposed framework successfully replicates these behaviors while achieving higher rewards and greater data efficiency compared to standard RL baselines. Furthermore, it exhibits superior performance in learning to walk on uneven terrain, a capability that baseline models fail to achieve. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2000/DIC. This work investigates Ward relations within conformal quantum theory, specifically focusing on a two-dimensional Toda model based on the Lie algebra sl(3). We establish Ward relations for sl(3) and explicitly calculate them using a basis of local sl(3)-invariant operators. Furthermore, we demonstrate that local Ward relations can be derived from global Ward relations. Finally, we examine specific local Ward relations and their potential utility in computing the three-point functions of primary fields. Additionally, we explore the connection between Ward relations and monodromy matrices. This research serves as a generalization of our earlier study on the sl(2) Toda model. Our findings are supported by explicit calculations performed with the computer algebra system FORM. The paper includes an appendix detailing the construction of local sl(3)-invariant operators. Recent advancements in Connection Networks have introduced a novel, highly efficient architecture for processing relational data, surpassing prior state-of-the-art methods. Concurrently, Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in modeling complex distributions, including those of natural images. This study seeks to integrate these two fields by training Connection Networks within a GAN framework. We propose training a Connection Network discriminator using a triplet loss to enhance the learning of the image distribution. Our approach yields two primary benefits: first, the adversarial training of the network significantly boosts the sample accuracy of the generator; second, the generated samples exhibit greater diversity. We validate the efficacy of Relation GANs with triplet loss across three datasets, achieving state-of-the-art results on MovieNet and GoogleNet and competitive performance on IMDB-5K. Furthermore, we provide qualitative evidence of improved sample diversity. The code is accessible at https://github.com/abhishekgupta1997/RelationGANs.

Twin-field quantum key distribution (TF-QKD) has recently become a leading solution for long-distance quantum communication, surpassing the Shannon limit by utilizing an interferometric setup where remote users share a random local oscillator phase. This same interferometric principle can be applied to twin-field quantum key exchange (TF-QKEx), enabling the secure transmission of quantum keys alongside qubits. TF-QKEx offers the potential to extend quantum communication channels beyond the Shannon capacity, making it a viable alternative to classical communication methods. However, the reliance on local oscillators in TF-QKEx necessitates phase synchronization between remote users, a process that is highly complex and susceptible to errors. This study presents a practical TF-QKEx protocol that eliminates the need for phase synchronization, thereby significantly simplifying the system architecture. We demonstrate that this approach maintains security levels comparable to those achieved with phase synchronization. Furthermore, we show that the performance of our proposed protocol is similar to that of the original TF-QKEx scheme. These findings indicate that TF-QKEx can be implemented without phase synchronization, substantially reducing hardware complexity. Additionally, we outline a future experimental setup for TF-QKEx that operates without phase synchronization. This research paves the way for the practical deployment of TF-QKEx, which can be integrated into existing quantum communication systems to transmit quantum keys alongside quantum information. TF-QKEx is expected to play a crucial role in the future development of quantum communication networks. Our proposed scheme is currently being tested in a laboratory setting. Identizing objects with open vocabularies is a core challenge in computer vision, essential for practical applications. While current methods rely on learning fixed vocabularies of common objects, they struggle to generalize to rare or unseen items. This paper introduces a novel approach that enables models to recognize a broader range of objects by utilizing pseudo bounding-box annotations. These annotations are automatically generated from image captions, which describe both open-world and common objects. We demonstrate that these pseudo boxes can be effectively integrated into existing models to enhance their ability to detect diverse objects. Our experiments show that this method significantly improves the accuracy of open lexicon identification models. Furthermore, we evaluate our approach on the newly released Visual Genome dataset, achieving state-of-the-art results. The code and data required to reproduce these results are publicly available at https://github.com/visg/lexicon-pseudo-boxes. We conducted a multi-wavelength analysis of the PDR gas, ionized gas, and atomic gas associated with the S1 cluster in the Rho Ophiuchus cloud. Utilizing archival data from the Hubble Space Telescope (HST) and the Spitzer Space Telescope, alongside new observations from the VLT and ALMA, we mapped the spatial distribution of ionized gas (via [O III] 5007 Å), atomic gas (via $^{12}$CO J=2-1), and PDR gas (via [Fe II] 1.644 $\mu$m and [C II] 158 $\mu$m). Our findings reveal that the ionized gas distribution is asymmetric, extending 0.2 pc along the cluster's rotation axis, whereas the atomic gas is more symmetric and confined to a smaller region. The PDR gas exhibits a morphology similar to the ionized gas but is shifted toward the cluster's rotation axis. We propose that the ionization of the PDR gas is driven by the S1 cluster's rotation axis, which aligns with the cloud's magnetic field. Furthermore, the PDR gas appears to shield the ionized gas from the atomic gas, while the atomic gas shields the PDR gas from the ionized gas. The PDR gas is likely heated by the cluster's UV radiation field, with its morphology shaped by the magnetic field and the cloud's internal pressure. Finally, the atomic gas is predominantly heated by cosmic rays, a process that is less efficient than PDR heating. These results suggest that the heating mechanisms for ionized, atomic, and PDR gas are distinct, and that the PDR gas may play a critical role in the thermal balance of the cloud. Additionally, the PDR gas could be the primary source of the [Fe II] 1.644 $\mu$m emission observed in the cloud. The differing thermal structures of these gas components may influence the evolution of the cloud and the S1 cluster. This study underscores the necessity of observing the cloud across multiple wavelengths to understand the heating and thermal balance of its gas. Future research should focus on the interplay between the cloud's magnetic field and the PDR gas, as well as the impact of PDR gas on the cloud's thermal equilibrium. The remarkable success of the Transformer architecture in Natural Language Processing (NLP) has sparked significant interest in applying it to Computer Vision (CV). This survey reviews recent advancements in integrating Transformers into Sight, offering a comprehensive overview of current research. We begin by examining the foundational Transformer architecture and its core mechanisms, followed by a detailed analysis of various adaptations, such as Vision Transformers and Vision-and-Language Models. Furthermore, we evaluate performance across key CV domains, including image classification, object detection, segmentation, and image generation. Finally, we discuss open challenges and potential future directions for Transformer research in CV. This survey serves as an essential resource for researchers and practitioners navigating the evolving landscape of CV and AI. The associated repository can be found at https://github.com/ashishkumar2000/Transformers-in-Sight. The review is also available in Spanish at https://github.com/ashishkumar2000/Transformers-in-Sight/blob/main/Transformers-in-Sight-Spanish.pdf. This study employs a factor model to forecast mortality rates, deriving common factors from the Lee-Carter framework using principal component analysis. We evaluate whether time-varying or time-constant factor loadings yield superior mortality predictions. Our results indicate that time-varying loadings significantly enhance forecast accuracy, particularly for longer life expectancies. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this enhanced performance is more pronounced in countries with higher forecast errors. Finally, we apply the method to predict mortality rates in China, revealing that life expectancy for both men and women will surpass 80 years by 2050. Additionally, the gap between male and female life expectancies is projected to narrow, reaching approximately 3.5 years. These findings underscore the necessity for policymakers to prioritize health and social security investments to mitigate the adverse social and economic impacts of an aging population. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2019/Mortality_Prediction. The data utilized in this research can be found at https://github.com/ChenYi2019/Mortality_Prediction/tree/master/Data. Given the open-source nature of our work, the methodology is easily adaptable for forecasting other countries' mortality rates. We encourage researchers to replicate our findings to validate the robustness of our approach. Finally, we welcome any comments or suggestions. Neural Architecture Exploration (NAE) has recently demonstrated remarkable success in automating the creation of neural networks for image classification. However, the high computational costs associated with training and evaluating these architectures have hindered their widespread adoption. To address this, researchers have developed various techniques to reduce the time required for searching image classification models. This paper investigates the root causes of disruption in NAE and introduces a novel method to mitigate it. Our approach involves a new metric designed to predict the disruption level of an architecture, which is calculated using a small, pre-trained, and lightweight convolutional neural network. We evaluate this metric across three NAE scenarios, demonstrating that it effectively anticipates disruption in each case. Leveraging this metric, we propose a new strategy to alleviate disruption by reusing the features of architectures known to be non-disruptive. Experimental results confirm that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance, delivering up to 2.5x speedup and 1.5x accuracy improvements compared to existing state-of-the-art approaches. The code is available at https://github.com/DeepLearningResearch/Examining-and-Alleviating-Disruption-in-NAE. Furthermore, we have released a new Python library, NAE, to facilitate the use of our methods, which can be installed via pip install NAE. The library is hosted at https://github.com/DeepLearningResearch/Examining-and-Alleviating-Disruption-in-NAE. Finally, we have made our trained models available for download at https://github.com/DeepLearningResearch/Examining-and-Alleviating-Disruption-in-NAE/tree/master/models. We establish that a proper geodesically complete CAT(0) square complex $X$ with fundamental group $\Gamma$ cannot simultaneously satisfy the following conditions:
  1. $|\Gamma| \leq |\Vtx{X}|$;
  2. $\Gamma$ acts freely on $X$;
  3. $\Gamma$ acts minimally on $X$; or
  4. $\Gamma$ acts cocompactly on $X$ and possesses a center of order $1$ or $2$.
  Additionally, we demonstrate that an infinite fundamental group acting cocompactly on a proper geodesically complete CAT(0) square complex must have abelianization of order at least $3$.
  We further prove that each of these four limitations extends to geodesically complete nonpositively curved $4$-dimensional Riemannian manifolds.
  Finally, we examine the analogues of these findings for geodesically complete CAT($\kappa$) environments.
  As a corollary, we show that a proper geodesically complete CAT($\kappa$) environment $X$ with $\kappa < 0$ and fundamental group $\Gamma$ cannot have $|\Gamma| < |\Vtx{X}|$.
  This resolves a question posed by P. Glickenstein and provides a partial answer to a query by J. D. Hamilton.
  The proof relies on a novel application of the Morse lemma to geodesic spaces.
  Additionally, we present a new proof of a theorem by J. Anderson and T. Baird, which characterizes the fundamental groups of compact nonpositively curved manifolds as precisely those that are minimally non-amenable.

  We further establish that the isometry group of a proper geodesically complete CAT($\kappa$) environment $X$ is amenable if and only if $X$ is isometric to a finite-dimensional Euclidean space.

This paper introduces a novel approach to assessing translator performance, designed to overcome the inherent limitations of the traditional, one-dimensional fluency-based evaluation. We propose a framework that integrates fluency scores with translator-specific information, such as their source language, to enhance the reliability of the assessment process. Within this framework, we utilize a Bayesian method that synthesizes fluency scores with information from multiple previous evaluations of the same translator. By modeling the translator's performance as a random variable, we calculate a dependability score that indicates the likelihood of consistent future performance. We demonstrate that the scores generated by this framework exhibit a strong correlation with human judgments of performance. Furthermore, we show that the framework's performance improves as more evaluations are incorporated. Finally, we offer recommendations for applying this framework in both research and industrial contexts. The code required to replicate our results is accessible at https://github.com/abhishekgupta1997/Dependability-Evaluation.

We establish sum rules for energy absorption across the entire spectrum of energy loss in inelastic scattering processes, specifically within both quantum mechanical and semi-classical regimes. These sum rules are derived using general formalisms applicable to any open system where a projectile interacts with a target, resulting in the absorption of energy and the emission of secondary particles. The approach is sufficiently broad to encompass quantum mechanical descriptions of electronic excitation in atom-atom collisions, as well as semi-classical models for particle absorption in matter. Notably, the derived sum rules remain valid even when multiple channels are open, regardless of whether they are directly or indirectly accessible. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the ratio of total absorption cross sections for a specific inelastic channel between two different projectiles is independent of the specific properties of the projectiles themselves. This result follows from a fundamental property of the S-matrix, which implies that the sum rules for total absorption cross sections for any given inelastic channel are universal. Consequently, these derived sum rules can serve as valuable tools for testing the accuracy of various theoretical models and numerical simulations regarding energy absorption in inelastic collisions. Additionally, we apply this formalism to the optical theorem and its extensions to multichannel systems, revealing a novel sum rule for the total absorption cross section in inelastic electron-atom collisions. Finally, we discuss the connection between these sum rules and the energy-weighted sum rules found in nuclear physics. In this context, we derive a general sum rule for energy absorption in inelastic scattering, which holds true for both quantum mechanical and semi-classical frameworks. This finding is particularly significant for ion-atom collisions, where it enables the calculation of total absorption cross sections for inelastic channels without requiring knowledge of the projectile's internal structure. We also examine the relationship between energy absorption and the momentum-weighted sum of response functions, a concept central to sum rules in nuclear physics. Finally, we illustrate the utility of these sum rules by comparing the total absorption cross sections for inelastic electron-atom collisions against various theoretical models. Our analysis indicates that the sum rules are well-satisfied by the theoretical predictions. However, we observe that the sum rules are not well-satisfied by experimental data, a discrepancy that may be attributed to the limited energy range of the available measurements. This conclusion is supported by an analysis of the energy-weighted sum rule, which exhibits a similar pattern of deviation. These findings underscore the critical need for high-precision measurements of inelastic scattering cross sections to accurately test the sum rules for ion-atom collisions. Fully connected neural networks, characterized by extensive parameter counts and high-dimensional weight spaces, often struggle with overfitting, necessitating the sifting of critical attributes from the initial weight initialization. This study examines the sifting process through the lens of the Winning Ticket Hypothesis, which posits that a small, randomly selected subnetwork within a fully connected network can replicate the performance of the fully connected counterpart when trained from the same initial weights. By utilizing the sparsity of subnetworks to represent the transition from fully connected architectures to their distilled components, we demonstrate that the sifting process is intrinsically linked to the sparsity of subnetworks. Furthermore, we reveal that the fully connected network does not necessarily contain the optimal subnetwork required to achieve the performance of its pruned, sparse architecture. Finally, we explore the relationship between subnetwork sparsity and the complexity of the sifting process. These findings offer valuable insights for future research aimed at enhancing the efficiency of weight sifting. The code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi1998/Sifting. We introduce a two-temperature model that accounts for valley and phonon temperatures within a valley-phonon system, specifically focusing on interaction mechanisms in two-dimensional materials. This framework is applied to silicene, a two-dimensional semiconductor featuring highly anisotropic electron-phonon coupling. Our findings indicate that the relaxation dynamics of both valley and phonon temperatures are governed by the anisotropy of the electron-phonon coupling. Additionally, we demonstrate that the valley temperature remains stable against phonon decay channels. These results offer a quantitative framework for analyzing the complex dynamics of phonons and valleys in two-dimensional substances. Furthermore, the proposed model is applicable to other two-dimensional materials, including transition metal dichalcogenides, where it can aid in the design of valley devices. Finally, the methodology employed is versatile and can be utilized to investigate electron-phonon coupling in various other two-dimensional materials. This competition addresses a significant challenge in unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA): the absence of labels in the target domain. To mitigate this, existing methods typically align the source and target domains to minimize distribution discrepancies. However, these approaches often overlook differences in visual importance, leading to performance degradation. Multidimensional scaling (MDS) serves as a powerful tool for visualizing high-dimensional data by mapping data points into a lower-dimensional space while preserving their relative distances. However, conventional MDS methods are ill-suited for data residing on a sphere, such as orientation and spherical harmonics, because Euclidean space cannot accurately represent spherical relationships. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel approach that adapts MDS for spherical data. Our method, Spherical Neighbor Embedding (VMF-SNE), substitutes the Gaussian kernel used in standard techniques with a Von Mises-Fisher (VMF) distribution, which is defined on a sphere. By employing the von Mises-Fisher distribution to calculate distances between points on a sphere, we ensure more accurate distance preservation. We demonstrate the efficacy of VMF-SNE across various spherical information processing tasks, including spherical orientation representation, classification, and clustering. Furthermore, we evaluate its performance against existing state-of-the-art methods for representing spherical orientation. The experimental results confirm that VMF-SNE effectively learns spherical orientation representations and surpasses current state-of-the-art approaches. Quantum emulation of fermionic systems is a critical step toward achieving a quantum advantage in simulating quantum chemistry. While the quantum phase estimation algorithm is the standard approach, it demands extensive quantum error correction, pushing current noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) processors beyond their capabilities. Our findings indicate that the resulting fermionic state can accurately predict the ground state energy of the system. This method is expected to significantly advance the investigation of strongly correlated fermionic systems within the NISQ era. Hitchin provided an explicit formula for the relation that characterizes the moduli space of Higgs bundles associated with the $A_2$ quiver. Specifically, we show that the monodromy representation corresponding to a Hitchin relation is, up to a conjugation within $\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb{R})$, equivalent to the Veech relation derived from an affine translation surface. Furthermore, we establish that the Hodge locus defined by the Higgs bundle with a Hitchin relation remains invariant under conjugation in $\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb{R})$. These findings offer fresh perspectives on the interplay between Higgs bundles and translation surfaces. Additionally, we present several examples of Veech relations and their respective Hodge loci. This result confirms a conjecture proposed by the second author in [BZ20]. We also provide a conjecture and an example illustrating the scenario where the Hodge loci of a Veech relation and its corresponding stratum of holomorphic differential forms are disjoint. This paper investigates how distributed teams impact the success of Scrum projects. By analyzing data from 127 Scrum initiatives across 27 companies within the Brazilian software sector, we examined 22 specific practices. Our findings indicate that remote work does not inherently increase the likelihood of project success; instead, success is driven by how effectively teams manage communication and coordination. We observed that successful remote teams place a stronger emphasis on these factors compared to their on-site counterparts. Furthermore, we identified that the most critical practices for remote success involve fostering a strong team culture, ensuring clear role assignment, and implementing regular team reviews. These insights offer valuable guidance for managers aiming to enhance the performance of remote Scrum teams. Additionally, we highlight that certain practices, such as daily stand-ups, are less critical for success in a remote context than in an on-site one. This research is unique in its application of both ordinal and binary logistic regression to study the success factors of distributed Scrum teams. The study's limitations include a sample size of 127 projects, a single-industry focus, and data collection via an online questionnaire. This paper presents an algorithm for computing the persistent homology of colorful alpha complexes. Unlike traditional alpha complexes, which are minimal vertex covers for the second barycentric covering, colorful alpha complexes are constrained to use only one vertex per simplex's original cover. This study examines the maximum potential GDoF loss resulting from the limitation of power control to binary levels in interference networks. We demonstrate that the extremal GDoF gain of optimal power control over its binary counterpart is $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$ for specific network topologies, where $K$ represents the number of users. This finding indicates that the previously established lower bound of $\Omega(\sqrt{K})$ is tight up to constant factors for these extremal cases. Furthermore, we identify that these topologies share a common structural characteristic: the existence of a user whose interference channels are sufficiently strong to render all other users' transmissions effectively irrelevant. We also present several additional topologies that adhere to this property and achieve the same extremal GDoF gain, with the previously analyzed case being a subset of these. Additionally, we establish a lower bound of $\Omega(\log K)$ for the GDoF loss of binary power control in other network topologies and provide a tight upper bound of $O(\log K)$ for the two-user case. Finally, we propose a conjecture suggesting that the extremal GDoF gain of optimal power control is bounded by $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$ across all network topologies. The proofs in this work rely on a novel technique that converts interference networks into equivalent bipartite graphs, enabling the application of established results from graph theory. This methodology may offer a promising avenue for future research in this area. This paper investigates the computational requirements for managing the execution of multiple tasks. Specifically, we examine a real-time multitasking system where an external scheduler sequentially assigns each task to a shared computing resource. We analyze the relationship between a task's execution time and its input size, demonstrating that this relationship is not necessarily linear. Furthermore, we explore the link between a task's output size and its input size, noting that the output can be significantly larger than the input. We show that both multitasking management and input-output size considerations are critical when designing scheduling algorithms. Our primary contribution is the introduction of a new computational model that simultaneously accounts for multitasking management and shared resource usage. This model incorporates input and output sizes, as well as computation time, into a unified framework. We present a problem within this model that is closely related to the well-known Bin Packing problem. Finally, we demonstrate that the specific nature of computation and storage in this model renders the standard First Fit algorithm ineffective. To address this, we propose a new algorithm and prove that it achieves an asymptotically optimal approximation ratio. Additionally, we extend this approach to a more complex scenario where tasks may require preliminary processing before their primary computation. We provide an approximation algorithm for this extended problem and establish a lower bound on the ratio between the number of resources used by our algorithm and those required by an optimal solution. Our analysis indicates that this lower bound is asymptotically tight for this general case. We conclude by discussing the model's relevance to real-world scenarios, such as parallel computing and distributed systems. These environments often face challenges including network latency, bandwidth limitations, and the need for task pre-processing, all of which are addressed within our proposed model. We believe this model offers a valuable framework for analyzing the resource efficiency of multitasking management systems. Our findings suggest that the techniques developed in this paper can be applied to a wide range of multitasking problems, leading to more efficient resource utilization. We hope this work will inspire further research into the theoretical foundations of multitasking management and their practical applications. We introduce a new algorithm for this model that achieves an optimal approximation ratio, and we discuss its potential applications in parallel computing and distributed systems. This paper presents a model for the dynamic behavior of a monopod, including its base, capable of leaping across granular media. The system is modeled as a single degree-of-freedom (SDOF) mass-spring-damper framework where the damper represents a non-linear spring interacting with the granular medium. We developed a mathematical model for the monopod's interaction with the granular surface and conducted numerical simulations to assess its dynamic response. Our findings indicate that the proposed model accurately replicates the observed response of the monopod on yielding terrain. Furthermore, we identified that the initial displacement of the monopod serves as a critical parameter for determining the required input energy to traverse the granular surface. Finally, we demonstrated that the monopod can successfully leap over the surface by applying a specific amount of input energy. These results offer valuable insights for the design of mobile robots intended for such environments. Additionally, we propose that the robot's mobility can be enhanced by adjusting the mass of the system. The proposed model and these results are expected to be valuable for researchers in the field of robotics. The complete code is available at: https://github.com/ahmed-ibrahim/leaping-monopod. Over-the-air (OTA) software updates are essential for the widespread adoption of Internet of Things (IoT) devices, yet they introduce significant risks to system reliability. To address this, our paper introduces a dependable OTA update mechanism leveraging Long-Term Evolution (LTE) technology, designed to mitigate the potential failures associated with the process. We implemented this mechanism in a real-world environment and evaluated its performance within an extensive-scale IoT mesh network. Our experimental results demonstrate that the proposed solution effectively handles the challenges posed by a complex mesh network, ensuring that OTA updates occur with zero system outages. Furthermore, we show that the mechanism maintains system reliability even when OTA operations fail, while also reducing the time required to update the network. Additionally, our approach enables the concurrent updating of multiple device classes, thereby eliminating the need for network partitioning. We contend that this method offers a practical and scalable dependable OTA update strategy for IoT mesh networks. The corresponding source code is accessible at https://github.com/dependable-iot-software-upgrades. To our knowledge, this represents the first extensive-scale evaluation of a dependable OTA upgrade mechanism for LTE-based IoT devices. The paper is structured as follows: Section II reviews related work; Section III details the system model; Section IV presents the OTA update mechanism; Section V describes the experimental setup; and Sections VI and VII discuss the experimental results and conclude the study, respectively. Finally, Section VIII outlines the paper's contributions. We investigate the transition from many-body localization (MBL) to delocalization in the disordered Fermi-Hubbard model, which occurs at a critical disorder strength $D_c$ known as the MBL shift. We demonstrate that the spreading rate of Fock-space propagator wavepackets, characterized by the exponent $\theta$, exhibits a universal scaling behavior near $D_c$. Specifically, $\theta$ approaches a universal value of $\theta^* = 0.5$ as the system size $N$ increases, following the relation $\theta^* = \lim_{N\rightarrow\infty} \theta(D_N)$, where $D_N$ denotes the disorder strength corresponding to a fixed distance from the critical point in the thermodynamic limit. Furthermore, we find that the multifractal spectrum $f(\alpha)$ displays a universal profile near $D_c$, with the spectrum's width increasing linearly with the system size. These findings indicate that the universal scaling of the spreading rate and multifractal spectrum persists well beyond the MBL-delocalization transition. Additionally, we show that the scaling of the spreading rate aligns with the multifractal spectrum derived from the spectral singularity spectrum. These results provide strong support for the existence of a universal critical point situated at the MBL shift. Finally, our study offers a quantitative analysis of the finite-size scaling of the shift, yielding an estimate for the subleading correction to the system size dependence of $\theta$. These conclusions are corroborated by extensive numerical simulations. Our findings suggest that the shift represents a genuine finite-size effect in the thermodynamic limit, with the universal critical point becoming accessible only when the system size is sufficiently large. This insight is crucial for the accurate characterization of the delocalization transition and the universal critical properties of the thermodynamic system. We also discuss the implications of our results for the experimental observation of the MBL-delocalization transition. Specifically, we show that the universal scaling of the spreading rate can be observed experimentally when the system size is large enough to be close to the critical point. This provides a practical guideline for future experimental studies of MBL and its critical properties. We conclude by discussing the potential applications of our findings to other quantum many-body systems. Our results suggest that the shift is a generic phenomenon that can be observed in a wide range of quantum many-body systems, providing a framework for the study of the universal critical properties of the thermodynamic system. This paper addresses the challenge of visiting numerous target locations using a large fleet of mobile robots, where each vehicle is assigned a specific maximum travel distance. The mission involves an interactive element, as target visitations occur sequentially rather than simultaneously. We introduce the concept of the cost-limited interactive exploration problem (CLIEP) and demonstrate that it is closely linked to the metric multidimensional matching problem. Consequently, we show that CLIEP is NP-hard and proves that, under the standard complexity assumptions P ≠ NP and FNP ≠ FP, no fully polynomial-time approximation scheme exists for it. Furthermore, we propose a novel algorithm capable of producing a solution within a factor of 2.5 of the optimal cost. Finally, we validate the effectiveness of this algorithm through simulations involving the exploration of multiple target areas by robot fleets. Experimental results indicate that our proposed method outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches. The code is accessible at https://github.com/ashishkumar12345/CLIEP. Additionally, a video of the associated experiment can be found at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=22222222222. Quantum machine learning (QML) has emerged as a promising avenue for investigating the computational capabilities of quantum computers. Although QML models are anticipated to match the performance of their classical counterparts, they have received comparatively less attention regarding adversarial robustness. This paper introduces the first framework for generating adversarial instances and disturbances tailored to quantum classifiers. We demonstrate the utility of this framework by creating adversarial examples for a quantum perceptron and by proposing disturbance generation techniques based on both classical and quantum adversarial training methods. Furthermore, we establish the relationship between classical and quantum adversarial distances via a novel concept known as quantum adversarial sensitivity. Finally, we provide numerical evidence indicating that the proposed framework effectively identifies adversarial instances and disturbances within the feature spaces of quantum classifiers. Additionally, our results show that the quantum perceptron is more resilient to adversarial instances than its classical equivalent, while adversarial training enhances robustness against quantum disturbances. However, we observe that the quantum adversarial sensitivity is significantly higher than in the classical case, suggesting that quantum classifiers may be more sensitive to adversarial inputs. These findings are supported by numerical experiments. The source code for this framework is available at: https://github.com/QuantumAIResearch/Classical-and-Quantum-Adversarial-Instances-and-Disturbances-for-Quantum-Classifiers. This study examines Steklov eigenvalues within two families of three-dimensional domains: the deformed spheres parameterized by Legendre polynomials and the mean curvature dumbbell domains. Our findings indicate that, in both scenarios, the Steklov eigenvalues exhibit linear behavior, consistent with observations in convex settings. Furthermore, the corresponding eigenfunctions maintain compact support within the interior of each domain. We also demonstrate that the Steklov problem on these domain families can be formulated as a system of ODEs, which is computed using the collocation method. The paper concludes with an analysis of the condition number of the resulting linear system and its implications for the method's accuracy. Finally, we establish that the spectral condition number for the discrete Steklov problem on the sphere scales as $O(h^{-2})$, where $h$ represents the mesh size. These results suggest that the collocation method may not be the optimal choice for computing Steklov eigenvalues. To address this, we introduce a novel approach utilizing the Nyström method, which demonstrates superior accuracy. Our numerical experiments confirm that this new method is highly effective for both spherical and non-spherical domains. Additionally, we explore the relationship between Steklov eigenvalues and the geometry of the underlying domain. By leveraging the computed eigenvalues, we derive a new isoperimetric inequality specifically tailored to dumbbell-shaped regions. Our results indicate that the spectral properties of these dumbbels are more sensitive to their geometric shape than those of other domains with comparable volume. Finally, we examine the spectral behavior of the discrete Steklov problem on the sphere, presenting a spectral analysis of the discrete operator and its connection to the continuous spectrum. We also discuss the spectral properties of the discrete Steklov matrix. The paper ends with a discussion on the spectral graph theory of the discrete Steklov problem. These conclusions are supported by extensive numerical experiments. Overall, our work provides a comprehensive analysis of Steklov eigenvalues and eigenfunctions across various geometries, offering new insights into their spectral properties. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 reviews the Steklov problem and its variational formulation; Section 3 derives the ODE system for the Steklov problem on deformed spheres; Section 4 presents the numerical results; and Section 5 discusses the spectral graph theory of the discrete Steklov problem. Conformance checking evaluates the extent to which system behavior aligns with a process model. While infix and postfix alignments offer efficient methods for calculating trace fitness, they often struggle to deliver detailed diagnostic information. To address this, we introduce infix-postfix alignments, a novel class of full alignments that blend characteristics of both existing approaches. These infix-postfix alignments are specifically designed to generate diagnostic data comparable to that of full alignments. Furthermore, they enable the efficient computation of trace fitness using an algorithm based on infix-postfix distance, which offers significant computational advantages over standard full alignments. Additionally, the paper demonstrates the practical utility of infix-postfix alignments in advanced techniques such as indeterminate conformance checking and the integration of external knowledge. Finally, an implementation is provided, and various case studies are conducted to assess its performance. The results indicate that the proposed approach achieves computational efficiency on the order of magnitude better than full alignments. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/fernando-garcia/infixpostfix. The accompanying case studies utilize process models from the German insurance industry, the German automotive sector, and the European Space Agency. These models are derived from real-world scenarios involving invoice processing, car rental services, and satellite data processing, respectively. The case studies employ extensive trace datasets comprising 10,000 traces, with lengths ranging from 100 to 1,000 events. In contrast, the examples used to illustrate the techniques involve much shorter traces. This paper introduces a deep convolutional neural network (DCNN) model designed to simulate the radio transmission characteristics of cellular networks. The model accepts a 2D image as input, representing the network layout where pixel intensity corresponds to building height, and generates an output image depicting the Equivalent Path Loss Exponent Map (EPLEM). We developed two distinct DCNN architectures, 3D-DCNN and 2.5D-DCNN, which differ in the dimensionality of their internal feature maps. Both models were trained using a dataset of 3D city layouts paired with their corresponding EPLEMs. Extensive experiments were conducted to evaluate the models' performance and scalability. The results indicate that the 3D-DCNN achieves an average pixel-wise accuracy of 99.1% and a mean squared error of 0.001. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that DCNNs offer a more efficient alternative to traditional ray-tracing methods for radio propagation modeling. Finally, we outline potential future research directions regarding the application of deep learning in cellular network simulation. This work establishes the rigorous semantics for both a temporal planning language and its corresponding planner, which are verified within the same logical framework. This study examines the sensitivities of low-carbon energy system growth models, which are frequently employed to design future energy infrastructure. We develop a model featuring an endogenous investment schedule and analyze how variations in key parameters influence system growth. Our findings indicate that the model is highly sensitive to assumptions regarding the cost of capital, the rate of technical progress, and the discount rate. Consequently, the capital cost of energy systems and the pace of technology advancement are critical determinants of the transition to low-carbon economies. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this model framework is sufficiently flexible to be applied across a broad spectrum of energy systems. Ultimately, we argue that model sensitivities must be rigorously analyzed to ensure the reliability of policy recommendations derived from energy system growth models. This paper investigates the global-in-time well-posedness of the Vlasov-Poisson system within bounded domains featuring absorbing or reflecting boundaries. We establish existence and uniqueness of solutions for both nonlinear systems and those with modified collision operators, addressing challenges related to boundary singularities and particle confinement. Furthermore, we demonstrate the stability of linear systems and explore applications in plasma physics, specifically deriving a linear Fokker-Planck equation from the linearized Vlasov-Poisson system under reflecting boundary conditions. This derivation utilizes the theory of semigroups on Banach spaces to prove the existence of a unique solution and the stability of the corresponding adjoint system. Additionally, we provide a global existence result for the linear Vlasov equation with absorbing boundaries and linear background charges, supported by appropriate estimates. Finally, we outline an iterative scheme to prove the well-posedness of the nonlinear Vlasov-Poisson system under reflecting boundary conditions. The present study represents the first global well-posedness result for the Vlasov-Poisson system with absorbing boundaries in a confined region. Furthermore, it marks the first global well-posedness result for the Vlasov-Poisson system with reflecting boundaries in a confined domain that does not rely on small initial data assumptions. Our methodology extends to the Vlasov-Maxwell system under electric boundary conditions and to the full Maxwell-Poisson system in three dimensions. The findings are applicable to both steady-state and time-dependent problems. The study begins with an analysis of the linear problem, followed by an examination of the nonlinear problem. Finally, we present numerical simulations of the Vlasov equation with absorbing boundaries in a bounded domain. These simulations employ a finite element method for spatial discretization and a backward differentiation formula for temporal integration, demonstrating that the numerical solution remains stable over time. The work concludes with a discussion of the results and potential future research directions. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 presents the problem formulation; Section 3 provides a preliminary analysis of the problem; Section 4 establishes the well-posedness of the linear problem; Section 5 analyzes the linear problem with a modified collision operator; Section 6 addresses the nonlinear problem; and Section 7 presents numerical simulations. Ultrasonic standing waves can induce significant shifts in the mechanical properties of colloidal gels. In this study, we demonstrate that applying a continuous ultrasonic field during the aggregation of a polystyrene latex suspension in a glycerol matrix can continuously and reversibly modify the gel's mechanical characteristics. Specifically, the gel's storage modulus can be tuned across a broad spectrum, spanning from that of the liquid phase to approximately 100 Pa. We propose that this rheo-acoustic softening stems from the formation of a nonequilibrium acoustic gel, where particles arrange into linear chains aligned with the ultrasonic wave. Furthermore, we investigated the gel's evolution kinetics under both acoustic and non-acoustic conditions, revealing that the aggregation process is markedly slower within the acoustic field. Finally, we examined the gel's structural organization using small-angle light scattering, finding that the acoustic field suppresses the development of large-scale fractal structures. These findings offer new insights into the dynamics of colloidal gels and their potential applications. Additionally, they suggest that ultrasonic fields could serve as a tool for controlling the mechanical properties of colloidal gels.

The Collatz Conjecture remains an unresolved mathematical mystery, positing that any positive integer $n$ will eventually reach 1 through a simple iterative process. For each iteration, if the current value is even, it is halved; if odd, it is multiplied by 3 and incremented by 1. The conjecture asserts that this sequence invariably terminates at 1, a claim supported by the fact that all tested numbers up to $10^{10}$ do indeed converge. This paper aims to elucidate the conjecture and provide a proof utilizing automata theory. Specifically, it demonstrates that for any $n$, there exists a finite deterministic automaton with an initial state equal to $n$ that generates a sequence converging to 1. This approach offers a novel perspective grounded in computational theory, potentially facilitating a more intuitive grasp of the problem. The study begins with a review of fundamental automata concepts, followed by an examination of the conjecture's history and an analysis of its validity through specific examples. The core of the argument establishes the automata-based proof, which represents a significant contribution to the literature. The paper concludes by discussing the conjecture's implications and suggesting avenues for future research. By leveraging the principles of automata theory, this work provides a fresh and promising avenue for comprehending the enduring enigma of the Collatz Conjecture. Ultimately, this methodology not only proves the conjecture but also opens new possibilities for investigating its intricate nature. Ultimately, this research offers a unique and valuable contribution to the ongoing quest to solve this timeless puzzle. The findings have the potential to inspire further exploration and innovation in the field of number theory. Classifying STEM documents is a critical step for building domain-specific language models. However, existing methods often fail to yield satisfactory results, and their underlying causes are not well understood. This study addresses STEM document categorization by modeling it as a multi-label classification task and enhancing performance through the integration of mathematical entities and their interconnections. We demonstrate that mathematical formulas serve as highly discriminative features for distinguishing document types. Furthermore, we show that leveraging the semantic relationships between these mathematical entities provides additional context, further refining the categorization process. Our results indicate that incorporating both mathematical entities and their connections significantly boosts the effectiveness of STEM document categorization. This paper presents a new algorithmic framework designed to determine which job offers to release in a matching environment. We examine a scenario where multiple companies, each with a specific set of candidate preferences, simultaneously select and submit offers to a group of candidates. Each candidate then chooses the most desirable offer they receive. The objective is to design an algorithm that ensures all participating companies receive at least as many offers as they would from a predetermined algorithm, thereby guaranteeing a form of ex-post fairness. We focus on the case where all companies aim to secure stable job assignments. We establish an upper bound on the number of offers an algorithm can reliably select and present a novel algorithm called "Reliable Matching" that achieves this bound. Furthermore, we extend these findings to settings involving multiple candidates per job and to scenarios with unknown candidate arrival rates, effectively creating a new online matching algorithm. Our results demonstrate that Reliable Matching performs at least as well as a randomized algorithm in both offline and online contexts. Additionally, we explore a related problem concerning fair offer sharing among companies and analyze the performance of a corresponding algorithm. Finally, we validate our theoretical findings through simulations. The Python implementation of Reliable Matching is available at https://github.com/robertk1995/reliable-matching. This paper introduces SummScore, a cross-encoder-based metric designed to evaluate summary quality. By utilizing the SummEval dataset, SummScore demonstrates a strong correlation with its ground truth scores while offering superior computational efficiency. Furthermore, it exhibits robustness in assessing narrative texts, as evidenced by its high alignment with SummEval scores. Ultimately, SummScore serves as an effective and efficient tool for evaluating summary excellence. The implementation can be accessed at https://github.com/ChenYi-1999/SummScore.

We introduce a new approach for restoring signals from noisy quadratic measurements, utilizing a non-convex optimization framework that is both computationally efficient and capable of accurately recovering signals with sparse frequency content. Our method's theoretical performance is evaluated through simulations, which demonstrate that it effectively restores signals with limited bandwidth even at extremely low signal-to-noise ratios. The rapid signal restoration is achieved by leveraging the sparse frequency domain representation, a capability that existing time-domain techniques struggle to match. This advantage is realized by integrating the theoretical foundations of compressed sensing with a novel non-convex estimator. Our proposed technique is anticipated to find applications in various domains, including quadratic sampling, holography, and holographic interferometry. Furthermore, we illustrate its utility in reconstructing holograms from severely degraded data. The code required to execute the algorithm is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ashishkumar1992/NonConvex-Quadratic. Keywords: Holography, Non-convex optimization, Quadratic sampling, Sparse recovery. MSC 2010: 94A12, 94A17, 94A12.

LiDAR and monocular vision are the two most prevalent sensors used in autonomous driving. Although many fusion methods exist, they often rely on complex fusion spaces, intricate fusion strategies, or extensive parameter tuning. This paper introduces BEVFusion, a straightforward yet resilient framework that fuses these modalities within a bird's-eye view representation. The approach employs a simple yet effective fusion strategy that eliminates the need for camera intrinsics, LiDAR extrinsics, or point cloud registration. Furthermore, the method is highly adaptable, easily extending to other sensor types and fusion objectives. Extensive experiments across three datasets demonstrate that BEVFusion matches or surpasses state-of-the-art results in object detection and segmentation tasks. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/CAI-DUT/BEVFusion. Additionally, the model can be downloaded from https://drive.google.

This study examines the dissipation scales of liquid turbulence through both experimental and theoretical frameworks. Utilizing high-speed imaging, we measured the spatial extent of velocity fluctuations in the dissipation range for gaseous and supercritical fluids under turbulent conditions. Our findings indicate that the Kolmogorov length scale, defined as $l_K = (\nu^3/\varepsilon)^{1/4}$, remains consistent across gases, supercritical fluids, and gases at the critical point, provided the ratio $l_K/l_0$ (where $l_0$ is the jet diameter) is sufficiently small. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the probability distribution of liquid velocity fluctuations follows a Gaussian distribution, with a standard deviation $\sigma$ satisfying $\sigma \approx u_r = (2\varepsilon/3)$, where $u_r$ represents the root-mean-square velocity. These results confirm that velocity fluctuations in the Kolmogorov range of liquid turbulence adhere to the same statistical laws observed in gases. Additionally, we analyze the thermal characteristics of liquid turbulence, demonstrating that temperature fluctuations in the Kolmogorov scale are governed by the Prandtl number. Specifically, when the Prandtl number is small, the thermal Kolmogorov scale is significantly larger than the velocity counterpart, whereas it becomes comparable when the Prandtl number is large. These conclusions are supported by theoretical derivations and experimental data. Finally, we discuss the potential applications of liquid turbulence in enhancing heat transfer and the mixing of heat and mass. The findings are expected to benefit researchers in the fields of liquid turbulence and heat transfer. Keywords: liquid turbulence, Kolmogorov length scale, velocity fluctuation, temperature fluctuation, liquid heat transfer.

This study presents a numerical analysis of the thermal profile generated by a pulsed laser in a liquid, with the objective of elucidating complex self-induced diffraction patterns. The investigation examines the laser-liquid interaction across a broad spectrum of parameters, including pulse duration, spot radius, fluence, and propagation distance. By employing a two-dimensional model, the research numerically solves the heat diffusion equation within a liquid medium. The resulting temperature distribution is subsequently utilized to determine the liquid's refractive index via the thermo-optic effect. Furthermore, the numerical results are compared with experimental diffraction patterns obtained from a CCD camera, which captured the propagation of a laser beam through a liquid. This validation confirms the model's ability to accurately represent the laser-induced thermal profile in a liquid. Finally, the research explores the formation of various diffraction patterns, such as dark rings, bright rings, and dark spots, by analyzing the interplay of laser parameters. These findings are discussed in relation to potential applications in laser processing and microfabrication. Ultimately, the study demonstrates that the proposed model can effectively predict the liquid's thermal profile and the resulting complex diffraction patterns. The code used for the numerical simulations is available at: https://github.com/ahmedhassan1998/numerical-simulation-of-laser-induced-thermal-profile-in-a-liquid. The corresponding MATLAB file can be found at: https://github.com/ahmedhassan1998/numerical-simulation-of-laser-induced-thermal-profile-in-a-liquid/blob/master/ThermalProfile.m. Keywords: Laser interaction, Liquid, Diffraction pattern, Numerical simulation. PACS: 42.50.-j, 42.60.Lc, 42.60.Fc, 42.60.Fn.

Design conversations are a common phenomenon in software engineering, where developers frequently discuss various design aspects. These discussions are often conducted in natural language, making them difficult to process. However, such conversations can yield valuable insights, such as design decisions, rationale, and alternative solutions. Consequently, there is a growing interest in mining design conversations to extract this useful information. This paper introduces Conclusion Stability, a concept that enables the detection of consistent conclusions within design conversations. By leveraging Conclusion Stability, we can identify design decisions and their accompanying rationales. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach through a comprehensive evaluation on 1,000,000 design conversations extracted from 10,000 issues across 10 open-source projects. Furthermore, we assess the effectiveness of Conclusion Stability in two key scenarios: (1) enhancing the quality of design decision detection, and (2) improving the retrieval of design rationales. Our results indicate that design decisions identified by Conclusion Stability achieve higher consistency scores than those found by state-of-the-art methods. Additionally, rationales retrieved using Conclusion Stability outperform those from existing approaches in terms of human judgment. Finally, we illustrate the utility of this technique by applying it to the detection of design decisions and rationales in the Apache Commons project. The code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2019/ConclusionStability. To our knowledge, this represents the first attempt to mine design conversations using natural language. We hope this work will inspire further research in this area. The source code for our Conclusion Stability method is available at https://github.com/ChenYi2019/ConclusionStability. This paper is written in Chinese. The English version can be found at https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.01001. The Chinese version is available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.01001. In contemporary data analytics, the volume of data generated daily has grown so rapidly that it necessitates new methods for storage and processing. This surge in data is driven by the proliferation of data sources, such as sensors and social media, which produce information in various formats, including streams, documents, and databases. This paper introduces H-STREAM, a hybrid system designed to handle these diverse data formats. The H-STREAM architecture is built upon Hadoop, a widely adopted open-source framework for big data processing. By leveraging Hadoop's capabilities, H-STREAM enables the processing of data streams in a scalable and fault-tolerant manner. Furthermore, it offers a unified programming model that simplifies the integration of stream and batch processing, allowing developers to write code that operates seamlessly across both environments. This research aims to facilitate the development of data processing applications that can access and process both data streams and data files (such as JSON documents) within a single, integrated system. The paper details the H-STREAM architecture and outlines the methods for processing data streams and files using this framework. Additionally, the study includes a proof of concept demonstrating the processing of various data formats, such as streams and JSON files, within H-STREAM. The paper also provides a comparison between H-STREAM and other big data processing systems, including Hadoop, MapReduce, and Spark. Finally, the paper addresses the challenges and limitations inherent in H-STREAM processing. Overall, this work contributes to the advancement of big data processing by offering a unified solution for handling multiple data formats. The paper concludes by suggesting future research directions focused on optimizing H-STREAM for improved performance and scalability. H-STREAM is available for download at https://github.com/abhishekkumar123/H-STREAM. Keywords: Big Data, Analytics Pipeline, Hadoop, H-STREAM, Data Streams, JSON Documents.

This work introduces a non-resonant approach to calculating the singular part of the cross section for producing top quark associates such as $t\bar{t}b$, $t\bar{t}\bar{b}$, $ttt$, and $\bar{t}tt$ at hadron colliders. The methodology relies on the soft-collinear effective theory (SCET$_1$) and the soft-collinear-cubic effective theory (SCET$_2$) within the narrow-width approximation. We apply this formalism to the $tt\bar{b}$ and $tt\bar{t}\bar{b}$ production channels at the LHC and the FCC-hh, respectively, and compare our findings with existing state-of-the-art results. Furthermore, we provide predictions for the $ttt$ and $t\bar{t}t$ channels at the HL-LHC and FCC-hh, which may prove valuable for future phenomenological studies. Our findings indicate that the relative difference between the singular approximation and the full cross section is approximately 10% for $tt\bar{b}$ and $tt\bar{t}\bar{b}$, and roughly 20% for $ttt$ and $t\bar{t}t$. Additionally, we have made the code used in this study publicly available. These results can be readily incorporated into any public event generator. The code is accessible at https://github.com/AlirezaHosseinpour/soft-collinear-cubic. The corresponding arXiv manuscript is available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.00001.
