Neural Machine Translation (NMT) models have demonstrated significant potential for automatically translating SPARQL, a query language used to access graph databases. Nevertheless, current SPARQL NMT systems are constrained by the length of context knowledge bases (KBs), which hinders their ability to accurately model long queries. This paper introduces a replication mechanism designed to divide large KBs into smaller, manageable fragments for NMT training. The mechanism operates in two stages: first, it partitions the KB into disjoint fragments, and then, for each source sentence, it identifies a relevant subset of these fragments to concatenate into a unified input for the NMT model. We evaluated this approach across various SPARQL n-grams, comparing different replication strategies and fragmentation methods. The results indicate that our replication mechanism enhances performance, particularly for NMT models tasked with generating longer sequences. Furthermore, we conducted experiments on a dataset of triplets comprising 10 million sentences and KBs, demonstrating that our method enables the training of SPARQL NMT models on knowledge bases approximately 100 times larger than previously feasible. The source code and data required to reproduce these findings are available at https://github.com/GraphDB/kb-replication. Finally, we have integrated the mechanism into the GraphDB knowledge base server, allowing users to query individual instances or federated graphs by specifying the relevant knowledge source. This paper introduces a straightforward approach to venue assessment that serves as an effective alternative to traditional citation-based metrics for gauging research quality within specific fields. Our methodology involves training classifiers to predict conference or journal names from abstracts, training data of which is publicly accessible. We demonstrate that these classifiers yield a reliable quality signal by evaluating them across three distinct dimensions: (1) their ability to distinguish between top-tier and other venues, (2) their stability when applied to new venues, and (3) their consistency relative to citation-counting methods. Our models surpass existing abstract-based scoring systems and, in several instances, outperform established citation-driven metrics. Furthermore, we illustrate how these models can be utilized to detect non-reproducible claims in scientific literature. The code and models supporting this study are available at https://github.com/alexandervolkov/venueinsights. The findings presented here were featured in the Proceedings of the 16th ACM International Conference on Web Search and Mining (WSDM 2023). Alexey Volkov's contribution to this research was supported by a Google PhD Fellowship.

This paper examines the application of neural networks in regulatory contexts. We begin by reviewing the primary characteristics of these networks, followed by an analysis of their advantages and limitations. Subsequently, we explore various validation techniques, detailing their methodologies and implications. Finally, we conclude by addressing key challenges and open questions within this field. The discussion is grounded in literature from mathematics, statistics, computer science, and engineering. Given the absence of comprehensive surveys on this topic, we aim to provide a foundational resource for researchers and practitioners engaged in neural network regulation. Additionally, we examine the ethical and societal dimensions associated with these models. Our objective is to establish a solid foundation for future research and to facilitate a more responsible and transparent deployment of neural networks in real-world settings. We believe this survey will be valuable to both the academic community and industry professionals. Furthermore, we believe the issues raised will stimulate broader discussions on the ethical implications of neural network usage. We have also made our bibliography available online at \url{https://github.com/afg2000/neural-network-validation}. This survey was prepared for the special issue of the \emph{International Statistical Review} titled "Machine Learning and Data Science: Challenges and Opportunities for Statistics," edited by S. Larochelle, A. Bouchard-Côté, and O. Chapelle. The editors invited contributions on diverse topics related to machine learning and data science, with a specific focus on challenges and opportunities for statisticians. We selected this subject to highlight the expanding role of neural networks in regulation, thereby addressing a gap in current literature and promoting ethical considerations within this domain. We anticipate that this survey will inspire further research and foster more extensive discussions on the ethical dimensions of neural network applications. \textbf{Keywords:} Artificial Intelligence, Data Science, Ethics, Machine Learning, Neural Networks, Regulation. \textbf{MSC2020 subject classification:} 62-07, 68T01, 68T07, 68T15, 90C40. \textbf{Primary Area:} 68T07, 68T15. \textbf{Secondary Area:} 68T01, 68T15, 90C40. \textbf{Related fields:} 68T01, 68T15, 90C40. \textbf{Related fields:} 68T0

We introduce a method for grouping objects based on a hierarchy of pairwise overlap graphs, utilizing a technique called "functorial" traversal. This name is derived from category theory, reflecting our conceptualization of the grouping process as a functor that maps overlap graphs to sets of object clusters. The procedure begins with a comprehensive binary clustering of all objects, subsequently refining this partition by traversing the overlap graphs in a functorial manner along a specified hierarchy of connections. A connection is defined as functorially traversable if an edge exists between the components containing the source objects. The resulting grouped output preserves all information from the overlap graph hierarchy, including indirect overlaps. Furthermore, the method offers a formal guarantee that it produces the coarsest partition that remains consistent with the hierarchy. We demonstrate the method's utility through two applications: (1) a formalization of the coarse-graining process in the Standard Model of particle physics, and (2) a new approach for image segmentation that leverages object detectors and pairwise pixel similarity. The latter application is supported by experimental results on the MS-COCO dataset. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the method's properties, including its computational complexity. Streaming retrieval within large-scale databases is a demanding task that necessitates efficient and effective solutions. While tensor completion has shown promise in this area, it often struggles with visual data, producing blurry images that hinder retrieval. This paper introduces a novel approach called patch monitoring-based streaming tensor ring restoration (PSTR). The method first divides input images into patches, which are then downsampled into a low-rank tensor. Subsequently, a patch similarity matrix is constructed using these inputs, and a similar reference image is selected to serve as a prior for filling missing pixels. Finally, a patch-based optimization is performed using this prior to recover the image. Experimental results demonstrate that PSTR achieves superior performance in both accuracy and computational efficiency. Furthermore, PSTR exhibits robustness in handling complex scenarios, such as image rotation and occlusion, that typically challenge tensor completion methods. The study also explores the impact of various hyperparameters on the proposed model. Overall, PSTR is well-suited for streaming retrieval in big data environments. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi1997/PSTR. The paper is available in English at https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.01007. This paper establishes that, with the exception of types (A, B, C, D, E, F, G, I, J, K), the Nichols algebras associated with traditional quantum groups over finite fields are finite-dimensional. Consequently, this demonstrates that certain finite-type Nichols algebras cannot be generated by admissible braided auto-automorphisms. Furthermore, we provide an explicit construction for the algebras in these finite cases. In a subsequent publication, we will outline the infinite-dimensional Nichols algebras corresponding to the exceptional groups. This study demonstrates that the kink-concavity property is synonymous with the log-kurtosis condition $\kappa_\omega(t) \propto t^{2/3}$, which serves as the foundation of the ZK theory for fully developed turbulence. The equivalence is established through the analysis of isotropic Gaussian fields, where the log-kurtosis condition is shown to be equivalent to the fourth-order cumulant condition $\kappa^{(4)}_\omega(t) \propto t^2$. Furthermore, the research confirms that the log-kurtosis condition is necessary for the development of inertial wave chaos in stratified fluids. Consequently, the findings indicate that the ZK spectrum represents a universal description of energy transfer in both compressible and incompressible fully developed turbulence. This paper introduces a straightforward algorithm, ISS[$\lambda$], designed to determine if two finite graphs are isomorphic. The algorithm operates in non-deterministic polynomial time relative to the number of vertices and the maximum degree. We establish that, provided $\lambda \geq 2$, ISS[$\lambda$] is guaranteed to standardize every finite graph G where the product of the number of vertices and the maximum degree does not exceed $4^\lambda$. Furthermore, we present an algorithm that tests whether a specific finite graph G belongs to a maximum weight autonomous set, ensuring this process requires no more than $2|G|+1$ evaluations of the graph's adjacency matrix. Finally, we propose an algorithm that constructs such a set for any finite graph G within polynomial time. The proposed ISS[$\lambda$] algorithm is a modification of the approach described in [1]. This paper investigates the thermodynamic properties of electrically tuned monolayer graphene. We calculate the internal energy, entropy, and temperature as functions of particle number, area, and chemical potential. Furthermore, we derive the system's thermodynamic temperature and entropy, examining their behavior in the limits of low and high temperatures. Finally, we establish the low-temperature specific heat capacity and explore its applications. These findings are supported by numerical computations and statistical mechanics principles. Ultimately, graphene emerges as a potent candidate for developing high-performance electronic and optoelectronic devices. Additionally, our results provide valuable insights for researchers in thermodynamics and physics. This study was conducted within the framework of the International Conference on Mathematics and Theoretical Physics (ICMTP-21). This study reports the first low-frequency radio observations of the binary system CR Draconis, conducted using the LOFAR telescope. The observations captured two distinct radio bursts from the active M-dwarf component, CR Dra, with a peak flux density of 1.2 Jy at 138 MHz. The polarization characteristics of these bursts indicate that they are generated by the electron cyclotron maser instability. The burst durations, ranging from 10 to 20 minutes, are significantly longer than those typically observed in other flare stars, suggesting a stable magnetic field configuration. The energetics of the bursts imply a magnetic field strength of approximately 1.5 kG. Furthermore, the bursts' duration and energy indicate that the electron beam is not monoenergetic, pointing toward a gradual acceleration mechanism. The observed bursts are interpreted as the result of a large flare event, with the prolonged emission attributed to the extended reconnection process. Additionally, the bursts exhibit a periodicity of 1.2 hours, consistent with the binary period, which supports the hypothesis that the bursts are modulated by the binary interaction. These findings suggest that CR Draconis is a promising candidate for future observations aimed at studying the fundamental properties of electron cyclotron maser radiation. Ultimately, this research provides a foundation for future observations of active M-dwarfs at low frequencies. (Abridged)

The virtual human avatar (VHA) stands as a vital instrument for social virtual reality (VR), enabling users to visually communicate and collaborate within immersive 3D environments. While current state-of-the-art methods for generating VHAs typically rely on mapping 3D body skeletons to textured meshes, this approach often results in unrealistic movements and subpar textures. Our method, Articulated Neural Depiction (AND), overcomes these limitations by utilizing 2D neural depictions (2DNDs) instead. By training a model to translate skeletal data into 2DNDs, we can subsequently animate these depictions to generate VHAs. This strategy offers two primary benefits: first, it produces realistic animations that are invariant to scale, rotation, and background clutter; second, it renders VHAs that are aesthetically pleasing and culturally diverse. We demonstrate the efficacy of AND through a series of experiments, including the creation of a large-scale dataset containing 1,000 videos of individuals from 100 distinct ethnic groups performing 10 different actions. The results indicate that AND outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques. Furthermore, we have integrated AND into a mobile application, allowing users to select VHAs from a diverse library and express themselves through virtual personas. This capability holds significant potential for enhancing social interaction and communication within social VR platforms. The dataset and mobile application are accessible at https://github.com/and-vc/Avatar-App. Our research was conducted while the first author was a student at the University of Washington. Additional details regarding the application can be found at https://avatarapp.io. Image intensification is a prevalent technique in image processing that alters image contrast and brightness. While human perception of intensified images is influenced by the specific adjustments to contrast and brightness, it remains unclear which modifications are most significant to humans. This study addresses this gap by conducting a human evaluation to identify the relative importance of contrast and brightness adjustments. The findings indicate that contrast adjustments are generally more critical than brightness adjustments. Furthermore, an automatic evaluation using the structural similarity (SSIM) metric yielded results consistent with human assessments. However, when evaluated through deep learning, the structural similarity model (SSIM-D) demonstrated a stronger correlation with human judgments than the original SSIM metric. We demonstrate that the Chern-Simons knot invariant for the link $6^2_{13}$, which involves the three-parameter family of quantum $sl(2,\mathbb{C})$ invariants, can be expressed using Askey-Wilson $q$-orthogonal polynomials. This finding offers fresh insight into the structure of these knot invariants and establishes a direct link between Chern-Simons theory and hypergeometric series. Furthermore, we identify the specific linear combination of quantum $R$-matrices within the Chern-Simons diagram that yields the desired knot invariant. We also examine the relationship between these knot invariants and the corresponding braid group representations of the Askey-Wilson algebra. Finally, we explore the potential for extending this approach to other knots and the $6^3_{22}$ link. Our work is grounded in the recently established correspondence between the $R$-matrices of the Askey-Wilson algebra and the Chern-Simons $R$-matrices. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive review of the Askey-Wilson algebra and its representation theory. This study examines the thermodynamic characteristics of two-dimensional frustrated antiferromagnets composed of triangular units connected by weak links. The interaction within each triangle is modeled as a linear combination of bilinear and trilinear forms, while the interactions between triangles are represented by a bilinear term. We demonstrate that the model exhibits a phase transition driven by temperature, with the nature of this transition shifting from second-order to first-order as the ratio of trilinear to bilinear intratrimer coupling increases. Furthermore, we show that the model's parameter space is divided into two regions: one featuring a single ordering wavevector and another containing two distinct wavevectors. The boundaries between these regions are defined by two continuous lines and a discontinuous line. Additionally, we identify two reentrant regions where magnetic order reemerges at lower temperatures following a nonmagnetic or spin-liquid state at higher temperatures. These reentrant regions are bounded by first-order transition lines. Our findings are supported by data from cluster Monte Carlo simulations. We also provide an analytical explanation for the model's phase diagram, which aligns with the numerical results. Finally, we explore the potential of this model to describe the temperature-dependent magnetic behavior of real materials. Specifically, we suggest that it can account for the reentrant magnetic ordering observed in the layered triangular lattice compound Cu$_3$SnS$_4$. This interpretation relies on the existence of a first-order transition and the presence of a reentrant region within the model's phase diagram. We further show that the model's phase diagram is consistent with the available experimental data for Cu$_3$SnS$_4$. Finally, we discuss the phase diagram of Cu$_3$SnS$_4$ in light of our theoretical results. We conclude that the experimental phase diagram of Cu$_3$SnS$_4$ can be qualitatively reproduced by our model, provided that the intercluster interactions are anisotropic. This conclusion is based on the existence of an anisotropic phase diagram in the model, which includes a reentrant region, contrasting with the isotropic phase diagram. We also discuss the implications of this finding. Our results indicate that the phase diagram of Cu$_3$SnS$_4$ cannot be accurately described by an isotropic model. Recent advancements in large language models (LLMs) have made them increasingly capable of responding to complex, open-ended questions, including those related to education. However, their performance in zero-shot educational question-answering remains inconsistent. To address this, we introduce a novel meta-learning framework designed to enhance the LLM's zero-shot capabilities in this domain. Our approach involves iteratively generating synthetic data, filtering it, and assembling it into training datasets. We evaluate various meta-learning strategies to determine the optimal method for adapting LLMs to zero-shot education tasks. Experimental results demonstrate that our framework significantly boosts performance, achieving up to a 15.4-point improvement over GPT-3 (175B) in zero-shot educational question-answering. This study examines the implications of recent LHC findings on the $Z_3$-symmetric Next-to-Minimal Standard Model (NMSSM) within the context of the Electroweak Phase Transition (EWPT). We analyze the stability of dark matter candidates, specifically focusing on a lightest odd parity state ($L_p=1$) that is either a pure neutralino or a neutralino/ino mixture. Our analysis reveals that the identified LHC Higgs boson at 125 GeV is predominantly composed of the lightest CP-even NMSSM component, $\hat{a}_{11}$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the NMSSM can accommodate a dark matter neutralino lighter than 13 GeV, provided its higgsino fraction is minimal. In this specific scenario, the NMSSM predicts an enhanced EWPT, a feature potentially detectable through gravitational wave observations. Additionally, we show that a lighter Higgsino is viable if the Higgsino mixing angle, $\theta_{h^0}$, is small, whereas a neutralino/ino dark matter candidate with a mass between 13 GeV and 135 GeV requires a higgsino fraction below 0.15. These findings indicate that the NMSSM can successfully address the Higgs boson problem, the nature of dark matter, and the possibility of a first-order phase transition. Finally, we discuss the prospects for identifying gravitational waves associated with this EWP transition. The paper concludes with a discussion of the NMSSM's viability in light of current experimental constraints. The analysis was conducted using the software packages NMSSMTools and EWPT. We introduce a straightforward technique for redshifting (sub)millimeter sources by applying a Sudoku-like grid to their spectral energy distributions (SEDs). This method is demonstrated using the source B1410+1020, identified in the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array's Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Survey (ALMA-ALS) at 1.1 mm, which we show has a redshift of z=3.95. We further demonstrate that this approach is straightforward to implement and can be readily extended to other (sub)millimeter wavelengths. The primary advantage of this technique is that it enables the rapid identification of robust redshifts for (sub)millimeter sources without requiring prior knowledge of galaxy luminosity evolution. Additionally, we outline a strategy for utilizing this method to investigate the evolution of star-forming galaxies at z>3. Our findings indicate that the z=3.95 redshift for B1410+1020 is secure, and we argue that the (sub)millimeter galaxy population at z>3 is likely more abundant than previously estimated. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the high-z Sudoku method is a valuable tool for identifying the most reliable redshifts for (sub)millimeter galaxies at z>3. By applying this technique to the ALMA-ALS sample, we identify 11 galaxies with z>3, including B1410+1020. We also present a preliminary analysis of the ALMA-ALS source counts at z>3, yielding a number density of $\log_{10}N(z>3)=10^{(10.0\pm0.1)}$ Mpc$^{-3}$. This result is consistent with other recent measurements of the (sub)millimeter galaxy population at z>3. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for the evolution of star-forming galaxies at z>3. The paper includes a data release of 11 galaxies with z>3.95, with a median redshift of z=4.95 and a median 1.1 mm luminosity of $L_{1.1mm}=1.1\times10^{13}$ L$_{\odot}$. We present results from extensive Monte Carlo simulations of Higgs theory involving simple and adjoint scalars within $SU(3)$ gauge theory in four dimensions. Our analysis reveals that the limitation-deactivation transition, which governs the restoration of the $SU(3)$ center symmetry, belongs to the same universality class as the confinement-deconfinement transition in pure $SU(3)$ gauge theory. This finding holds true across various gauge choices, including both Landau and Coulomb gauges. Furthermore, by incorporating non-abelian gauge interactions, the limitation-deactivated phase becomes metastable, giving rise to a first-order transition to the deconfined phase. Finally, we estimate the critical exponents and the ratio of the latent heat to energy density at the limit-deactivation transition. These values align with those of the pure $SU(3)$ gauge theory, confirming the universality of the transition, and we also examine the dependence of these quantities on the Higgs mass. Additionally, we explore the implications of these findings for the high-temperature phase diagram of QCD. Finally, we discuss the potential for a first-order transition between the deconfined and limit-deactivated phases, a scenario that could be experimentally investigated through the study of the QCD phase diagram. This possibility is particularly relevant in the context of the quarkyonic phase, which may exist at high chemical potential and low temperature. Our investigation of the limit-deactivated phase is motivated by the observation that the Coulomb potential between static sources in this phase exhibits a linear rise at short distances, a feature that could be tested in future experiments. We conclude by outlining the necessary experimental conditions to observe this phenomenon. The antiferromagnetic phase transition in the metallic compound Cr$_2$Al, which occurs at $T_{\rm N} = 280$ K, has been extensively researched, yet the magnetic structure within this antiferromagnetic region remains unresolved. This study employs neutron powder diffraction to determine the magnetic structure and analyze the exchange interactions. The data reveal that the chromium spins are arranged in-plane according to a propagation vector of $k = (1/2, 1/2, l)$, where $l$ is an arbitrary parameter. The magnetic moment is measured at $2.0(1)$ $\mu_{\rm B}$, aligning with prior theoretical predictions. Furthermore, the exchange interactions are modeled using the Fourier transform of the magnetic structure factor, $J(k)$, which exhibits a pronounced peak at $k = (1/2, 1/2, 0)$, offering a clear explanation for the observed magnetic arrangement. These findings suggest that Cr$_2$Al serves as a representative system for investigating the interplay between magnetic exchange interactions and crystal structure. Additionally, the results indicate that the previously reported magnetic field-induced phase transition is likely a consequence of the magnetic structure's sensitivity to external fields. Finally, the study confirms that the earlier proposal of a charge density wave in Cr$_2$Al lacks experimental support. These outcomes are consistent with recent density functional theory calculations. The complete magnetic structure data are accessible at http://www.icsm.riken.jp/Neutron/. This study introduces a kinetic model that captures the effects of an intermolecular potential by utilizing a speed-dependent collision frequency. The equilibrium distribution is defined as a Maxwellian where the temperature corresponds to that of an adiabatic process driven by the intermolecular potential. We demonstrate that this speed-dependent collision frequency generates additional internal energy within the post-collision state, thereby mimicking the influence of an intermolecular potential. The proposed model is assessed against two standard benchmarks: the shock tube problem and the plane Couette flow. Numerical results indicate that the proposed model aligns well with the Navier-Stokes equations under small Knudsen number conditions and successfully represents the physical impacts of an intermolecular potential. Furthermore, we observe that the planar Couette flow exhibits greater sensitivity to an intermolecular potential than the shock tube problem. Finally, we extend the proposed model to the Boltzmann equation by incorporating an angular-dependent weight function. This extension shows that the effects of an intermolecular potential are more pronounced in the plane Couette flow when compared to the angular-independent case. These findings suggest that the angular-dependent weight function is more effective at capturing the effects of an intermolecular potential than the standard Boltzmann kernel. Additionally, the proposed model is shown to be consistent with the conservation laws of mass, momentum, and energy. Finally, we confirm the well-posedness of the model by establishing the positivity of the solution and proving its stability. To achieve this, we derive an appropriate entropy and establish an appropriate convex entropy inequality. These theoretical results are supported by numerical experiments. The model is expected to be valuable for investigating the physical effects of an intermolecular potential in gas flows. This work is dedicated to Professor Shuichi Takata on the occasion of his 60th birthday. Semantic interpreters function as a bridge between neural networks and the natural world, translating between the discrete states a network perceives and the continuous elements of the real world. While prior research has explored training these interpreters using minimal data, such approaches often yield interpreters that fail to generalize to novel instances. This study demonstrates that by leveraging a few hand-crafted, high-level observations about an environment, interpreters can be trained to generalize to new instances. We introduce an algorithm that utilizes these observations to train semantic interpreters with negligible data, requiring only a few examples to identify novel instances. We validate the efficacy of our method across two distinct domains: color segmentation and object tracking. Our findings indicate that the trained interpreters successfully generalize to new instances and successfully identify novel instances. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the high-level observations employed are sufficiently natural for human experts to comprehend. Overall, our research advances the capability of trained interpreters to generalize to new instances and facilitates the practical application of neural network interpretations in novel situations. The upcoming 100-TeV proton-proton collider and the 20-100-TeV Electron-Ion Collider (EIC) are poised to become the next major facilities for nuclear and particle physics. The EIC is designed to investigate the internal structure of protons and nuclei by scattering high-energy electrons against protons or ions. To ensure high-performance data collection, the EIC will require advanced tracking detectors featuring exceptional spatial resolution and rapid data readout capabilities. This paper outlines the current state of silicon sensor technology and its application in the LHC Upgrade tracking system, while also presenting a roadmap for developing silicon sensors and readout electronics tailored to the EIC. Additionally, the study will demonstrate the potential of these silicon sensors through recent experimental results. Keywords: Electron-Ion Collider, Silicon Sensors, Readout Electronics. 1. Following the LHC's completion, two further accelerators are anticipated: the High-Luminosity LHC (HL-LHC) and the Future Circular Collider (FCC). The HL-LHC will enhance the LHC's luminosity by a factor of ten, whereas the FCC will be a proton-proton collider with a center-of-mass energy of 100 TeV. Concurrently, the Future Circular Collider (FCC) is being considered as a potential site for a high-energy nuclear physics experiment known as the Electron-Ion Collider (EIC). The EIC will utilize a proton beam from the Future Circular Collider in Heavily Ion mode (FCC-eh) and an electron beam from a linear accelerator to collide with energies up to 20 TeV. The primary objective of the EIC is to probe the internal structure of the proton and nucleus. To achieve this, the EIC must deliver high-precision data, necessitating a tracking detector with a small point-to-point resolution of approximately 5 $\mu$m and a large acceptance of 1.5 m$^2$. Furthermore, the tracking system must operate with a high rate capability of 100 kHz per interaction vertex. The EIC will be constructed at Brookhaven National Laboratory (BNL) in the United States. We report on the detection of pulsations in the low-luminosity active galactic nucleus (LLAGN) Mrk 365, characterized by a period of 10.5 days and an amplitude of 0.15 mag in the r band. This discovery is significant because it marks the first identification of pulsations in a LLAGN with a mass below 10^6 Msun, a finding that challenges the conventional view that stochastic fluctuations dominate accretion processes in low-accretion scenarios. Furthermore, the variability amplitude of Mrk 365 is comparable to that of the prototypical pulsating AGN, Mrk 335, despite a mass difference exceeding an order of magnitude. This suggests that the amplitude of fluctuations in LLAGN is not directly tied to the black hole mass, indicating that accretion processes in low-accretion-rate AGN may be more complex than previously assumed. Additionally, we observed a correlation between the r and i bands in Mrk 365, which may be attributed to the accretion disk. These observations collectively suggest that the accretion process in LLAGN is not governed by the standard Shakura-Sunyaev (SS) model. Instead, we propose that the accretion flow in LLAGN is likely governed by a magnetized thin disk, which can account for the observed variability. This study underscores the need for further research into the accretion processes of LLAGN. Our findings provide a new perspective on the nature of LLAGN and their associated accretion mechanisms. This study presents spectropolarimetric observations of HD 58260, a rapidly rotating Ap star, conducted using a discharge spectropolarimeter. By analyzing the variation of the longitudinal magnetic field with the rotating star, we derived the radial magnetic field profile. Our results indicate that the magnetic field is predominantly dipolar, with a total flux of approximately 1.5 kG. The derived radial profile aligns with the model proposed by Mathis et al. (2014), which posits that the magnetic field is anchored in the stellar core and expands outward. Furthermore, the observed profile suggests the presence of a magnetic equator. These findings are corroborated by the results of a magnetic field model developed by the authors. Additionally, we determined the star's inclination angle to be $i = 80.5 \pm 0.5$ degrees, consistent with previous literature. Finally, we estimated the star's age to be $1.1 \pm 0.1$ Gyr. These conclusions are supported by the analysis of the line profile of the neutral line Fe I 6067.8 Å, which exhibits a broadening characteristic of Stark broadening. This indicates that the line is formed in a plasma environment with an electron density of $n_e \approx 10^{16} cm^{-3}$, a condition typical of a discharge rather than a stellar atmosphere. Consequently, the line is likely formed in a chromospheric layer, and the observed broadening is attributed to the Stark effect. We conclude that the discharge spectropolarimeter is a highly effective tool for investigating the magnetic field of HD 58260. We conducted ALMA observations of the H30$\alpha$ line at 1.15 mm to investigate the star formation characteristics of NGC 5253, a starburst galaxy known for its low metallicity. Our analysis of the spatial distribution of H30$\alpha$ emission reveals a pattern consistent with the star-forming regions identified in the optical spectrum. By comparing our findings with prior observations of the H41$\alpha$ and H56$\alpha$ lines, we examined the physical conditions of the HII regions. Our results indicate that the H30$\alpha$ emission is primarily driven by the H0 recombination process, with an electron temperature ($T_e$) of approximately 10,000 K. Furthermore, the H30$\alpha$ emission is more intense in the central regions of NGC 5253 compared to the H41$\alpha$ and H56$\alpha$ lines, suggesting that the HII regions responsible for the H30$\alpha$ signal are younger than those producing the H41$\alpha$ and H56$\alpha$ emissions. These observations suggest that NGC 5253 is currently undergoing a starburst event. Additionally, we analyzed the relationship between the H30$\alpha$ line and the H$\beta$ line to explore the star formation history of NGC 5253. Our data reveal a strong correlation between the H30$\alpha$ emission and the optical H$\beta$ emission, implying that the HII regions generating the H30$\alpha$ signal are younger than those older than 10 Myr. We introduce the notion of constant orbit equivalence stiffness, which extends the concept of constant orbit distance to virtually cyclic group actions. This new concept maintains many desirable properties of distance, including its ability to ensure orbit separation and serve as a coordinate system. We demonstrate that a constant orbit equivalence stiffness exists precisely when the action is equicontinuous, and in such cases, it is not unique. Furthermore, we establish that within the class of smooth actions, the existence of a non-unique continuous orbit equivalence stiffness implies the existence of a $C^1$ orbit equivalence stiffness. Finally, we examine the relationship between orbit stiffness and orbits with finite distance, showing that while finite distance actions are necessarily equicontinuous, finite distance stiffness within this class is not necessarily continuous. Additionally, we prove that if a virtually cyclic group action possesses a $C^k$ orbit equivalence stiffness, then the action itself must be $C^k$ equicontinuous. Finally, we note that our definition of orbit equivalence stiffness aligns with the classical metric distortion concept found in the literature. This study introduces a new class of nonparametric estimators for conditional expectation functions, $\mu(X) = E[Y \mid X]$, grounded in nearest-neighbor methodology. The proposed estimator, $m_n(X)$, is defined as the average of paired samples $(Y_1, Y_2)$ where the corresponding $X$ values fall within a pre-defined, data-driven neighborhood around $X$. We establish that $m_n(X)$ converges in probability to $\mu(X)$ as the sample size increases. Furthermore, we develop a plug-in estimator for the asymptotic variance of $m_n(X)$ and demonstrate its consistency. These findings are supported by a simulation study. Additionally, we apply this estimator to two real-world datasets: the 1990 US Census Public Use Microdata Sample (PUMS) and the 1996-2000 Current Population Survey (CPS) Annual Social and Economic Supplement (ASEC). The application includes calculating the poverty rate as a function of family size and the average number of children as a function of family income. Finally, we compare our proposed estimator against existing alternatives. The code required to replicate all results is available at \url{https://github.com/abhishekbhagat/NNCE}. This study introduces a state assessment framework grounded in state estimation, specifically for determining the basic reproduction number and initial infected population within epidemiological models. The proposed assessment relies on constructing observers that generate dynamic estimates of these two key parameters. We demonstrate that for a significant subset of standard epidemic models, this estimation problem can be reduced to a state reconstruction challenge. To address this, we develop a state estimator utilizing a high-gain observer, a method selected for its simplicity and rapid convergence. Furthermore, we extend this approach to a broader range of epidemic models by employing a composite observer. The efficacy of our methodology is validated through numerical simulations. Additionally, we examine the application of our state assessment technique to real-world data, utilizing a discrete-time epidemic model fitted to the observed cases. In this context, we construct data-driven observers to estimate the parameters of the fitted model. Finally, we provide a comparative analysis of the proposed observer techniques against existing methods in the literature. This entire methodology is implemented in the open-source Python package `epidemic-observer`. Our findings indicate that the high-gain observer delivers superior performance compared to several techniques reported in prior studies. The Python package, along with all associated code and data, is publicly accessible at https://github.com/epidemics/epidemic-observer. Temporal Knowledge Graph Completion (TKGC) focuses on predicting missing subject-predicate-object triples within a temporal context. This study theoretically investigates Kerr-lens mode-locking (KLM) within high-peak-power ultrafast laser systems. The analysis demonstrates that ultra-short pulse durations can be achieved by appropriately selecting the filling factor, defined as the ratio of the intra-cavity spot size to the Kerr-lens focal length. Furthermore, it is shown that resonance at the inverse gain cross-section ($\sigma_g^{-1}$) is not a necessary condition for stable KLM. Finally, the paper establishes that laser systems operating at high peak powers can function effectively with apertured KLM, opening a pathway for developing ultrafast lasers with very high power levels. These findings are supported by numerical simulations. The theoretical framework is applied to analyze the Kerr-lens mode-locked Yb:YAG crystal utilized in the 100 W, 200 fs Yb:YAG/Yb:CaF$_2$ thin-disk laser recently presented at the Optical Society of America's Conference on Lasers and Optical Engineering (OSAC) by the Institute of Physics of the Polish Academy of Sciences. The results indicate that ultra-short pulses are achievable in this system, with a fundamental mode limit of approximately 170 fs. Additionally, the potential for generating even shorter pulses via dual-carrier wave Kerr-lens mode-locking is demonstrated. Ultimately, this work provides a comprehensive theoretical and numerical examination of KLM in high-peak-power ultrafast lasers. The presented theory is general and applicable to any Kerr-lens mode-locked laser system. The paper concludes with a discussion of the theory's limitations and an outline of future research directions. This work was conducted in collaboration with the Institute of Physics of the Polish Academy of Sciences.

Keywords: Kerr-lens mode-locking, ultrafast lasers, ultrafast laser theory, ultra-short pulse generation, high-peak-power lasers.

Existing literature on high-dimensional expansions, such as those by Nisan, Schulman, and Vadhan, or O'Donnell, typically relies on random walks over groups to define independent random subsets (disjoint influences) of the original variables. This paper introduces an alternative approach that replaces random walks with covers of the variable set. This method offers greater flexibility, enabling expansions to be constructed directly from the variable structure rather than solely based on group actions. The approach includes a definition of "unbiasedness" and a Fourier analysis tailored to these expansions. The authors demonstrate an upper bound on bias and establish a Parseval identity analogous to the classical Fourier analysis on the discrete cube. Furthermore, the paper explores applications within probabilistic communication complexity, specifically regarding index functions, and includes a discussion on the relationship between this technique and the analysis of property testing algorithms. The work concludes with an outline of a conjecture concerning the optimal bias bound.

Keywords: high-dimensional expansions, probabilistic communication complexity, property testing.

The study investigates the magnetic properties of the centered honeycomb lattice antiferromagnet GdInO$_3$ through both experimental measurements and theoretical modeling. Experimental results indicate that GdInO$_3$ exhibits a three-sublattice antiferromagnetic (AFM) ordering with a Néel temperature of $T_\mathrm{N}=4.5$ K. At temperatures below $T_\mathrm{N}$, the experimental exchange interactions are derived using the Bonner-Fisher method and the equal-time spin correlation technique. Theoretical analysis employs a Heisenberg AFM model incorporating both nearest-neighbor ($J_1$) and next-nearest-neighbor ($J_2$) exchange interactions. By fitting the exchange-coupling parameters to the experimentally derived values, the ratio $J_2/J_1$ is determined to be $0.15\pm0.01$. This ratio aligns with the theoretical prediction of $0.167$ for a three-sublattice AFM state in a centered honeycomb lattice. Furthermore, the theoretical exchange interactions and the corresponding magnetic structure are illustrated. The magnetic ground state is identified as a non-collinear AFM state, consistent with the experimental data. Finally, the magnetic phase diagram is constructed, and the temperature dependence of the magnetization is calculated. The theoretical findings regarding the temperature dependence of the magnetization show good agreement with the experimental observations. These results provide a comprehensive understanding of the magnetic properties of GdInO$_3$. Additionally, the research demonstrates that the Bonner-Fisher method is effective for extracting exchange interactions in a centered honeycomb lattice. The findings are also applicable to other two-dimensional centered honeycomb antiferromagnets, such as the recently discovered EuInO$_3$. The accompanying data repository contains the raw experimental data, including magnetization curves and the temperature dependence of the exchange interaction parameter $J_1$. The source code used for the theoretical analysis is also provided. This paper introduces a model designed to estimate the increase in bit error rate caused by nonlinear impairments during optical transmission. The framework relies on the assumption that dual-polarization nonlinearities generate crosstalk between them, which is modeled as additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN). The efficacy of this approach is demonstrated across various four-dimensional (4D) modulation schemes, specifically QPSK, 16-QAM, and 64-QAM, as well as different system configurations, including RZ-DPSQ and DQPSK. The results indicate that the proposed model achieves accuracy within 1 dB of the actual bit error rate. Furthermore, the model is computationally efficient, requiring only a few seconds to execute on a standard personal computer. This efficiency stems from the model's independence from simulation parameters such as fiber length, span length, and the number of spans. Consequently, the model is applicable to any transmission system utilizing dual-polarization modulation. Additionally, the paper presents a novel modulation format combining QPSK with 64-QAM, offering a spectral efficiency of 10 b/s/Hz. Finally, the study demonstrates how the model can be utilized to determine the optimal power distribution between the two dual-polarization channels. This optimization capability is illustrated using QPSK and 64-QAM formats, which offer the highest and lowest spectral efficiencies, respectively. The findings reveal that the power split between the two channels varies depending on the specific system configuration employed. Ultimately, the paper concludes that the proposed model is highly accurate and serves as a valuable tool for analyzing and designing dual-polarization modulation systems. It enables the rapid evaluation of various system parameters, such as modulation format, power allocation, and dispersion management, thereby facilitating the optimization of dual-polarization transmission systems. This capability is demonstrated by optimizing a QPSK/64-QAM format, achieving a spectral efficiency of 10 b/s/Hz with a power allocation of 40% for QPSK and 60% for 64-QAM. The resulting system exhibits a total split nonlinearity penalty of 0.1 dB, representing a 25% reduction compared to the conventional QPSK-only format. This optimization is achieved without incurring any dispersion penalty. Furthermore, the model is used to assess the performance of a 100-Gbit/s dual-polarization system employing QPSK and 16-QAM formats, achieving a spectral efficiency of 6 b/s/Hz.

This study presents a data collection and analysis process designed to identify signs of depression in social media posts. The research relies on a dataset comprising 1,000 users, divided into two equal groups: 500 individuals diagnosed with depression and 500 without. The analysis involves examining user profiles to detect indicators of depression, a task evaluated through two metrics: the accuracy of profile classification and the detection of specific depression-related indications. The primary finding is that while individual indications are often weak, their combination allows for the detection of depression signs in 70% of profiles. Additionally, the study identifies the specific indications that contribute to this detection. The results suggest that this detection mechanism can be utilized to generate features for future machine learning models aimed at identifying depression in social media content. Furthermore, the paper outlines potential applications for these findings, including the development of online support services for depressed users and the creation of features to enhance the accuracy of existing mental health assessment tools. Finally, the study addresses the ethical implications of its findings and results.

This study introduces a new stochastic compartmental model designed to simulate the spatial dissemination of COVID-19. The framework incorporates two compartments for infected individuals: isolated and non-isolated. For each compartment, the system tracks both isolated and non-isolated healthy individuals, alongside isolated and non-isolated infected individuals, as well as isolated and non-isolated susceptible individuals. The analysis focuses on isolated and non-isolated regions, examining both the existence and uniqueness of the stationary distribution and the local stability of the unique positive solution. Furthermore, simulation results are presented to validate the proposed methodology. The findings indicate that increasing the isolation rate of both healthy and infected individuals in non-isolated areas significantly reduces the population count in both zones. Additionally, the model demonstrates that a higher transmission rate in non-isolated areas leads to a higher population of both healthy and infected individuals in isolated areas. Finally, it is observed that a higher isolation rate for both healthy and infected individuals in isolated areas results in a lower population of both healthy and susceptible individuals in non-isolated areas. These outcomes suggest that implementing isolation measures in non-isolated regions can effectively mitigate the spread of COVID-19. The paper concludes by outlining potential directions for future research. The research utilizes the Random Phase Approximation (RPA) to calculate the energy and strength of the ISGMR, incorporating the effects of monopole-quadrupole coupling. This work examines the dynamics of a particle subject to Coulomb resistance, where acceleration reverses sign whenever the particle's velocity becomes zero. This system serves as a simplified representation of frictional models found in mechanical engineering and physics. We demonstrate that, under specific conditions, the stick-slip behavior of this particle results in an infinite sequence of alternating slip and stick phases within a finite timeframe. Furthermore, we establish conditions guaranteeing that the particle's position remains bounded during slip phases and that it eventually ceases movement in a finite time. The analysis is conducted using a continuous feedback control law, which can be viewed as a smooth approximation of discontinuous control strategies commonly employed in control theory literature. Our approach relies on a combination of classical techniques, including Zeno convergence and comparison lemmas, alongside recent findings by the authors and their collaborators regarding the behavior of Filippov differential inclusions. These findings are subsequently applied to model a frictional mass-spring system regulated by a continuous feedback controller. We prove that, given appropriate parameter selection, the system's convergence to an equilibrium point occurs in finite time and is non-oscillatory. Additionally, we show that the convergence to any other equilibrium is asymptotic and potentially oscillatory. Finally, we support these theoretical findings with numerical simulations. The proofs utilize tools from recent literature on the behavior of differential inclusions, and the examples are drawn from applications in control theory. Consequently, this paper may offer valuable insights for researchers in both mathematics and engineering. Notably, the engineering applications are formulated using continuous control laws, which are advantageous for implementation on digital computers. This contrasts with many results in the engineering literature that rely on discontinuous control laws, which are difficult to implement digitally. We believe this study contributes to the field by bridging mathematics and engineering through the use of continuous control laws. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 reviews preliminary concepts and lemmas; Section 3 analyzes the one-dimensional case; Section 4 addresses higher-dimensional scenarios; and Section 5 presents an application involving a mass-spring system with Coulomb friction. The paper concludes with a discussion of open problems. Finally, Section 6 presents numerical simulations that corroborate our findings. Section 7 offers concluding remarks. Sequential recommender systems are designed to predict a user's next item based on their past consumption history. However, in real-world scenarios, users often have multiple distinct goals, and traditional sequential recommender systems often fail to effectively address these hidden intents. To tackle this challenge, we introduce the Hidden User Intent (HUI) framework, which enables a sequential recommender to adapt to and satisfy various user intentions. This framework comprises two key components: the Multi-Head Intent Learning (MHIL) module and the Intent Satisfaction (IS) module. The MHIL module learns diverse user intents by utilizing multiple head networks, each specializing in a specific intent. Subsequently, the IS module dynamically selects the most relevant head network for a given history to ensure intent satisfaction. We evaluated the HUI framework across three real-world datasets, comparing it against several baseline methods. The experimental results demonstrate that our framework significantly outperforms the baselines, achieving substantial improvements in both overall recommendation quality and the ability to satisfy varied user intents. Furthermore, we conducted ablation studies and statistical significance tests to verify the effectiveness of the proposed framework. Finally, we analyze the HUI framework's performance to provide insights into its advantages and limitations. Overall, the HUI framework offers a promising solution for building recommender systems capable of handling varied user intents. Low-rank matrix completion is a widely used technique for reconstructing full-rank matrices from sparse observations. However, many real-world datasets exhibit groupwise heterogeneity, where distinct subsets of data follow different underlying patterns. This study investigates the feasibility of achieving consistent estimation and inference for all entries in a collection of low-rank matrices when data is organized in a way that reveals these group structures. We establish the necessary conditions for achieving minimax optimal rates of estimation and inference for a set of varying-rank matrices under a common sparsity regime. Furthermore, we introduce a novel algorithm designed to estimate the number of groups and their corresponding indicators. We provide a theoretical analysis of the proposed method, demonstrating that it achieves the optimal rates previously identified. Additionally, we present simulation results that validate our theoretical findings and explore potential applications in genomics. Our method outperforms existing approaches that either ignore groupwise heterogeneity or assume a fixed number of groups. Finally, we apply our methodology to a real-world genomic dataset to identify distinct cell types. The code required to replicate our theoretical and simulation findings is available at https://github.com/abhishekgupta1997/MatrixCompletion.

The study of topological quantum systems relies fundamentally on symmetry, as most current theoretical frameworks are limited to systems possessing at least one symmetry operation. This research aims to establish a comprehensive and fundamental theory applicable to all topological systems, regardless of the absence of symmetry. We demonstrate that the absence of symmetry in a topological system can be effectively modeled by introducing an additional particle-hole symmetry operation that anti-commutes with the system's Hamiltonian. Furthermore, we prove that this modified Hamiltonian system is topologically equivalent to the original system featuring symmetry. Consequently, established theories for systems with particle-hole symmetry can be directly applied to analyze original systems that lack symmetry. This approach offers a more fundamental and complete understanding of topological systems devoid of symmetry. Additionally, we examine a specific case where the topological classification of original systems without symmetry differs from that of systems with particle-hole symmetry, revealing that the former is determined by the second Ext group of the C*-algebra associated with the original system, whereas the latter is determined by the second Ext group of the C*-algebra associated with the hypothetical system that includes particle-hole symmetry. This distinction highlights the necessity of the K-theory approach for achieving a more fundamental and complete understanding of topological systems without symmetry. Finally, we validate our theory by successfully reproducing the complete topological classification for all possible Hamiltonians of 1D, 2D, and 3D systems lacking symmetry. Our findings indicate that all previously reported topological phenomena in original symmetry-less systems can be understood through the lens of particle-hole symmetry, thereby reinforcing the validity of our proposed theory. This work represents a significant advancement toward a more fundamental and comprehensive understanding of topological systems without symmetry. Our theory is expected to facilitate the discovery of new topological materials that are free of particle-hole symmetry. Additionally, we anticipate that this framework will enable the development of new topological quantum devices that do not rely on particle-hole symmetry. Recent anomalies in lepton flavor universality tests, specifically in $b\to s\ell^+\ell^-$ transitions, have prompted a proposal to introduce a new observable, $\mathcal{R}_{\mu e} = N(\mu^+ \mu^-)/N(e^+ e^-)$, to further investigate these discrepancies. This study examines the feasibility of measuring this ratio at the LHCb experiment. Utilizing the LHCb 2016 dataset, we analyze the $\bar{B}^0\to K^{*0}\mu^+\mu^-$ decay and calculate the ratio of the branching fraction for $\bar{B}^0\to K^{*0} \mu^+ \mu^-$ against that for $\bar{B}^0\to K^{*0} e^+ e^-$. Our findings indicate that the LHCb experiment can achieve a precision of approximately 10% for this quantity. Additionally, we introduce a semi-inclusive variant of $\mathcal{R}_{\mu e}$, defined as $\mathcal{R}_{\mu e}^{\rm semi} = \sigma(\bar{B}^0\to X_K\mu^+\mu^-)/\sigma(\bar{B}^0\to X_Ke^+e^-)$, and demonstrate that this semi-inclusive ratio can be determined with an even lower uncertainty. Consequently, $\mathcal{R}_{\mu e}^{\rm semi}$ serves as a valuable tool for probing new physics effects. We also provide a preliminary estimate of the sensitivity of this observable to new physics contributions. Finally, we discuss the potential of this measurement to constrain new physics models, with a specific focus on the $C_{10}$ Wilson coefficient. This paper introduces a decentralized regulation strategy for linear multi-channel networks that supports a distributed architecture, enabling distributed parameter estimation and distributed computation. The control law relies on a distributed feedback mechanism, where each channel's regulation is governed by its own state and those of its neighbors. Additionally, the control law features an adaptive component that utilizes the state variables of its neighbors. This approach ensures that the closed-loop system's state converges asymptotically to a desired reference state, with the distributed adaptive parameters reaching a steady state. A key advantage is that the steady-state distributed parameters are constant, allowing each channel to be regulated by a time-invariant distributed feedback mechanism. The paper also establishes sufficient conditions for the distributed regulation of state and output variables. Furthermore, it demonstrates that distributed output regulation is achievable even when the network parameters are unknown, provided the network topology remains constant. Simulation results are included to validate the effectiveness of the distributed regulation approach. The proposed methodology is applicable to various network types, including those with distributed computation, and can be utilized for distributed distributed parameter systems. Applications span diverse domains such as power networks, electrical machines, mechanical systems, and fluid networks. The global COVID-19 pandemic has caused widespread fear and significant loss of life, prompting researchers to develop various diagnostic tools to assist medical professionals. This study introduces a novel two-phase approach designed to aid clinicians in diagnosing and predicting the disease. In the first phase, a BERT-based classifier determines if an individual is infected. The second phase evaluates disease progression by categorizing patients into one of two groups: those experiencing no symptoms or in the initial phase, and those exhibiting severe symptoms or having entered the second phase. The model was trained and assessed using a dataset of 1,000 clinical records. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves a 95% accuracy rate in the initial phase and an 85% accuracy rate in the second phase. These findings indicate that the system is effective for early detection and the prediction of disease symptoms. The eco-evolutionary process encompasses both evolutionary changes, driven by genetic variation and selection, and ecological dynamics, resulting from the interaction between genetic makeup and environmental factors. This study examines how environmental fluctuations influence the rate of evolution, specifically analyzing the impact of varying time scales. By employing a quantitative framework, we demonstrate that when environmental duration is short relative to the time required for genetic adaptation, evolution proceeds rapidly. Conversely, when environmental duration is long, the evolutionary rate slows down. Furthermore, we identify the critical parameters that govern the speed of eco-evolution, revealing that both the absolute value and the variance of environmental change rates are essential. Ultimately, this research provides a foundation for understanding the fundamental mechanisms driving eco-evolutionary dynamics. By integrating both ecological and evolutionary perspectives, our findings offer a comprehensive understanding of the processes occurring within ecosystems. This holistic approach is essential for comprehending the dynamics of both natural and artificial ecosystems, as well as the mechanisms behind their stability and resilience. Consequently, this work aids in predicting the outcomes of environmental changes and the emergence of new species. Additionally, it establishes a basis for managing environmental factors to achieve desired results, such as accelerating the development of beneficial traits in crops and livestock. Finally, these insights are applicable to other systems, including the brain, where the interaction between ecological and evolutionary factors is crucial for understanding behavior and disease. By applying these findings, we can better understand the dynamics of brain disorders and develop strategies to mitigate their effects. Overall, this research advances our understanding of the complex interactions between ecology and evolution, providing valuable insights for addressing global challenges related to environmental change and human health. Self-supervised speech models have recently demonstrated significant potential for speech representation learning. While numerous studies have explored various architectures and pretraining strategies, the antagonistic susceptibility of speech self-supervised models to different training conditions remains underexplored. This paper investigates such vulnerabilities, specifically focusing on the impacts of diverse educational regimens and their effects on downstream tasks. Our findings indicate that self-supervised models trained with multiple acoustic modalities exhibit superior downstream performance compared to those trained on single-modality data. Furthermore, we demonstrate that training objectives designed to predict masked segments of the input sequence are more effective than those requiring the prediction of augmented segments. Finally, we establish that the vulnerability of these models to downstream tasks is primarily driven by the susceptibility of their representations to perturbations. Overall, this study underscores the critical importance of education in speech self-supervised learning. This paper introduces a method for assessing the impact of missing data on Bayesian sensitivity analysis through the use of E-values. We demonstrate the approach using a clinical trial example. Furthermore, we extend the methodology to handle missing data arising from both non-compliance and non-convergence. Finally, we illustrate the utility of this framework with two case studies drawn from the literature. The E-value approach is particularly effective for quantifying the influence of unobserved data on sensitivity analysis conclusions. The initial framework, which addresses absent data, is straightforward to implement and can be applied across a broad spectrum of scenarios. Additionally, it facilitates the quantification of uncertainty linked to the absence of data, a feature that is often difficult to achieve with other methods. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 reviews the E-value and its application in sensitivity analysis; Section 3 presents the proposed framework for evaluating the effects of missing and non-compliance data; Section 4 applies the method to missing and non-compliance data within a clinical trial context; Section 5 examines two examples from the literature; and Section 6 offers concluding remarks. The accompanying code is available at https://github.com/abhishekkumar2000/Evalue. Keywords: Missing data, Non-compliance, E-value, Sensitivity analysis. Furthermore, we explore the quantum plane's link to the quantum group $SU_q(1,1)$ and the Lie algebra $sp_q(2)$. We also investigate the action of $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2,\mathbb{R})$ on the quantum plane and the resulting quantum orbits, which include the quantum disk, upper half-plane, and strip. Additionally, we detail the action of the discrete quantum group $\mathbb{Z}_q^2$ on the quantum plane and its associated quantum orbits, such as the quantum disk, upper half-plane, and strip. Finally, we analyze the actions of both the quantum group $SU_q(1,1)$ and the Lie algebra $sp_q(2)$ on these quantum orbits. This work serves as a foundation for further research into the quantum geometry of these spaces. Our findings are supported by explicit formulas and can be viewed as a comprehensive overview of the quantum geometry of the quantum disk, quantum half-plane, and quantum strip. We introduce a novel analytical framework for modeling finite-size corrections in quantum critical systems, grounded in wavefunction overlaps. This approach amalgamates the standard operator algebra method with a universal matrix product state ansatz. The resulting theory accurately predicts all universal data, including corrections to the scaling form of wavefunction overlaps, entanglement entropy, and one-point functions of local operators. Furthermore, it enables the determination of the complete set of relevant and marginal boundary operators based on their finite-size scaling behavior. By applying this method to the Ising chain, we achieve high-precision results that align exceptionally well with both exact solutions and density-matrix renormalization group findings. Additionally, we demonstrate its efficacy on the $\mathbb{Z}_3$ Haagerup model, a recently discovered quantum critical system lacking a conventional field-theoretic description. In this case, our approach yields the full spectrum of relevant and marginal boundary operators, alongside precise estimates for entanglement entropy and entanglement entropy density. These outcomes represent the most accurate results to date and significantly surpass the capabilities of density-matrix renormalization group techniques. Finally, we discuss the method's applicability to higher-dimensional systems. This work is conducted in collaboration with J. B\'{e}rard, J. Bergli, and M. B\'{a}r\'{a}sz. Part-of-speech (POS) tagging serves as a fundamental NLP task, typically approached by training neural networks on extensive, high-quality annotated corpora. However, applying these models to historical texts often yields unreliable results due to the scarcity of sufficient training data and the significant challenges posed by archaic vocabulary and syntax. To address this, we propose a new method for labeling historical documents that generates an upper confidence bound for POS labels, thereby enhancing the dependability of the output. This approach employs a set-valued forecast to represent the confidence level of each token's assigned category. We evaluate the efficacy of various set-valued forecasting techniques and introduce a novel strategy for integrating them into neural POS taggers. Our results demonstrate that this method produces more reliable labeling for historical collections compared to standard point-valued predictions, while also showing that the proposed system can leverage unlabeled data to improve overall reliability. We further assess the tagged outputs by analyzing the semantic coherence of the resulting segmentations. The code and data required to replicate our experiments are accessible at https://github.com/alexanderkollmer/set-valued-pos-tagging. A leading method for mitigating quantum errors is the application of quantum error correction codes. However, these codes demand substantial overhead in terms of both qubit counts and operational complexity. To address this, we propose a quantum error reduction protocol utilizing concealed inverses, which enables error correction with significantly fewer qubits and reduced complexity. This approach functions as a hybrid between quantum error correction and quantum error mitigation. We demonstrate the implementation of this protocol within superconducting quantum processors, which are highly susceptible to decoherence and operational errors. Our findings indicate that the overhead per qubit and the operation count can be decreased by up to 90% and 70%, respectively, compared to standard quantum error correction. Furthermore, we show that this protocol can achieve high-fidelity results for the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) and the variational quantum eigensolver (VQE). Specifically, for QAOA, we successfully executed a 14-qubit problem with a success probability of 50%, whereas for VQE, we achieved a chemical accuracy of $10^{-4}$ on a 9-qubit system. These results suggest that our proposal offers a promising avenue for advancing quantum computing capabilities. The article introduces a new statistical technique designed to estimate extreme thresholds and their associated copula for high-dimensional spatial datasets. This approach is particularly relevant in marine engineering for predicting "conditional peaks," which represent the most severe sea states a ship or offshore platform might encounter given specific environmental conditions. The proposed method relies on two primary components: a local Poisson process to estimate the threshold and a local copula to model conditional extremes. To ensure the method's practicality, the authors develop efficient estimators for both parts and validate their performance through simulation studies and a real-world application. The results demonstrate that the technique yields accurate estimates and produces meaningful predictions for conditional peaks in spatial data. Furthermore, the study confirms that the method remains effective even when data quality is reduced due to missing observations. Finally, the authors provide an open-source R package, \texttt{spatialPeaks}, to facilitate the implementation of this approach. Current pre-trained vision-language models (VLPs) often struggle to capture the visual semantics of images, particularly when the image-text pairs are not naturally aligned. To address this limitation, we introduce VT-CLIP, a framework that leverages images of objects to generate visual-directed texts, thereby enhancing the image representations of VLPs. This approach is grounded in the hypothesis that visual-directed texts are more effective at revealing an VLP's latent visual knowledge. We validate this hypothesis through an ablation study on the ImageNet dataset, demonstrating that VT-CLIP yields a 3.5% improvement in top-1 classification accuracy compared to the baseline. Furthermore, we extend this methodology to the COCO dataset, showing that VT-CAPTION produces more visually directed captions than the baseline, as evidenced by higher scores on the SPIDErs metric. Additionally, we observe that VT-CLIP improves the performance of various downstream tasks, including zero-shot classification and image description generation. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/ai4bme/VT-CLIP.

Controlling open quantum systems is a fundamental challenge in quantum information science, with applications spanning quantum simulation, thermodynamics, and chemistry. This study introduces a method utilizing operator-valued time-dependent Hamiltonians to steer open quantum systems, demonstrating that the method is universal and capable of achieving arbitrary unitary evolution. We illustrate its utility through a universal noisy quantum simulator for matrix multiplication, which remains robust against both coherent and incoherent noise. This approach offers a versatile framework for addressing diverse problems, such as the universal preparation of quantum states and their corresponding density matrices. Furthermore, we show that the universal state preparation protocol is inherently resilient to both types of noise. Additionally, we introduce an operator-valine model for quantum thermodynamics, which enables the universal extraction of work from quantum batteries against thermalization effects. These findings underscore the broad applicability of operator-valued time-dependent control, particularly in the presence of quantum noise. Our work establishes a pathway toward universal quantum simulators and devices that function effectively despite environmental noise. The associated software is publicly accessible. Furthermore, we establish that if $X$ is an $F$-regular local Noetherian algebraic $k$-scheme, it necessarily admits a compact formal Hilbert polynomial. We also examine the relationship between the compact formal Hilbert polynomial and the local Hilbert polynomial. Additionally, we define the compact formal dimension for $k$-local rings and prove that an $F$-regular local Noetherian algebraic $k$-scheme $X$ is $Q$-Gorenstein if and only if its compact formal dimension equals the codimension of its associated graded ring. Finally, we extend the definition of the compact formal dimension to $k$-local rings that are not necessarily algebra schemes. In this generalized setting, we characterize $Q$-factorial $F$-regular local Noetherian algebraic $k$-schemes as those whose associated graded rings exhibit a formal Hilbert polynomial of degree zero. We further characterize factorial $F$-regular local Noetherian algebraic $k$-schemes as those where the local Hilbert polynomial of the associated graded ring has a degree no greater than the Krull dimension of the scheme. Moreover, we demonstrate that factorial $F$-regular local Noetherian algebraic $k$-schemes satisfy the strong $F$-regularity criterion. We also characterize factorial $F$-regular local Noetherian algebraic $k$-schemes as those where the local Hilbert polynomial of the associated graded ring has a degree equal to the Krull dimension of the scheme. Finally, we characterize $F$-regular local Noetherian algebraic $k$-schemes by noting that their local Hilbert polynomials are polynomials in the variable $q^{d}$, where $d$ represents the Krull dimension of the scheme. Quantitative image analysis in radiology and pathology is a rapidly expanding field that relies on the standardized reporting of image analysis outcomes. While DICOM is the established standard for image data, there is currently no equivalent standard for describing annotations or analysis results. This absence hinders the reproducibility of results and complicates data exchange between institutions. To address this, we present highdicom, a Python framework designed to facilitate the encoding and exchange of image annotations and analysis results. This tool is particularly relevant for radiology and histopathology, offering a unified approach to describe annotations across both modalities using the same encoding scheme. The framework adheres to the DICOM standard and integrates with pydicom, the most widely used Python library for DICOM handling. Additionally, it supports annotation schemes from the Data Dictionary for Pathology and Imaging Research (DDPIR) and the Histopathology Annotation Scheme (HASC). We demonstrate the framework's capabilities by generating annotations for the TCGA breast cancer dataset and a whole slide image from the Digital Pathology Challenge 2018. The highdicom package is freely available on PyPI and GitHub. The framework's ability to generate annotations for large, complex image datasets indicates its potential for scalable and efficient processing. By enabling the exchange of image annotations, highdicom is poised to significantly enhance the reproducibility of image analysis. Furthermore, it offers a flexible and extensible solution for developing new annotation schemes, thereby supporting the growing field of quantitative image analysis.
