Furthermore, we utilize this method to analyze the Hodge structures associated with K3 surfaces possessing a high count of algebraic 2-cycles. Additionally, we examine the connected components of the K3 moduli space where the count of additional 2-cycles remains constant. Our approach relies on the Torelli theorem for K3 surfaces and an algebraic analysis of the period domain. In the concluding section, we establish a conjecture regarding the rationality of the L-function for K3 surfaces with a large number of algebraic 2-cycles. This conclusion is achieved by explicitly calculating the zeta function of a specific finite graph, which encodes the necessary local data for the K3 surface. We present a straightforward estimation technique grounded in Euler's polyhedral formula, which yields the exact genus for thick graphs. This approach utilizes the expansion properties of adjacency matrices to determine graph embeddability on surfaces and integrates these findings with the structure theory of matrix powers. Our work establishes the first genus estimation bound for highly connected graphs, proving that for any thick graph $G$, the genus $\gamma(G)$ equals $c_G + o(|V(G)|)$ as $|V(G)|$ grows, where $c_G$ denotes the number of edges in a spanning forest of $G$. This result further indicates that the genus of a thick graph is nearly entirely determined by its spanning forests. Additionally, we derive a lower bound for the genus of $k$-expander graphs that is independent of the number of vertices. Our findings also extend to multigraphs, enabling the genus estimation of multi-expander graphs. We demonstrate that the genus of a multigraph $G$ satisfies $\gamma(G) \geq \lfloor \frac{e(G)-f(G)}{2} \rfloor$, where $e(G)$ and $f(G)$ represent the counts of edges and faces, respectively, in an embedding of $G$ on a surface. This result strengthens a longstanding conjecture by J. Kahn and M. Szabó, who proposed that $\gamma(G) = \lfloor \frac{e(G)-f(G)}{2} \rfloor$ for all multigraphs. We also provide a constructive proof of a theorem by B. Mohar and S. Oum regarding the characterization of the genus for thick multigraphs. Finally, we offer a concise proof of a conjecture by B. Mohar and S. Oum concerning the genus of $k$-expander multigraphs. This paper introduces a randomized Newton approach designed for high-dimensional distributed convex optimization. In this framework, a master node coordinates a collection of worker nodes, each trained on a subset of data and performing a specific computational task. The master node then integrates the outputs from all workers to update the solution. The proposed Distributed Randomized Newton (DRN) method achieves a per-iteration complexity of $O(d)$, where $d$ represents the feature dimensionality. This efficiency is made possible by restricting the Newton search direction to the null space of the master's gradient, thereby minimizing the communication overhead associated with solving the Newton system. We demonstrate that DRN converges to a first-order stationary point with a rate of $O(1/k)$, matching the performance of fully centralized Newton methods. Furthermore, under a data distribution assumption, we prove that DRN converges to a second-order stationary point at a rate of $O(1/k^2)$. Additionally, we establish that DRN attains an optimization error of $O(1/k)$ for smooth non-convex problems. Numerical experiments conducted on both synthetic and real-world datasets validate the method's effectiveness. The code is accessible at \url{https://github.com/ChenchenWang1997/DRN}. This research examines neural network-based models for identifying hate speech in Hindi and Bengali, employing both transfer learning and data augmentation techniques. We evaluated various architectures, including LSTM, Bi-LSTM, CNN, Bi-GRU, and Bi-LSTM-CNN, utilizing BERT pre-trained embeddings for the Hindi language. Our primary contributions involve the first comprehensive investigation into hate speech detection for both languages, the application of transfer learning to Bengali, and the use of data augmentation to enhance performance on both Hindi and Bengali datasets. Experimental results indicate that the Bi-LSTM-CNN model yields the highest accuracy for both languages, achieving 99.1% accuracy on the Hindi dataset and 98.1% accuracy on the Bengali dataset when using pre-trained BERT embeddings. Furthermore, we observed that data augmentation improves model performance on both Hindi and Bengali datasets. Finally, we provide a detailed analysis of the most and least frequent classes within the Hindi and Bengali hate speech datasets. High-resolution gas time projection chambers (TPCs) utilizing solid-state detectors are capable of measuring the recoil energy and trajectory of particles generated by nuclear reactions. These devices offer superior sensitivity and a broader detection cross-section compared to individual target experiments, making them ideal for measuring rare and forbidden transitions in beta decay, as well as detecting dark matter candidates like neutrinos and majoranas. This study presents a theoretical framework for characterizing the performance of such TPCs through three key metrics: the average number of electrons per primary ionization ($\bar{n}_e$), the average number of clusters per primary ionization ($\bar{N}_c$), and the average cluster size ($\bar{S}_c$). The approach employs a modified Birks' law to simulate the distribution of electron density within microscopic clusters and applies a Poisson distribution to model the count of these clusters. The proposed model is validated against experimental data from a 2017 study involving a $^{214}$Po source. Furthermore, the paper derives the average number of "lost" electrons and discusses the impact of the average ionization size on cluster formation. Finally, the framework is applied to evaluate the performance of a TPC targeperiment using $^{212}$Po as the source. The results indicate that a 100 cm$^3$ TPC filled with 300 mbar of Argon can achieve a resolution of 1.5 keV FWHM, with an expected average of 10 electrons per cluster. These findings suggest that gas TPCs can achieve recoil energy resolutions comparable to those of solid-state detectors. Additionally, the methodology for estimating the average electron count per cluster is applicable to other detector types, such as bolometers and semiconductor detectors. This work serves as a foundation for developing a comprehensive performance model for gas TPCs, which will facilitate the optimization of experimental parameters, including gas type, pressure, and volume. The code used for these calculations is publicly available at https://github.com/alejandro-ruiz-ruiz/TPC_Performance_Model. Commercial driving represents a labor-intensive sector with profound implications for individuals, families, and communities. The rise of technology, including telematics, electronic logging devices, and telemarketing tools, has transformed driver supervision, evaluation, and performance assessment. Nevertheless, the widespread adoption of telematics has intensified scrutiny on drivers, often resulting in unfair assessments and evaluations. This study examines the development of a new moderation framework designed to enhance the fairness of driver performance evaluations. By integrating various contextual factors—such as weather conditions, traffic volume, and time of day—into the analysis of driving data, the proposed method employs machine learning to generate route-specific benchmarks. These benchmarks are used to moderate driver performance, thereby mitigating the impact of external contextual variables. The approach is validated using a comprehensive dataset of over 100,000 trips from a major North American trucking company. Results indicate that these benchmarks effectively account for contextual variations in driving behavior, with statistical significance confirmed through hypothesis testing. Furthermore, a simulation study demonstrates that incorporating route-specific benchmarks significantly improves the accuracy of driver performance assessments. The study concludes that route moderation serves as a more effective mechanism for achieving fair evaluations of commercial drivers. The methodology is implemented in an open-source Python package, and the associated data and code are publicly accessible. This work offers a novel, interpretable, and extensible framework for moderating driver performance, which can be readily applied to other industries and contexts. The findings are expected to influence future research and the adoption of moderation techniques in commercial driving evaluations. We introduce a novel approach to modeling complex systems by treating them as a stochastic process within a high-dimensional Gaussian field manifold. This manifold is defined by a set of random variables, each representing a system configuration, with their joint probability distribution specified by a Gaussian functional. The deterministic dynamics of the complex system are represented as a geodesic pathway traversing this manifold. We establish the necessary and sufficient conditions for a stochastic field to admit geodesic geodesic pathways and derive the corresponding geodesic equation. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this geodesic equation can be decomposed into a set of coupled stochastic differential equations. As proof of concept, we apply our framework to two physical systems: a driven Brownian particle and a pendulum driven by white noise. In both cases, we show that the geodesic equation yields the standard stochastic equations of motion. Our methodology offers a unified framework for modeling a broad class of complex systems as geodesic pathways within stochastic field manifolds. This approach is particularly valuable for analyzing high-dimensional systems where the stochastic dynamics of individual components are interdependent. Additionally, our framework facilitates the analysis of complex systems using geometric techniques and provides a pathway for discovering new models of complex systems through geometric reasoning. The paper includes detailed mathematical derivations and explicit examples. All mathematical proofs can be verified using the accompanying Python code, which is provided in the supplementary materials. We believe this work will inspire further research into the application of geometric methods to stochastic processes. This paper examines the temporal dynamics of the (the) film market, specifically analyzing how the presence of a blockbuster in a given year influences the duration of positive and negative returns in subsequent years. This study theoretically examines the impact of a zigzag-edge defect graphene nanoribbon on electron transport within a two-terminal setup connected to metallic leads, focusing on how gate voltage and spin polarization influence this process. The research demonstrates that incorporating such a defect enables the regulation of both electron and spin currents. Specifically, the spin-dependent conductance can be tuned from a high-regime linear-bias regime to a low-regime linear-bias regime. Furthermore, the system exhibits spin-polarized quantum resonant tunneling, where the spin polarization of the tunneling current is controlled by adjusting the gate voltage. These findings suggest that the proposed device could serve as a promising candidate for developing spintronic technologies. Additionally, the study highlights that edge defects in graphene nanoribbons can be leveraged to advance both electronic and spintronic applications. Finally, the results indicate that the device operates effectively at room temperature. These outcomes were achieved by solving the discrete Landauer-Büttiker formalism equations for a two-terminal system, utilizing a tight-binding model for the graphene nanoribbon and nearest-neighbor coupling for the metallic leads. The theoretical framework was validated by comparing the calculated band structure and density of states with existing literature. The model was further extended to investigate the device's performance under varying conditions, including different lengths, widths, and edge defects. The study also explores the potential for achieving higher spin polarization by analyzing the device's behavior under different spin-polarization configurations. Overall, this work provides a comprehensive theoretical analysis of the relationship between edge defects and electron/spin transport in graphene nanoribbons, offering valuable insights for the development of new graphene-based electronic and spintronic devices. The findings are expected to have significant implications for the fields of physics, materials science, and engineering. Additionally, the research has the potential to contribute to the advancement of quantum computing and other emerging technologies. The concept of the Hamiltonian cycle can be extended to define $k$-Hamiltonian $n$-vertex graphs, meaning graphs with $n$ vertices where every subset of size $k$ is contained within some Hamiltonian cycle. This paper introduces and examines this notion, demonstrating a necessary and sufficient condition for a graph to be $k$-Hamiltonian based on its Hamiltonian independence number. Furthermore, we present a novel Hamiltonian cycle theorem that parallels Ore's Theorem. Utilizing this new theorem, we establish that the pancyclic property is a sufficient condition for a graph to be $k$-Hamiltonian.

Additionally, we introduce the notion of a $k$-independent set, which parallels the traditional definition of an independent set. Leveraging this concept, we derive a sufficient condition for $k$-Hamiltonicity. We also provide a straightforward algorithm to determine the $k$-independence number of a graph and employ this algorithm to prove that the $k$-independence number of a pancyclic graph does not exceed $k+1$. Finally, we explore the relationship between $k$-Hamiltonicity and other graph properties, including $r$-regularity, $r$-partiteness, and $r$-colorability. Notably, we demonstrate that for a $k$-independent graph with $n$ vertices, the $k$-Hamiltonian number is bounded above by $\frac{n}{k+1}$. This result is achieved by adapting the well-known proof that the chromatic number of a perfect graph equals its clique number.

As an application of our findings, we extend Dirac's Theorem. We show that for a graph $G$ with $n$ vertices where $n$ is even, if the degree of every vertex $v$ satisfies $d(v) \geq \frac{n}{2} + \frac{n}{4} - 1$, then $G$ possesses a Hamiltonian cycle. Additionally, we provide an example illustrating that this bound is the best possible. We also examine the case where $n$ is odd, proving that if $d(v) \geq \frac{n}{2} + \frac{n-1}{4} - 1$ for all vertices $v$, then $G$ contains a Hamiltonian cycle. We further illustrate that this bound is also optimal when $n$ is odd.

This study employs a multiparticle correlation analysis of Au+Au and isobar collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\textrm{NN}}}=$ 200 GeV to investigate the collective behavior of high-transverse momentum (high-$p_{\rm T}$) particles. By utilizing the three-dimensional balanced average flow framework, we examine both the magnitude and orientation of the average flow vector for various particle species, including high-$p_{\rm T}$ charged particles, electrons, muons, and jets. Our findings indicate that the orientation of the average flow vector remains consistent across different particle types within each collision system. Furthermore, the data reveal that the orientation of the average flow vector for high-$p_{\rm T}$ particles in isobar collisions differs significantly from that observed in p+p collisions. These results offer new insights into the mechanisms driving collective flow in high-energy nuclear collisions and suggest that a hydrodynamic model incorporating initial-state fluctuations can account for the observed phenomena. Additionally, the observed differences in the average flow vector orientation between isobar and p+p collisions may reflect distinct initial-state fluctuations. Finally, the fact that the average flow vector points in the same direction for both high-$p_{\rm T}$ particles and low-$p_{\rm T}$ particles in isobar collisions suggests that the initial conditions for these two particle types are likely similar. These conclusions are supported by the AMPT and EPOS-LHC models. Overall, this research provides a novel perspective on the collective motion of high-$p_{\rm T}$ particles in high-energy nuclear collisions. The methodology employed can be applied to future experiments, such as the Energy Upgrade at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (eRHIC) and the Electron-Ion Collider (EIC). Furthermore, the findings may offer valuable insights for future collider facilities, including the Future Circular Collider (FCC) and the Super Proton Proton Collider (Super Proton Collider). This study introduces a sparse-grid-driven adaptive spectral method designed to reconstruct the linear Koopman operator within state-space models. By utilizing spectral basis functions derived from orthogonal polynomials, the approach offers enhanced interpretability and superior performance in extrapolation. The adaptive spectral technique constructs a sparse-grid-based linear Koopman model, enabling efficient exploration of high-dimensional state spaces. Furthermore, the method employs a greedy selection strategy to identify the most informative states for linear Koopman operator analysis. Applications to various dynamical systems demonstrate the proposed technique's effectiveness in predicting system dynamics and in extracting interpretable, low-dimensional linear models from nonlinear systems. Additionally, the method is applied to analyze the dynamics of a nonlinearly coupled power grid, where the resulting linear model facilitates the design of a low-dimensional controller. The paper concludes with a discussion of the technique's limitations and potential future research directions. This study introduces a novel complex scaling approach grounded in the density functional theory of the electron ground state. By employing a complex coordinate transformation on spatial variables, the method generates a scaled electron density that maintains the essential physical characteristics of the original, including the ground state energy, orbital energy, and total kinetic energy. To address the practical challenges of applying this transformation to extensive atomic and molecular systems, the paper proposes a practical implementation utilizing Gaussian-type orbitals. This "outside complicated scaling method" is computationally efficient, requiring only the adjustment of scaling parameters for outer regions. The technique's validity is confirmed through applications to helium, the hydrogen molecule, and the neon atom. Furthermore, the method's potential for strong-field physics applications is demonstrated by analyzing ionization and absorption spectra. These spectra are derived from the ground state energy's dependence on the scaling parameter, with the kinetic energy's sensitivity to this parameter serving as an indicator of excited states. The approach offers a fresh perspective for investigating atomic and molecular systems within intense electric fields. Additionally, the method's utility extends to other scenarios involving large deformations of the electron density, such as those caused by external magnetic fields. The Sinkhorn-Byzanzer algorithm is a well-established iterative method for solving the Schrödinger problem, defined by a system of linear equations derived from an irreducible stochastic matrix. This matrix is constructed from a pair of discrete probability measures and a discrete, non-negative, irreducible cost function, ensuring the problem's solution always exists. However, when the cost function is replaced by a continuous function defined on a closed set, existence is guaranteed only if a solution exists; otherwise, the problem is deemed unsolvable. This document demonstrates that the Sinkhorn iteration still converges to the optimal solution in this scenario, provided a specific condition is met: the infimum of the entropic risk must be attainable by a valid probability distribution supported on the closed cost function domain. Furthermore, this condition is sufficient to ensure that Sinkhorn iterations converge to the optimal solution regardless of their initial starting point. The paper also presents illustrative examples, including one that highlights the necessity of this condition. These findings extend previous work by the authors, which established the existence of solutions and convergence of Sinkhorn iterations for continuous costs under stricter assumptions. The current results are particularly applicable to a broad class of problems in information theory, such as the Blahum-Arizananda algorithm for computing channel capacity, and to continuous optimal transport issues. Finally, numerical experiments confirm that the Sinkhorn method remains effective even when solutions do not exist. This study presents the measurement of top-quark pair production in proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s}=5.02$ TeV, utilizing the ATLAS detector at the LHC. The analysis focuses on events where both top quarks decay leptonically. A total of 22.6 fb$^{-1}$ of data was collected during the LHC Run 2 period. The differential cross-sections are determined as functions of the invariant mass, transverse momentum, and rapidity of the $t\bar{t}$ system, along with the individual rapidities of the top quarks. The primary uncertainty in these differential measurements stems from the limited event statistics. Additionally, the absolute cross-section is calculated, yielding a value of $\sigma_{t\bar{t}} = 822 \pm 10$ (stat) $\pm 14$ (syst) pb, which aligns with the predictions of next-to-next-to-leading order (NNLO) perturbative QCD. The observed distributions are also compared against various theoretical models. Furthermore, the study examines the production of $t\bar{t}$ events accompanied by one or two additional jets. The cross-sections for these specific channels are also determined. Finally, the study investigates the production of $t\bar{t}$ events with at least three jets, specifically those containing at least one or two jets with transverse momentum exceeding 200 GeV. The cross-sections for these categories are also calculated. The differential cross-sections are compared with leading-order (LO) and next-to-leading-order (NLO) perturbative QCD predictions, as well as with results from other experiments. This study examines the localization dynamics of a central site within a ring of $N$ sites connected to it. The ring is governed by a localized Anderson model, while the central site follows either a localized or delocalized Anderson model. We demonstrate that although the central site can be localized even when the entire system is delocalized, its localization dynamics are significantly slower than those of the global system. Furthermore, we establish that the localization length of the central site scales with the global localization length as $l_{\rm center}\sim l_{\rm global}^{0.5}$. These findings were validated through numerical simulations of the system's time evolution. Additionally, we derived analytical expressions for the localization length and the time required for localization, which align well with the numerical results. Finally, we explored the impact of the initial state on both the localization length and the dynamics of localization. These outcomes are anticipated to be applicable to various coupled systems, including those found in physics, chemistry, and biology. Our results may also hold relevance for the design of materials and devices, such as those involving quantum dots and quantum wells. Specifically, the observation that a central site can be localized despite a delocalized global system could be leveraged to engineer devices with specific functional properties. For instance, the central site could serve as a memory unit, while the rest of the system functions as a bus for data transfer. This could be achieved by adjusting the coupling strength between the central site and the rest of the system. Additionally, the coupling strength could be tuned to control the rate of localization at the central site. These concepts are expected to be useful in the development of quantum information devices. Finally, our findings may contribute to the design of new materials with unique characteristics, such as those exhibiting memory properties. For example, the localization of the central site could be utilized to create materials with enhanced stability under varying environmental conditions. The coupling strength could be adjusted to achieve the desired level of central site localization. Overall, our findings have broad implications across diverse scientific and technological fields. By enabling the design of systems with specific properties, our findings could lead to advancements in quantum computing, energy harvesting, and many other areas. For example, the localization of the central site could be harnessed to create more efficient solar cells or to develop new types of quantum sensors. The coupling strength could be adjusted to achieve the desired level of central site localization, thereby optimizing the performance of these devices. In conclusion, our findings have far-reaching implications for a wide range of scientific and technological disciplines

The paper aims to establish new inclusion relations within the Janowski category by utilizing generalized Bessel functions as markers. It  integrates these functions, which possess specific convexity characteristics, into inequalities and inclusion relations to generate novel results and unify existing ones. The study emphasizes the inclusion relations of the class $\mathcal{SB}_B(\alpha,\beta)$, defined as $\mathcal{SB}_B(\alpha,\beta):=\Big\{f\in\mathcal{A}:\frac{zB'(z)}{B(z)}\prec\frac{1+\beta z}{1+\alpha z},\,\alpha,\beta\in(-1,1)\Big\}$, where $\mathcal{A}$ denotes the set of all functions analytic in the unit disk $\mathbb{D}:=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:\,|z|<1\}$. Additionally, the work examines the univalence of the function $\frac{zB'(z)}{B(z)}$ associated with these inclusion relations.

The pandemic-induced confinement measures altered human interaction patterns, thereby influencing urban mobility. This study examines the impact of the pandemic on interaction income inequality across various urban mobility contexts in France. Our findings indicate that the confinement significantly increased income inequality in urban interactions, a trend that was further amplified by behavioral shifts driven by the pandemic. Specifically, individuals with higher incomes relied more heavily on private transport modes, whereas those with lower incomes experienced a more pronounced reduction in face-to-face interactions. These results underscore the critical need to examine how behavioral changes during the pandemic intensified income disparities within urban social interactions. Furthermore, our results suggest that the pandemic's effect on income inequality was more significant than that of age, highlighting the pivotal role of income in shaping changes in urban interactions. These insights are essential for comprehending the social consequences of confinement and for designing policies aimed at mitigating the exacerbation of income inequality in urban interactions. The study's code and data are accessible at https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.14750050.

This study evaluates the performance of a nonlinear field-separated (NFS) preconditioner applied to a two-phase flow model based on the Richards equation, solving for saturation and pressure. The method utilizes a Newton-Krylov framework where the Jacobian-Krylov system is preconditioned by replacing the mixed-pressure subspace with two independent pressure spaces, thereby enhancing the properties of the resulting block-diagonal system. While the efficacy of nonlinear field-separated methods has been validated across various models, this work specifically examines their application to two-phase flow in heterogeneous porous media, addressing challenges such as low permeability contrasts and complex topographies. We assess the proposed NFS preconditioner against a standard block-diagonal approach and a recent block-triangular variant. Our findings indicate that the NFS preconditioner is highly effective for this specific model, demonstrating superior performance compared to both block-triangular and block-diagonal alternatives. Furthermore, the NFS method exhibits greater robustness when solving sequences of problems with progressively increasing permeability contrasts. Finally, the NFS preconditioner is recommended for use in high-performance computing environments. The study includes detailed results from a single-phase flow benchmark and a two-phase flow benchmark featuring both horizontal and vertical permeability contrasts. The latter was conducted in collaboration with the T2P2 project, a European initiative dedicated to advancing two-phase flow modeling in porous media. All simulations were executed on the SuperMUC-2 supercomputer at the Leibniz Supercomputing Centre in Munich, Germany. The source code is accessible via the open-source T2P2 project repository. The numerical experiments presented here were performed using a restricted subset of the full grid. The NFS preconditioner is anticipated to deliver even more significant performance improvements when applied to the complete grid. We introduce a method to measure heating rates and speeds within a two-dimensional Coulomb crystal by analyzing the temperature and state distributions of its normal modes. By comparing the experimentally determined temperature dependence of the spin decay rate with theoretical predictions, we can deduce the temperature distributions of the crystals' normal modes. This approach enables the investigation of heating rates and speed variations in the ion lattice. The study utilizes a two-dimensional lattice composed of $49$ $^{9}\mathrm{Be}^{+}$ ions, where lattice temperature is regulated via laser heating. The results indicate that the fastest heating modes correspond to those with the highest phase velocities. Furthermore, the observed heating speeds are independent of the initial lattice temperature and the specific heating method employed. These findings align with the hypothesis that heating is driven by spontaneous Raman scattering of acoustic phonons off the trapping laser. The maximum heating speed reaches approximately $1.5$ mK/ms, a rate that poses significant challenges for quantum information processing. This research was conducted using the 2D Coulomb crystal at the National Institute of Information and Communications Technology (NICT) in Japan. The NICT ion trap is renowned for its exceptional stability, facilitating the realization of long-lived spin qubits and high-fidelity quantum gates. The lattice's exceptional thermal stability is crucial for advancing quantum information processing capabilities. The methodology presented here offers a valuable tool for investigating heating mechanisms in ion traps, thereby facilitating the development of more efficient cooling techniques for quantum information processing. This study introduces a fully quantum mechanical approach grounded in time-dependent density functional theory (TD-DFT) to investigate the nonlinear enhancement mechanisms of tip-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (TERS). The method explicitly accounts for the complex electronic and light-matter interactions occurring at the junction between a silver nanoparticle and a tip positioned near a benzene molecule. By employing a realistic, experimentally derived excitation source, we demonstrate that TERS is driven by a combination of coherent Raman scattering and inelastic photon absorption. Furthermore, our findings reveal that the nonlinear amplification of the Raman signal in TERS is a direct consequence of the strong coupling between the electromagnetic field and the quantum states of both the metal and the benzene molecule. These results offer a comprehensive theoretical framework for modeling TERS and establish a foundation for future experimental investigations. Additionally, the proposed model is designed to be applicable to a broad spectrum of molecules and metal nanostructures. The accompanying Python code is publicly accessible. This study reports on microwave observations of 10 nearby galaxies conducted with the Sardinia Radio Telescope (SRT) as part of a survey designed to detect non-thermal emission and potential microwave background signals. The observations were carried out at 18 GHz (1.7 cm) and 22 GHz (1.3 cm) using the SRT's K-band. The selected galaxies were chosen based on their star formation rates, which were derived from optical imaging data. We identified a significant radio excess at 18 GHz relative to the 22 GHz band in NGC 4038/39 (Arp 273), a system undergoing a major merger. Additionally, we detected a radio excess at 22 GHz compared to the 18 GHz band in NGC 4435, a galaxy characterized by a high concentration of radio galaxies. These findings suggest the presence of a local spectral feature in the microwave range, which may be attributed to synchrotron emission from relativistic electrons within the galaxies. Furthermore, we observed a radio excess at 22 GHz relative to the 18 GHz band in NGC 4438, a galaxy with a low star formation rate. The data from this survey will be utilized to constrain the microwave background spectrum and to search for anomalous microwave emission. This study investigates the entropy shifts occurring during the phase transition in ammonium sulfate ($(NH_4)_2SO_4$), a well-established ferroelectric material. By employing a combination of calorimetry, dielectric measurements, and first-principles calculations, we demonstrate that the notable entropy variation linked to lattice soft modes cannot be attributed to the specific heat anomaly associated with the phase transition. Instead, our analysis indicates that configurational entropy plays a substantial role in driving the entropy change during the transition in this ferroelectric compound. These findings offer valuable insights for understanding the entropy alterations in other promising solid-state caloric materials. Furthermore, our results suggest that the entropy change in ammonium sulfate is not exclusively of pure electric origin, thereby challenging the conventional view that ferroelectricity is synonymous with electric caloric effects. Consequently, our work underscores the necessity of disentangling the diverse microscopic contributions to entropy changes in caloric materials to fully comprehend their underlying mechanisms. Ultimately, this research paves the way for developing a novel category of caloric materials that exhibit large caloric effects without relying on electric polarization. This could potentially lead to the creation of new caloric devices that are safer, more reliable, and more environmentally friendly than their electric counterparts. Additionally, our methodology is applicable to investigating entropy alterations in other materials, including those with non-ferroelectric natures. Finally, the first-principles approach employed in this study holds potential for advancing the understanding of entropy changes in various materials, which is essential for the future design of advanced caloric materials. Reinforcement learning (RL) models are frequently employed to analyze decision-making processes, yet the specific cognitive strategies individuals utilize to execute these computations remain poorly understood. This study introduces a method to identify the RL strategies most aligned with neural activity. We applied this approach to the BOLD signals of 20 participants performing a probabilistic learning task. By correlating midbrain activity with various candidate strategies, we found that BOLD responses primarily encode negative prediction errors utilizing an Rescorla-Wagner learning rate. These results indicate that while suboptimal RL strategies can emerge during learning, they do not correspond to distinct patterns of brain activity. Furthermore, the magnitude of the fMRI-encoded learning rate serves as a robust predictor of behavioral performance. These findings offer a framework for investigating the neural mechanisms underlying RL and suggest that the fMRI signal is a potent indicator of the learning rate, which may vary between individuals or across different tasks. Finally, we discuss the broader implications of these results for interpreting RL-based fMRI research. The data and analysis code are accessible at https://github.com/NeuroMLab/RL-fMRI. We have previously suggested that the root structure, which gives rise to the Dynkin diagram of the 8D real algebra $E_8$, can be physically realized through the entanglement of two 4D qubit systems, as depicted in a Schmidt decomposition. This paper extends that framework to the complexified version of the 4D qubits, thereby creating a physical model for the complex algebra of $E_8$. This extension enables a natural modeling of the 4D spacetime coordinates and the momentum vector associated with the 4D qubits. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the 240 momentum vectors correspond to the outcomes of a generalized Bell inequality experiment conducted on the 4D qubits, with locality defined by the entanglement structure. Consequently, contextuality is inherent in the observed results, aligning with the Kochen-Specker theorem. This representation provides a new perspective on the relationship between the basis vectors of the 4D qubits and the momentum vectors of the entangled state. The error rates associated with both classical and quantum computational assessments can be significantly reduced through post-processing. We introduce an iterative approach that leverages Bayesian statistics to enhance the accuracy of classical computation evaluations. This method is straightforward to implement, applicable to any computation, and capable of eliminating errors that scale linearly with the problem size. We validate this technique using quantum circuit simulations, demonstrating that it effectively mitigates errors arising from both classical readout and quantum simulation limitations. Furthermore, we show that our approach surpasses the performance of the standard majority vote method. Finally, we illustrate how this post-processing strategy can be employed to determine the computational complexity of problems. Our findings indicate that this technique is broadly applicable to the assessment of classical, quantum, and hybrid computations. This paper introduces a new framework called "collective autonomy," which enables robot systems to function as integrated entities by allowing individual robots to autonomously perceive, reason, and act. We outline the motivation behind this framework and demonstrate its application in a study where a group of robots autonomously learns to play a game of Go. The results indicate that the framework can facilitate the interaction between autonomous robot systems. Furthermore, we discuss the relationship between collective autonomy and existing concepts of collective intelligence, highlighting both their similarities and differences. Finally, we explore the potential of this framework for future research into creating autonomous robot systems capable of contributing to scientific discovery. We introduce HiTMap, a novel hierarchical topological map designed for navigation in unfamiliar settings. This H-TMap integrates a topological diagram of the environment with the spatial arrangement of its nodes, utilizing a new hierarchical topological diagram representation to bridge these two perspectives. The system learns the H-TMap through a single, unified training process that concurrently addresses topological diagram learning and spatial map representation. Furthermore, HiTMap supports graph-based path planning and provides a straightforward interface for navigation in unknown environments. Experimental results demonstrate that HiTMap achieves superior performance in both topological diagram and path representation compared to existing methods. Additionally, it offers a user-friendly interface that allows users to input topological information via a diagram editor, thereby facilitating navigation in unfamiliar areas. This paper introduces a two-dimensional array of complex sequences, grounded in multivariable functions, designed for two-dimensional localization. The Z-supplementary array features rows and columns that are mutually orthogonal, with each row and column containing exactly one zero-length sequence. This zero-length sequence is positioned at the center of the array. The study presents two distinct construction methods for these array sequences. Numerical simulations demonstrate that the proposed two-dimensional array achieves higher transmission capacity than conventional one-dimensional array codes. Furthermore, the analysis indicates that the array maintains robust performance even under severe conditions, including multipath fading, low signal-to-noise ratios, and large-scale transmission. These characteristics render the array particularly suitable for two-dimensional wireless localization systems. Additionally, the paper explores the application of these sequences in two-dimensional radar systems, specifically for target detection and parameter estimation. It is shown that the supplementary array enhances the radar's two-dimensional resolution. Finally, a closed-form expression for the mean square error of the parameter estimator is derived. Simulation results confirm that the proposed estimator outperforms the maximum likelihood estimator in terms of accuracy. Computed Tomography (CT) is a prevalent imaging technique in both medical and industrial contexts. However, conventional CT reconstruction methods often suffer from excessive sensor noise and the inability to distinguish between different materials. This study introduces a novel framework that simultaneously reconstructs images, mitigates sensor noise, and performs material breakdown. The proposed approach integrates a physics-informed variational model with a data-driven deep learning algorithm. Specifically, a physics-informed variational regularizer is developed to achieve these three objectives concurrently, while a deep learning algorithm is employed to optimize the resulting non-convex variational formulation. Numerical experiments validate the effectiveness of the proposed framework. The results demonstrate that the proposed method surpasses existing techniques in both image reconstruction and material breakdown capabilities. Furthermore, the proposed CT reconstruction outperforms traditional total variation-based methods by significantly reducing noise. Finally, the developed CT denoising and material breakdown framework proves to be more efficient than state-of-the-art approaches. This study examines how electron outflow and nonlocality influence gap surface plasmons as the space between two jellium slabs approaches zero. The analysis reveals that the impact of electron outflow diminishes significantly when the interval is nearly nonexistent, whereas the effect of nonlocality remains substantial under the same conditions. These findings are substantiated by numerical results. Furthermore, the research demonstrates that the local hydrodynamic model, which previously accounted for electron outflow, can now be effectively replaced by the local Planck model. This simplification facilitates the development of more efficient numerical algorithms for simulating plasmonic nanostructures. Finally, the paper derives the correct boundary conditions for the new model. Theoretically, these conditions indicate that the electric field within the vacuum gap must vanish, a result that aligns with the numerical simulations. Additionally, the derived boundary conditions successfully recover the known limit of surface plasmons on a single jellium slab. The consistency of these findings confirms the validity of the local Planck model. Finally, the surface plasmon energy for a nanoscale structure composed of two touching jellium slabs is calculated and compared against both local hydrodynamic and Planck models, showing excellent agreement. This confirms that the local Planck model accurately captures the essential physics of plasmons in plasmonic nanostructures. Consequently, the Planck model serves as a viable alternative to the local hydrodynamic model for the simulation and design of plasmonic devices. This conclusion is supported by the fact that the Planck model is computationally more efficient than the local hydrodynamic model. Overall, the local Planck model offers a robust framework for the simulation and design of plasmonic devices. This study introduces a novel approach to named entity recovery that leverages term importance feedback. We hypothesize that the semantic value of a sentence can be effectively captured by aggregating the importance scores of its individual terms. By utilizing a neural sentence-value model, we transform these sentence values into value embeddings and integrate them with standard semantic embeddings to train recovery models. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed term importance feedback model enhances context understanding, achieving state-of-the-art performance in named entity recovery across two large-scale datasets. Furthermore, we show that this model outperforms existing methods in low-resource scenarios by effectively utilizing the available training data. Finally, we provide an analysis of the learned term importance scores to validate the hypothesis that such scores accurately reflect the importance of terms within the sentence context. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2018/TIF4NER. This work was presented at EMNLP 2019.

We introduce a new category of interactive data visualization designed to facilitate engagement with single- and multi-channel time series and time sequences. These visualizations are grounded in the concept of temporal context, which we define as a collection of time points linked by shared events or semantic meaning. Temporal context is fundamental to numerous domains, including biological and financial events, historical records, and social media timelines. Our approach extends the principles of traditional 2D and 3D screen-based visualization to handle temporal data. We present a conceptual framework for designing interactive visualizations of temporal context and demonstrate their application through three motivating case studies. These examples illustrate how such visualizations can enhance user understanding of temporal context and its associated data. Furthermore, we outline the design and implementation of a proof-of-concept system that integrates these visualizations with time-aware information retrieval. This system enables users to interact with temporal contexts and their related data, thereby supporting more intuitive data exploration and analysis. We anticipate that this work will inspire further research into the visualization of temporal contexts and their connections to related information. Digital health records (DHRs) are essential for delivering high-quality, cost-effective care, yet their complexity and volume often hinder healthcare providers from deriving timely insights. While data mining and machine learning have been applied to DHRs, they frequently overlook the unstructured nature of clinical data and the diverse, heterogeneous patterns within it. To address these challenges, we introduce the Diverse Similarity Graph Neural Network (DiSeGNN), a novel framework designed to extract knowledge from digital health records. This approach constructs a patient knowledge graph to capture various relationships among clinical entities and leverages graph neural networks to identify diverse patterns for predicting clinical events. We validated DiSeGNN using a cohort of 1,000 patients with sepsis, demonstrating that it significantly outperforms several baseline methods in predicting sepsis onset. Furthermore, the model's ability to uncover diverse patterns from the data offers valuable clinical insights. These findings suggest that DiSeGNN holds promise for enhancing healthcare delivery and could be applied to other domains involving complex, heterogeneous data. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ashishkumar1990/DiSeGNN. This study examines the electric double layer (EDL) forming near a charged soft interface within an electrolyte solution that accounts for solvent polarization. Using a mean-field approach, we derive numerical solutions for the Poisson-Boltzmann equation incorporating solvent polarization effects. Our findings indicate that accounting for solvent polarization significantly alters electrostatic interactions between the charged soft interface and the electrolyte. Specifically, these effects substantially influence both the surface potential and the thickness of the electric double layer. Furthermore, we observe that solvent polarization can induce a transition from Debye screening to anti-screening behavior. These results offer valuable insights into the physical mechanisms governing electrostatic interactions at charged soft interfaces in electrolyte solutions where solvent polarization is relevant. Ultimately, this work underscores the necessity of including solvent polarization when analyzing electrostatic phenomena at charged soft interfaces in such environments. Software specifications are crucial for developing and maintaining software systems, yet they demand significant time and effort to create. While numerous approaches exist for generating specifications from requirements, they typically depend on structured inputs like formal descriptions or structured documents such as Word files. This paper introduces an approach that derives specifications from unorganized textual sources, such as web pages and emails. We outline the methodology and demonstrate its effectiveness through a use case involving the generation of specifications for the OpenStreetMap API from available text materials. The results indicate that the approach successfully produced high-quality specifications, with most requirements identified in the generated outputs also present in the original unorganized texts. Furthermore, we have released an open-source tool implementing this methodology, which is available at https://github.com/UnorganizedSpecs/UnorganizedSpecs. This tool is designed to be extensible, allowing users to incorporate their own domain-specific knowledge to enhance the quality of the generated specifications. We demonstrate how such extensions can be implemented and how they improve specification quality. Finally, we discuss the approach's limitations and outline potential future research directions. This paper introduces a collaborative network encoding framework designed to minimize the total energy consumption of a communication network. Within this framework, relays are permitted to jointly optimize their timetabling and network encoding power levels, while sources and sinks adhere to predefined schedules and encoding/decoding configurations. To address the resulting non-convex optimization challenge, we propose a suboptimal algorithm that simultaneously solves the joint timetabling and power distribution problem for the relays. This approach transforms the problem into a sequence of convex subproblems, leveraging the fact that the feasible region of the relay timing schedules forms a convex polytope. Furthermore, we establish the convergence of this algorithm and its resulting solution to an optimal problem, demonstrating through a case study that the proposed method achieves significant energy reductions compared to existing schemes. The case study findings indicate that the proposed solution is within 1.5% of the optimal solution. Additionally, we show that the computational complexity of our algorithm scales linearly with the number of relays. Finally, the proposed solution is implemented in C++ and made available as an open-source software package. The source code for this implementation can be accessed at: https://github.com/abhisheksingh123456789/Network-Encoding. This implementation includes a function that accepts a .mat file containing source and sink transmission schedules as input and outputs a .mat file with the optimized relay timetabling and power distribution results. The function also supports the inclusion of a .mat file with a user-defined cost function. The output includes a plot of the source, sink, and relay transmission schedules, along with the value of the cost function. The cost function is defined as the sum of transmission energies for all sources, sinks, and relays, weighted by a factor alpha. The alpha value is determined by the ratio of relay nodes to the total number of nodes in the network. The relativistic initial principles theory of Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states is applied to an Mn adatom and Mn dimers situated on Nb(110) surface. The study utilizes a hybrid density functional theory (DFT) framework, employing the HSE06 exchange-correlation functional to calculate the exchange coupling constant $J$ within the YSR formula. Spin-polarized tunneling conductance spectra are computed for these systems. Results indicate that the HSE06 functional yields YSR splitting values of $0.12\,\mathrm{eV}$ for an Mn adatom and $0.08\,\mathrm{eV}$ for an Mn dimer on Nb(110). Furthermore, the calculated tunneling conductance spectra align with experimental data, demonstrating that the HSE06 functional accurately predicts YSR splittings for transition metal adatoms and dimers on Nb(110). Finally, the influence of the interatomic distance between Mn atoms in dimers on YSR splitting is examined. This work establishes a foundation for future investigations into YSR states using hybrid DFT. The accompanying Python code is available at \href{https://github.com/abhisheksingh1997/relativistic-ysr}{https://github.com/abhisheksingh1997/relativistic-ysr}. The rise of 3D printing has made 3D objects easily accessible, leading to a surge in data sharing platforms like Thingiverse. However, this accessibility has introduced a proliferation of stereotypes and biases within shared 3D models. While existing research on bias mitigation in 3D-to-3D image filters has made significant strides, it has largely overlooked the critical issue of bias in 3D distribution images. This paper introduces a novel method to address bias in 3D distribution images, a domain previously unexplored. Experimental results demonstrate that our method effectively reduces bias in 3D point clouds, surpassing current state-of-the-art solutions. Furthermore, our proposed algorithm has been validated on the CARLA driving simulation dataset, confirming its efficacy in bias removal within 3D point clouds for this application. The model operates by processing the red, green, and blue color channels sequentially and integrating them through a specialized fusion mechanism. This approach eliminates the need for network preprocessing and avoids the complex, multi-stage pipelines typical of deep learning-based object detection methods. X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES) serves as a potent method for analyzing electron groups within atoms and molecules. While prior research has established a linear rate framework for these groups, it fails to adequately explain certain non-linear features observed in experimental data. This study introduces a non-linear rate framework to address such complexities. We demonstrate that the non-linear component of XANES spectra arises from the interaction between the core hole and the electron group, a phenomenon that can be modeled using a non-linear rate equation. Furthermore, we confirm the validity of this framework by comparing its predictions against both existing linear rate model results and actual experimental XANES data. The findings indicate that the proposed non-linear rate framework offers superior accuracy compared to the linear approach. Additionally, the theoretical analysis reveals that the non-linear rate framework encompasses the linear one as a specific instance. Finally, our results suggest that the non-linear rate model is particularly effective for describing the K-edge XANES spectra of light elements. These insights provide a robust foundation for future investigations into the physical mechanisms underlying K-edge XANES spectra. The accompanying Python code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi-1997/Non-linear-rate. Keywords: K-edge XANES spectra, non-linear rate, rate equation. Deep neural networks (DNNs) have achieved remarkable success in various communication signal classification tasks, including modulation recognition. However, DNNs are inherently susceptible to adversarial attacks, where carefully crafted perturbations are added to input signals to deceive the network into incorrect predictions. This paper introduces a robust training framework designed to enhance the resilience of modulation categorization against such adversarial threats. The proposed method employs a dual-network architecture: one network generates adversarial samples by combining original inputs with real-world noise, while a second "blend" network is trained to classify these adversarial samples. This approach enables the second network to develop robust feature extraction capabilities, significantly improving its accuracy when facing attacks. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques in both adversarial robustness and performance under normal conditions. Furthermore, the framework exhibits strong generalization across different modulation schemes and remains effective when tested on datasets generated by different transmitters. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/abdelrahimhassan/Blend-GAN. The findings were presented at the 2021 IEEE International Conference on Acoustics, Speech, and Signal Processing (ICASSP). Detecting and segmenting brain lesions in Multiple Sclerosis (MS) is a critical step for diagnosing and managing the condition. However, developing robust models that perform consistently across different sites remains difficult due to variations in MRI scanners and protocols. This study investigates the impact of domain shift caused by these variations and explores strategies to mitigate it. We evaluate two approaches: domain adaptation, which leverages data from multiple sites, and ensemble modeling, which combines models trained on single-site data. Our results indicate that neither approach is superior in all scenarios; domain adaptation proves more effective when the source and target domains are similar, whereas ensembles yield better performance when such similarity is absent. We conclude that a hybrid strategy, utilizing ensembles to establish a baseline and domain adaptation for refinement, offers the most promising path toward achieving consistent lesion segmentation across different clinics. This paper is the first to propose and assess the use of continual learning for MS lesion segmentation. The code and data are accessible at https://github.com/medicool/MS-Lesion-Segmentation. We introduce a novel contrastive learning technique designed for semi-supervised classification, which we term Manic Contrast. This approach leverages the inherent class-contrastive property found in self-supervised methods like SimCLR and NOCCL. Specifically, Manic Contrast maximizes the agreement between two pseudo-labels generated by a teacher network, where one is created by feeding an input through the student and the other by processing an augmented version of that input through the same teacher. The teacher is subsequently updated via a moving average of the student's parameters. We demonstrate that Manic Contrast is more straightforward and computationally efficient than the popular pseudo-labeling method, achieving superior or comparable semi-supervised classification accuracy across various datasets. Furthermore, we provide theoretical insights into the method's convergence behavior. Extensive experiments on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 reveal that Manic Contrast outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques in both supervised and semi-supervised contexts. Additionally, the method yields promising results when applied to semi-supervised object detection on the COCO dataset. The code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2019/ManicContrast. This paper introduces a framework for modeling machine intelligence regarding errors in dynamical systems. We represent the modeler as a dynamical system where the output is a model of a system of interest, and the error is defined as the discrepancy between the two models. We demonstrate that both the model and error outputs evolve over time, and under specific conditions, the error converges to a steady state. Furthermore, we show that when the error is additive, the modeler's dynamics can be decomposed into two distinct components: one capturing the behavior of the model and another representing the error dynamics. These findings provide a foundation for analyzing the behavior of modelers and can guide the design of modeling tools. The paper concludes with an application of these results to statistical models. Additionally, we outline several promising future research directions, including extending these results to nonlinear models, statistical models, and modelers. We also propose investigating the stability of errors within this framework and developing a unified theory for modeler behavior. Finally, we suggest that these results could inform the design of modeling tools and the analysis of modeler behavior in this domain.

We present the first detection of a core expansion wave in a massive star-forming region, specifically the Dragon infrared dark nebula. Utilizing 1.3 mm dust continuum observations from the Nobeyama 45 m telescope, we identified a shell-like structure surrounding the Dragon core with an average radius of 1000 AU and a thickness of 100 AU. By analyzing the radial profile of the dust continuum emission, we determined that the structure expands at a velocity of 0.15 km/s. This expansion is likely driven by the formation of a massive protostar at the shell's center, which is indicated by the detection of a compact, bright 1.3 mm source at the shell's core. The presence of this expanding shell offers a potential explanation for the observed filamentary structure in Dragon; we propose that these filaments formed as a result of the shell's expansion. Furthermore, the Dragon core exhibits a mass of 1000 solar masses and a mass-to-radius ratio of 1000 solar masses per parsec, both of which exceed the critical thresholds of 100 solar masses and 100 solar masses per parsec, respectively, required for the direct collapse scenario to form a massive star. These findings suggest that the direct collapse scenario is a viable pathway for the formation of massive stars. Additionally, we observed a large-scale shell-like structure around the Dragon core with a radius of 0.1 pc and a thickness of 0.01 pc, expanding at 0.1 km/s. This large-scale structure may have been triggered by the expansion of the inner shell. The discovery of this shell-like structure provides new insights into the formation of massive stars and the evolution of molecular clouds. Future observations will be conducted to investigate the physical properties of this large-scale shell. (Abridged)

We examine a two-dimensional model for liquid crystals featuring negative dielectric anisotropy, composed of spherical particles shaped like rigid wedges. These spheres self-organize into parallel rows, with the tip angles oriented in alternating directions. At elevated temperatures, these rows fluctuate and merge, creating a system that displays liquid density but exhibits solid-like orientational order. This order is nematic, characterized by long-ranged translational order perpendicular to the rows and long-ranged orientational order parallel to them. We demonstrate that orientational order can be broken by introducing a spatially varying twist in the orientation of the wedge tips, leading to a splay variation. The resulting phase retains long-ranged orientational order, meaning the phase correlation function decays as $1/x$, but it is orthorhombic due to the play effect, resulting in different elastic constants for splay and twist. This phase, which we designate as the nematic splay variation (NSV) phase, emerges from the nematic uniform (NU) phase through a first-order phase transition. We also identify a third phase, the nematic splay (NS) phase, where the splay variation is uniform; this phase is stabilized at high densities and low temperatures by the play effect. The NU to NS phase transition is second order, whereas the NU to NSV phase transition remains first order. Finally, we analyze the NU to NS phase transition in detail, demonstrating that it is mediated by a defect structure consisting of a pair of disclination dipoles. This finding indicates that the transition is neither first nor second order, but instead belongs to a new universality class. These findings are supported by Monte Carlo simulations and a theoretical analysis based on the Landau-de Gennes free energy. This paper investigates the preference ordering of subsets, a concept introduced by Barbera (1989) and later expanded by Barbera and Monge (1998). We concentrate on a specific scenario where an agent prefers a larger set of objects over a smaller one only if the larger set includes an additional object from a pool of desirable items. We demonstrate that satisfying a natural set of axioms leads to a full characterization of the resulting preference ordering. Furthermore, we analyze the computational complexity of this problem, establishing both tractable and NP-hard instances. Finally, we present polynomial-time algorithms for the cases that are NP-hard, and our findings regarding Barbera's original framework are consistent with the results of Barbera and Monge (1998). The paper concludes by discussing several open questions for future research. Additionally, we provide a supplementary section with computational results that highlight the practical performance of our proposed algorithms. Our Python implementation is available at https://github.

This study examines the thermodynamic and dynamic characteristics of a glass-forming liquid, specifically a polymer melt, across its supercooled state and upon vitrification. The analysis employs the canonical equation of state, which expresses internal energy as a function of temperature and specific volume. By applying a specific formulation of the thermodynamic scaling hypothesis, we demonstrate that the observed thermodynamic behavior can be derived from established dynamic properties. Furthermore, we show that the equation of state remains valid when the melt is vitrified at room temperature, allowing for the examination of glass structural entropy as a function of temperature. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for the broader understanding of glass-forming liquids. These results are grounded in extensive experimental data, including high-precision measurements of specific heat, thermal expansion, and viscosity, complemented by molecular dynamics simulations. Transformer language architectures have achieved remarkable success in natural language processing, yet their training frequently involves the retention of irrelevant context and the generation of inaccurate tokens. This paper introduces an innovative training framework designed to eliminate such redundant information and erroneous tokens. By leveraging the training dynamics of teacher models, we implement a mechanism that suppresses redundant data and enhances the accuracy of incorrect predictions. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach reduces redundancy in trained architectures while simultaneously improving overall performance. Furthermore, we provide an in-depth analysis of the proposed method, offering insights into its underlying principles and potential applications. This paper introduces a new framework for Neural Machine Interpretation (NMI) that enables models to generate tokens with an immediate focus on their subsequent look-ahead tokens. We contend that models are more prone to producing invalid tokens when they fail to anticipate how their current choices will impact future ones. To address this, we propose a focus-based attention mechanism that reallocates attention weights from previously generated tokens to the most recent look-ahead tokens. We evaluate this mechanism across three NMI tasks: English-to-SQL, SQL-to-SQL, and SQL-to-JSON. The results demonstrate that our approach surpasses state-of-the-art NMI methods on all three datasets. Furthermore, we show that this mechanism enhances the accuracy of downstream machine learning models trained on the NMI output. This paper investigates the relations and differential equations governing the values of the Kontsevich weights of the graphs used to represent the solution of the symplectic Todorov flow. We examine two approaches for evaluating the Kontsevich values associated with the curvature graphs of the symplectic Todorov flow, specifically: (i) an approach based on the relation graphs of the symplectic Todorov flow, and (ii) an approach derived from the differential forms of the Kontsevich values of the curvature graphs of the symplectic Todorov flow. The study includes a detailed calculation of the values for the Kontsevich graphs with one or two edges in these scenarios. Finally, we demonstrate that the two methods yield equivalent results. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive list of the values for the Kontsevich graph set with one or two edges, which is essential for the solution of the symplectic Todorov flow. These findings are derived from the author's doctoral thesis. Furthermore, we outline an algorithm for calculating the values of the Kontsevich graph set, which can be utilized to determine the values for graphs with three or more edges. The Python code is structured into two parts: the first part computes the values for graphs with a single edge, while the second part calculates the values for graphs with two edges. We establish a duality between $1/N$ deformations of large-$N$ conformal field theories and interacting conformal field theories in the same dimension. We demonstrate that if the interaction CFT possesses a unitary, discrete spectrum, the corresponding interaction in the "deformed CFT" must be marginal. We examine this duality within a broad range of interacting CFTs, including the epsilon expansion, the O(N) vector model, and the critical Ising model. We also explore the implications for the large-$N$ "deformed CFTs," which are shown to be free in terms of entanglement entropy but free with corrections of $O(1/N)$ in thermodynamics. We conjecture that these large-$N$ deformed CFTs are equivalent to the well-known "conformal bootstrap theories" derived from the epsilon expansion. Finally, we discuss the potential existence of similar theories in four dimensions, which could offer a large-$N$ window into the conformal bootstrap program. This work is a collaboration with S. We report on the detection of a gamma-ray spreading source (GRSS) located at the center of the Coma cluster, characterized by an observed angular radius of approximately 1.5 degrees and a differential photon spectrum with a power-law index of $\alpha = 2.1 \pm 0.1$. This GRSS is identified as a superposition of galaxies within the Coma cluster group, with individual galaxy spectra contributing an index of $\alpha = 1.7 \pm 0.1$. Our analysis indicates that the GRSS extends beyond the cluster's virial radius, and the Coma cluster represents the closest known GRSS. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the GRSS exhibits a jet-like morphology, with its axis aligned along the cluster's major axis. We also examine the potential connection between GRSSs and the dark matter halo distribution in galaxy clusters. Additionally, we identify a second GRSS in the Perseus cluster, which is more than twice as distant as the one in Coma. The spectral index of the galaxy component in the Perseus GRSS is $\alpha = 2.0 \pm 0.1$, compared to $\alpha = 1.7 \pm 0.1$ for Coma. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for GRSS physics and their relevance to the Fermi-LAT diffuse emission excess. Inspired by recent cosmological collider research, this study investigates the impact of non-Bunch-Davies initial states on cosmological collider signals. We demonstrate that initial features can substantially alter the amplitude of collider physics, with specific configurations enhancing the effect by several orders of magnitude. Furthermore, we find that the phase of these features serves as a sensitive probe for the pre-inflationary initial conditions of both the scalar and tensor modes. Finally, we show that the shape of the power spectrum can reveal characteristics of the post-bounce evolution, such as the duration of the radiation era, thereby providing additional constraints on the universe's early history. These findings suggest that incorporating initial features is essential for accurately interpreting cosmological collider signals. Consequently, our work establishes a framework for analyzing the pre-inflationary universe and offers a pathway for future investigations into the initial conditions of the early cosmos. Additionally, we have made our code publicly available to facilitate further research in this area. This study appears in Physical Review D.

This study introduces a new approach for visualizing the internal workings of deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) by examining the relationships between filters, image features, and semantic categories. Unlike traditional methods that rely on activation maps to localize visual features, our technique analyzes the weights of the CNN itself. We achieve this by training a linear model that maps filters to specific semantic classes. Utilizing these latent visual-semantical relationships, we can isolate and isolate individual filters to understand their distinct semantic contributions. Furthermore, our proposed filter-level semantical focus metric quantifies each filter's focus on its predicted class, offering deeper insights into the CNN's decision-making process. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method through visualizations and experiments on the CIFAR-10 and ImageNet datasets. The results show that our approach successfully identifies representative filters for each class and effectively distinguishes between them. Additionally, our method enhances classification performance, yielding a 2.0% improvement on CIFAR-10 and a 0.5% improvement on ImageNet. These findings indicate that our method yields more interpretable CNNs, which is a crucial step toward developing explainable AI. Recent experiments have indicated that long-range alluring interactions are vital for the emergence of superconductivity in cuprates. This study demonstrates that such interactions can be mediated by long-range phonons, which are generated through the dynamic coupling of electronic density fluctuations with structural distortions. We establish that these phonon-facilitated interactions are pivotal in establishing Cooper pairs within one-dimensional cuprates. Furthermore, we predict that these interactions can be experimentally detected through their impact on phonon spectral features. Our findings offer a potential pathway to investigate long-range superconducting correlations in cuprates and a novel method for detecting alluring interactions via their coupling with phonons. Additionally, this research expands the scope of materials capable of exhibiting phonon-mediated superconductivity. This study introduces an open-source dataset featuring fine-grained causal observations of personal activities, accompanied by a novel formalization of causal activity descriptions and causal Bayesian networks. To demonstrate the efficacy of this framework, we developed causal architectures for two domains: daily activities and physical exercise. We present Architectural Network Models (ANMs), a new class of Bayesian networks designed to capture causal relationships within activity networks. We provide theoretical proofs establishing ANMs as a valid subset of Bayesian networks and show that they can be learned from observational data using a novel algorithm. Furthermore, we propose a method for model selection to identify the most suitable architecture for a specific dataset. Finally, we validate the approach through experiments on two real-world datasets, including a user-generated social exercise platform. This study demonstrates the topological liquefaction of a metastable skyrmion lattice within the chiral magnet Co$_9$Zn$_9$Mn$_2$ (CoZnMn). Utilizing scanning Hall probe microscopy, we observed that applying a single magnetic field pulse transforms the periodic skyrmion grid into individual, randomly distributed skyrmions. This process involves the "liquefaction" of the metastable grid, which is driven by the nucleation of skyrmions at sample defects. We further elucidate the dynamics of pulse-induced skyrmion liquefaction and the subsequent evolution of these single skyrmions. These findings provide a foundation for manipulating and controlling skyrmion arrays in chiral magnets. Additionally, we show that single skyrmions can be re-integrated into the metastable grid through an annealing process, offering a pathway to stabilize them. This research holds significant potential for advancing the manipulation and control of skyrmion arrays in this class of materials.
